Alexandra’s undertakings were left unfinished by her swift death.Compare with Bellum [I.13.3] Hyrcanus succeeded to the whole inheritance; while his mother was still alive he had assumed the dignity of the priesthood. Aristobulus excelled in valour and wisdom. Matters were brought to a dispute and then to an encounter. When battle was joined, most deserted Hyrcanus and followed the other, who was the better man in war. Accompanied by those who had survived the battle, Hyrcanus fled into Antonia. Finding Aristobulus’s children and wife there, he secured his safety through these hostages, since Aristobulus took precautions by agreement lest anything harsh be done to his family. The brothers’ agreement was as follows: Hyrcanus was to relinquish the kingdom, and the whole right of rule was to pass to Aristobulus. Aristobulus was not, however, to leave Hyrcanus without honour; though excluded from the kingdom, he was to be allowed to hold another honour that Aristobulus himself would bestow. This settlement, also consecrated by the sanctity of the temple, secured the voluntary assent of both. They then parted in goodwill. After greeting one another, Aristobulus withdrew into the royal palace, and Hyrcanus went calmly into Aristobulus’s house.Compare with Bellum [I.14.1] But this change of affairs brought fear to some who remembered that they had taken sides against Aristobulus, and above all to Antipater. He was Idumaean by origin, distinguished among his people through his ancestors, a man of no small wealth and therefore of very great power. He was remarkably skilful at disregarding money in order to win favour. His counsels terrified Hyrcanus: a man who had relinquished rule could have no secure hope for his safety unless he sought protection by taking refuge elsewhere. Once he had bent Hyrcanus to his schemes, he suggested to King Aretas that help should be given to a man who had been ensnared into relinquishing his kingdom. It would be becoming to a king, he argued, to act as arbiter in restoring rule, and much finer still to order the restoration of what deceit had taken from a defrauded man to whom the birthright of kingship belonged. The one brother was shrewd and cunning, and therefore suspect to his neighbours; the other gentle and quiet. He would accept as the greatest benefit whatever an outsider bestowed on him, when even his brother had deprived him of the right to rule. Announcing to Hyrcanus that he had secured King Aretas’s favour, Antipater held out hope of flight and showed the way: Hyrcanus should go with him to Petra, situated in the territory of Arabia, where they would approach the king. Won over by Antipater’s pleas and gifts, the king gave Hyrcanus a very large force of fighting men to restore him to his kingdom. They numbered about fifty thousand infantry and cavalry. Driven back by them at the first encounter, Aristobulus fled to Jerusalem. Even there he was unsafe against so great a multitude of enemies: they would have captured him within it had Scaurus, commander of the Roman army, not lifted the siege on the occasion of another war, waged against Tigranes. He had been sent by Pompey, in whom fierce vengeance for the reception of Mithridates had blazed up, together with a resolve to carry the war against Tigranes’ father-in-law. For this reason he had ordered Syria to be ravaged by Scaurus, while he himself pressed Tigranes and Armenia.Compare with Bellum [I.14.2] As Scaurus approached Damascus, which Metellus and Lollius had utterly destroyed, the brothers’ envoys met him, each side begging for the support of Roman aid. Although inferior in strength, Aristobulus nevertheless outweighed his opponent by the money he offered. The decision of the contest in war was sold for three hundred talents, and the justice of the claim was weighed by its price. Once this money had been counted out to him, Scaurus ordered Hyrcanus and the king of Arabia to withdraw from the siege: if they remained, they were to know that they would have to fight a war against Pompey and the Romans. This threat dissolved the siege. Aretas made for Philadelphia, and Scaurus returned to Damascus. Aristobulus, who had scarcely been capable of warding off danger a moment before, gathered a force and pursued the enemy. At Papyron, as the place was called, he routed six thousand of the enemy in battle, together with Antipater’s brother Phallion. The hopes of Hyrcanus and Antipater collapsed: all their confidence had rested in the forces of Arabia.Compare with Bellum [I.15.1] But when Pompey the Great began to travel through Syria and arrived at Damascus, they sought help from the Romans, whose aid to their opponents had broken them and snatched victory from their hands. They approached Pompey as an arbiter of justice with no greed for money. They therefore began to rely on arguments, not gifts as before: a mind proof against the corrupting power of money was not caught in the snares of avarice and could hate, without payment, a man who had plotted against his brother’s honour. So they approached him with complaints calculated to arouse odium against Aristobulus for unworthily seizing what belonged to another, and to win favour for Hyrcanus. The right to rule belonged to him whether by the merit of his life or by the claim of his age, supported above all by his mother’s authority: she had had both the judgement to choose and the right to confer it. Aristobulus did not stay away long. Though he saw nothing in the Great man’s mind that would suit his schemes, he nevertheless presumed upon his purchase of Scaurus and boasted of their association. He therefore came clad in royal attire and surrounded by a more extensive display of pomp than usual. Distrusting the justice of his case, he meant to prevent any presumption that he would acquiesce and deny any hope that he would obey. But he could not long endure the Roman consul’s exalted position: though without a kingdom, the man was accustomed to command kings. When they reached the city called Diopolis, Aristobulus withdrew elsewhere, his swollen royal pride scorning the haughtiness of Roman dignity.Compare with Bellum [I.15.2] Aristobulus’s withdrawal gave no small cause for offence. The consul was so deeply stirred that Roman arms were immediately turned against Judaea, joined also by many Syrian auxiliaries. When Aristobulus learned that he was approaching the city of Scythopolis and then Coreae, where the territory of Judaea began, he fled into Alexandrium, a strongly fortified stronghold on a very high mountain. Learning this, Pompey ordered him to come down. But Aristobulus considered it unbecoming to obey a command as though from a master; immoderate in spirit, he thought he should face danger rather than obey an order. Looking down, however, upon the Roman camp packed with men, and warned by his followers not to provoke those to whose name and power almost the whole world had submitted, he came down. He used many arguments to establish that the kingdom had rightfully passed to him: it was owed to him by the bond of birth, or by the army’s judgement in following the stronger man and deserting the coward, or by the outcome of battle, or by the agreement of the treaty. He then returned to the fortifications. Again, when Hyrcanus had approached the consul, Aristobulus was summoned to judgement and presented himself. But seeing that the hearing was still being deferred, he returned to the stronghold. Poised between hope and fear, he thought that by obeying Pompey’s commands he could turn him to favour himself; yet he kept withdrawing into Alexandrium lest he again be forced to relinquish his rule. The king’s cunning did not escape the Great man. He ordered him to leave the fortifications and bind himself to do so by letters given to each of their keepers. Aristobulus obeyed commands he did not dare reject, but immediately hid himself within the walls of Jerusalem and began to prepare war against the Romans.Compare with Bellum [I.15.3] Pompey in turn pursued him as he fled, pressed him within his defences, and gave him no time to make preparations for war. News that Mithridates had ended the war by his death focused the Great man’s attention. Pompey was in the territory of the city of Jericho when word of the matter arrived. Near the city is a place where balsam is produced, growing upon shrubs which the farmers’ boys cut with sharp stones; through these incisions liquid drips, beautiful in its dew-like tears. From there the veteran soldier arranged his ranks and moved camp towards evening. At first light he stood before the walls of Jerusalem and unexpectedly poured in his armed forces.Compare with Bellum [I.16.1] Astonished by the sight of the deployment, the strength of the men and the eagerness of the soldiers, Aristobulus came forward of his own accord to beg pardon, offering money, the city and himself. Bending his words to a humbler tone of supplication, he had softened the consul’s indignation. But his plea proved fruitless because fulfilment of his promise was lacking: not only was the money refused, but Gabinius, who had come to claim what had been offered, was even shut out of the city. War descended upon them.Compare with Bellum [I.16.2] For the Great man placed Aristobulus under guard and began to survey the city walls and examine more closely where he might attempt an entry by force. But he observed the strength of the walls, which could not be stormed, and that the temple within the city was surrounded by fortifications hardly inferior to them. Those who entered would face a double danger, from the temple’s defenders and from the men holding the walls’ defences. For some time he hesitated, doubtful in mind and uncertain in judgement. Suddenly sedition arose within the city: Hyrcanus’s allies wished to admit Pompey, while Aristobulus’s defenders resisted. The former sought to open the gates to the Great man, the latter to bar them and wage war to prevent the Romans from taking away their king.Compare with Bellum [I.16.3] But those on the weaker side yielded to the greater number, whose ranks fear of Roman power had swelled. They withdrew into the temple and broke down the bridge that lay between city and temple, joining them by an open passage. The Roman army was thus admitted into the city, and with their own hands the Jews opened its gates to those who would soon storm both city and temple. David’s words were fulfilled: “God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple.” Thus they voluntarily handed over their royal quarters and relinquished the palace buildings. Piso, a man distinguished among his own people and experienced in military service, was charged with holding the royal palace and the rest of the city with a strong force. He carried this out diligently, as though he had led the Roman army there to defend these places rather than to occupy them.Compare with Bellum [I.16.4] For the assault on the temple, however, since resistance was stubborn, the Great man prepared the Jews—Hyrcanus’s allies, that is—so that, if possible, the Romans would not profane another people’s mysteries, and so that the Jews would fill the ditches with their own hands. In impious service and shameful obedience, their hands laboured at the basket, their minds at sacrilege. Yet the heaping up of material achieved nothing, since Aristobulus’s supporters resisted from the walls and hindered the work from above. Pompey’s first efforts would have been fruitless had he not, when the sacred days of religious observance came round, ordered his men to press on with heaping up mounds of earth. On those days it was the Jews’ ancient observance to refrain from all work. For only the practice of engaging in hand-to-hand combat had become customary even on the Sabbath: if battle was forced upon them and their lives faced the utmost peril, the Jews thought they must decide the matter by the sword; against other forms of conflict they had a religious scruple. Already the rampart had risen, already the siege engines had been brought up. The king’s men fought back, emboldened by the height of the walls; even when engaged in combat, they did not give way as the Great man came nearer.Compare with Bellum [I.16.5] Pompey marvelled at the men’s fierce spirits, the wall’s beauty and size, and the priests’ duties, nowhere relaxed amid the fury of war, as though there were profound peace. Nothing was lacking in the customary sacrifices. Amid the warriors’ missiles and the deaths of the slain, the blood of sacrificial victims was poured out; a victim was placed upon the altars. Those stationed before the altar were struck down. A third month already found the contest still undecided. Faustus, son of Cornelius Sulla, was the first, along with two centurions, one named Furius and the other Fabius, to break into the temple after a tower in the walls had been knocked down. Each had his band following him. Surrounding the temple’s interior on every side, they ran through with their swords whomever they found. Those fleeing were cut down; others, resisting, were slaughtered.Compare with Bellum [I.16.6] There was no mercy. Yet this savagery of the combatants did not interrupt the priests’ service. The enemy stood over them with drawn swords, but they carried out their accustomed duty without any disturbance. No kind of duty was suspended. Whatever belonged to the customary rites of purification, whatever concerned the observance of sacred worship, was fulfilled. So great was their care for their service—and if only it had been in the service of true devotion and faith! Still greater dangers also arose from their own people, which the Hebrews inflicted on one another. Inside, the fighting was fiercer, and the danger from the rebels nearer and twofold. A foreign enemy pressed from the front, a domestic one from the rear and the sides.Compare with Bellum [I.17.1] Thus, shut in on every side, some hurled themselves down, while others were consumed in the fires of their homeland. The priests, however, persevered in their duties to the very end, urging one another not to put the duty of religion below the protection of their lives. It would be well for them to give to devotion what was owed to necessity, and most noble if they could be buried in their homeland’s bosom. What good would it do to escape and outlive religion? Rather, to die together with their sacred service was a glorious deed. If anyone abandons it through fear of danger, that is sacrilege; if he fulfils it, that is sacrifice and the victory of devout suffering. Thus the priests, wearing their sacred fillets, were sacrificed among their own sacrificial victims; clad in their priestly robes, they lay on the ground among the bodies of the slain. Twelve thousand Jews were cut down there; few Romans were killed, more were wounded.Compare with Bellum [I.17.2] Yet amid that misery the Jews lamented nothing more deeply than that those previously hidden sacred mysteries had been uncovered and made manifest to the nations. Indeed, Pompey set aside such superfluous concerns. As he toured the burned ruins, intent rather on triumph, followed by many of his men, he saw the second tabernacle, which was open only to the chief priest on his customary entry. Looking inside, he saw the lamp, the table, the incense burners, the tablets of the covenant and the cherubim above them, a great quantity of spices scattered about, and two thousand talents of sacred money. Although these included a great deal of gold, he remained free of all greed and ordered that the treasure, and any sacred vessels also found, be kept untouched. On the day after the destruction he ordered the temple attendants to cleanse the temple’s interior and celebrate the customary sacrifices. He also gave Hyrcanus the primacy of the priesthood, having used his ready assistance in the exigencies of the siege. For though unfaithful to his own people, he was faithful to the Romans so that his own homeland might be stormed—but I think no one can be called faithful who has been unfaithful to his own people. Thus, in his own war, he gave far from perfunctory help to the enemies of his own people, if only by drawing away from Aristobulus’s alliance the multitude outside the walls that was supporting him. To all the ways in which Pompey proved an outstanding commander, whether in forestalling Aristobulus and diminishing his authority or in bringing the war swiftly to an end, he added this distinction: he kept moderation in victory. He bound the conquered to himself more by kindness than by terror, and executed only the instigators of the war with the axe. He also imposed tribute on the conquered, appointed a commander for Judaea, and fixed its boundaries.Compare with Bellum [I.17.3] Judaea was thus confined within its own boundaries. He also restored Gadara, which the Jews had destroyed, at the request of Demetrius, who had asked this favour for his homeland from his patron. In this matter, as in many others, Demetrius held a standing with the Great man beyond the usual measure of freedmen, even to the point of arousing envy. Pompey decided to take Aristobulus, his children and his father-in-law with him to Rome as captives. But one of the royal offspring escaped his guards on the journey and returned home. His name was Alexander; he was older than his brother and had two sisters. Thus the younger Antigonus and his sisters were taken to Rome; Pompey made for Cilicia and thence for Rome.Compare with Bellum [I.18.1] Meanwhile Scaurus, who held command in Syria, recovered the cities the Jews had invaded: inland, Scythopolis, Hippos, Pella, Samaria, Jamnia, Maresa, Azotus and Arethusa; on the coast, Gaza, Joppa, Dora and the place formerly called Strato’s Tower, afterwards named Caesarea under Herod’s rule, when he both adorned it and changed its name. Scaurus was preparing war against the Arabs. Holding Judaea between the Euphrates and Egypt under his jurisdiction, and Syria too, restored to its own boundaries, he wished to invade Petra, the capital of the kingdom of Arabia—whether from a desire for plunder, as I am more inclined to think, or for the sake of extending dominion. Hampered by the difficulty of the terrain, he could not break into it, but devastated many places both near the city and far away. While his army lingered in those places, hunger overtook it. A pitiful disaster would almost have occurred had Hyrcanus not supplied food to the struggling Romans through Antipater, and had he not, on Scaurus’s advice, urged Aretas to end the war with money. Thus the Arab rid himself of the enemy with three hundred talents: he bought off Scaurus. This was the price of his withdrawal. The affair strengthened Hyrcanus’s alliance with the Romans and fostered the security of profound peace, since through his efforts the Roman army had passed from severe scarcity to an abundance of grain in hostile territory and had found help at hand.Compare with Bellum [I.19.1] But Alexander, having escaped the Great man’s chains, first secretly gathered a suitable force over some time, then began openly to range through Judaea. Hyrcanus was thrown into alarm and lost confidence in his position; the Romans were pressed by concern lest the war grow. For Alexander had even resolved to rebuild the wall at Jerusalem that the Great man had destroyed. He had almost begun the work when Gabinius, who had succeeded Scaurus, energetically disposed of the other matters by which he had spread the terror of his name, and judged that Alexander’s attempts must be met. Alexander too thought he should not withdraw, but dared to decide the matter in battle with ten thousand infantry and fifteen hundred cavalry. He also repaired the strongholds of Alexandrium, Hyrcania and Machaerus, to serve as refuges for himself if circumstances demanded, or as obstacles to the enemy, since Arabia, not altogether faithful to the Romans, was nearby.Compare with Bellum [I.19.2] To meet him more quickly, Gabinius sent Mark Antony ahead with part of the army, to hinder the enemy’s march until he himself arrived with the entire force. Antipater came with picked men; Malichus and Pitholaus, supported by separate bands of Jews, also joined their strength to Antony’s. When Alexander saw them assembled—for Gabinius too was now present—he changed his plan and decided to fall back. But when he was no longer far from Jerusalem, he was forced to engage in battle, defeated, and fled. Nearly three thousand of his men were killed; the rest were captured or scattered. Scarcely a few remained with Alexander, to share his flight rather than dare further rebellion.Compare with Bellum [I.19.3] Finally, seeking peace from Gabinius, he even handed the strongholds over to the Romans, so that they would have no cause for suspicion. In this war Antony’s valour shone outstandingly, though everywhere he gave a distinguished demonstration of his courage.Compare with Bellum [I.19.4] Gabinius divided Judaea into five districts, to diminish the power from which arrogance arose in whoever gained control of affairs. The honour of the priesthood remained with Hyrcanus because of his gentle temperament, but Gabinius entrusted the care of the whole district of that region not to one man but to the people of Jerusalem in common. The other districts were assigned in the same way, apportioned among the leading citizens of Gadara, Amathus, Jericho and Sepphoris. Thus nothing would be left to the power of individuals, and the discharge of the districts’ duties, which called for public oversight, would not falter. This was welcomed both by the Romans, to relieve their fear of rebellion, and by the Jews, to lay aside resentment: the Hebrew people would live not under a king but under leading men, on the model of the Roman republic. There no single man commanded; rather, the best men, to whom office had fallen by lot, governed in turn, without kingdoms but arbiters of kings.Compare with Bellum [I.20.1] This was thought a prudent measure against the nation’s restlessness. But Aristobulus’s escape and return to Judaea stirred up very great disturbances. Many flocked back to him, attracted by the favour of an old friendship or by desperate circumstances for which they sought a remedy in public discord: they wished to mingle the lowest with the highest, and their other hopes had failed. On his return he began to build fortifications and repair Alexandrium. Learning this, Gabinius sent Sisinnius, Antony and Servilius with part of the army and stopped the work that had begun. For Aristobulus abandoned the fortifications and prepared for war. Since the force he led was greater in numbers than in experience, he rid himself of the burden of the unarmed multitude and mustered only eight thousand armed men. Pitholaus too joined him, having come voluntarily from Jerusalem with a thousand men. Battle followed—for the Romans were upon his neck—and for some time the fighting was vigorous. Roman valour nevertheless prevailed. Five thousand Jews were killed; Aristobulus broke through the line with a thousand men and withdrew into the defences of the stronghold of Machaerus, while two thousand scattered elsewhere. The Romans attacked the stronghold, but were held off for nearly two days, since Aristobulus fought with all his strength in the extremity of danger. Yet he could not hold out longer. Captured with his son Antigonus, whom he had taken with him when escaping from captivity, he was sent to Gabinius, and by him they were sent on to Rome. The senate put Aristobulus under guard but sent his children away to Bithynia. Gabinius is said to have indicated in letters that this had been promised to Aristobulus’s wife, to reward her diligence in handing the fortifications over to him.Compare with Bellum [I.21.1] After these events in Judaea, Gabinius thought he should dare some undertaking and prepared an expedition against the Parthians. But threatening developments on King Ptolemy’s side turned his advance back. For Gabinius changed his route from the Euphrates to Egypt, using in every matter the necessary services of Antipater and Hyrcanus—but Hyrcanus through Antipater. They helped the army with money, grain, arms and auxiliaries as well. Above all, the engagements around Pelusium would easily have deterred Gabinius had the Jews, familiar with the terrain and every aspect of that kind of warfare, not attended to everything. But while the army lingered, Alexander, Aristobulus’s son, was again preparing to throw himself into the other Syria as though into an unoccupied province. He would have done so had Gabinius not been stirred by the reports to hasten his return and send Antipater ahead to draw very many Jews away from Alexander’s alliance. Relying on their numbers, Alexander was preparing to destroy all the Romans he had found in the region. Even though many of the Jews had dispersed through Antipater’s intervention, he had not laid aside his audacity. He attacked with thirty thousand men around Mount Itabyrion, but fled when ten thousand were cut down. The scattering of the remainder ended the war. Gabinius arranged the public affairs of Jerusalem at Antipater’s discretion and departed. He subdued the Nabataeans in battle and secretly released Mithridates and Orsanes, who were fleeing from Persia; publicly, however, he told the soldiers that they had escaped by flight.Compare with Bellum [I.21.2] Crassus succeeded Gabinius. Before setting out for the Parthian war, he took away all the gold in the temple at Jerusalem and ordered that the two thousand talents Pompey had left untouched should also be removed. His joy did not last long: once he crossed the Euphrates, he lost his army and was himself killed.Compare with Bellum [I.21.3] Elated by this success, the Parthians thought they should cross into Syria. Cassius vigorously met them with an ambush and drove them from the boundaries of the province entrusted to him, inflicting no small loss upon the enemy. They had come on without restraint, thinking that no one would dare oppose them, and he had got ahead of them and caught them in narrower places. Thus, after many of their men had been cut down, they abandoned the war. Having repelled the enemy and secured the province, Cassius rushed into Judaea. He destroyed Tarichaeae and sold thirty thousand Jews into slavery. He also ordered Pitholaus to have his throat cut, suspecting him of a deceitful design to support Aristobulus’s side. Nor was Antipater uninvolved in that decision: he wished to exclude a rival for power as completely as possible.Compare with Bellum [I.22.1] He took as his wife a woman named Cypris, born to the most illustrious rank among the women of Arabia, and by her had four male children and one female. The males had these names: the first was called Phasael, the next Herod, the third Josephus, the fourth Pheroras; the daughter was Salome. For this reason a man outstandingly fitted to win the alliance of the powerful through gifts and friendship had secured the favour of the king of the Arabs above all others: he invoked the bond of kinship through the wife he had taken from the lands of Arabia. When preparing to fight Aristobulus, he sent his sons to the aforesaid king of the Arabs as pledges of mutual love. The king received them as an inviolable deposit, kept them in his house with the same care as his own children, and later returned them to their father when they were requested.Compare with Bellum [I.22.2] But while Aristobulus, defeated in war, was held in chains, his son Alexander refrained from battle under the terms of peace by which Cassius, about to return to the Euphrates, had bound him. The frontiers of Persia were troubled by no Parthian incursion, and an appearance of soothing tranquillity in the regions of the East relieved human anxieties. Caesar poured into Italy from the regions of Gaul beyond the Alps and drove Pompey and the senate across the Ionian Sea. Excluded from Italy, the Great man made for Emathia and ordered Roman forces from various places to follow him there, to prepare for war. Intent on these affairs, he had left Aristobulus in chains at Rome. Caesar was between the city of Rome and Pompey, following the Great man by short routes from the Flaminian Way to the Appian Way, to catch either the man himself or his army. He released Aristobulus from his chains, gave him military units as well, and sent him to Syria to bring Judaea to his side and press Pompey from the rear. But at the beginning of his attempts, once he reached the place, Aristobulus was killed by poison and left the undertaking unfinished. His death was attributed in common report to Pompey’s supporters. Thus Caesar’s arrangements were frustrated and Aristobulus’s ambitions defeated, in a strange variety of reversals: he had been safer as an exile among enemies, a captive in chains, than among his own citizens, master in his chamber, king at a banquet.Compare with Bellum [I.22.3] When Pompey learned that Aristobulus had tried to renew war against him in Judaea, he also ordered Aristobulus’s son Alexander to have his throat cut, deeply suspicious of his support for Caesar’s side. He gave the order to Scipio. In obedience, Scipio brought the accused before the tribunal to display the appearance of a trial. Accusers were also produced, and sentence was pronounced against a man who had disturbed the Roman republic by arms. Thus he was to be thought convicted of rebellion and struck with the axe, in the manner of enemy commanders, by the authority of law rather than in execution of an order.Compare with Bellum [I.23.1] When the deaths of both became known, Ptolemy, who had taken in Aristobulus’s brothers and his wife Alexandra, sent his son Philippion to the city of Ascalon to summon those mentioned. On arriving, Philippion received Antigonus and his sisters to take them to his father. Through familiarity and companionship a little flame of love stole upon the young man—surely forgivable, if tyrants knew how to forgive—and he took one of the sisters as his wife. His father Ptolemy could not endure this: he killed his son and married his own daughter-in-law. An outstanding censor of morals, who condemned in his son a marriage for which his consent had not been sought, so that he himself might be defiled by murder of kin and incest! Affairs changed when Pompey was killed: fleeing Caesar’s arms, he had offered his head to be cut off by an Egyptian eunuch. Yet he presented his head with the endurance fitting for a man who had so often conquered so many peoples. Seeing in his defeat the lot of an exile, a plaything of human reversals, he offered his neck to the sword, to receive death as his thanks from the man to whom he had given a kingdom.Compare with Bellum [I.23.2] After his death a change took place: many of the Great man’s friends sought Caesar’s friendship, and above all Antipater, endowed to an incredible degree with the ability to win the friendship of anyone he wished. For everyone needs resources, especially in preparations for war, when men who were enemies and opponents very often become all the dearer.Compare with Bellum [I.24.1] For Ptolemy, king of Egypt, had broken faith and was being pressed by Caesar himself in the gravest warfare. Mithridates of Pergamum, repulsed with all the force he had brought by the obstacles at Pelusium, had settled in the city of Ascalon. Despairing of passage and with his attempt frustrated, he no longer dared commit himself to battle on unfavourable ground and with inferior strength. Antipater first enlisted the Arabs to help him, then brought with him a strong, well-armed force of three thousand Jews. He also roused the powerful men of Syria to his aid: Ptolemy, who lived in Lebanon, Iamblichus, and another Ptolemy. Relying on their alliance, other peoples too were stirred to war. Supported by these additional forces, Mithridates approached Pelusium and, when denied passage, began a siege. There Antipater gave a distinguished demonstration of military ability. While the townspeople resisted and both sides fought with all their strength, he was the first to break into the city with his men, through a breach in the part of the walls where he himself was fighting, and he captured it.Compare with Bellum [I.24.2] Yet this was not the end of his labour and assistance. As the army advanced further inland, the Egyptian Jews around the district called that of Onias wished to resist and block its passage. Antipater again not only averted battle but brought it about that the very people who had prepared arms against them supplied the army with the necessities of human life. Hence the people of Memphis too turned their minds from battle and willingly joined Mithridates’s alliance. Having passed beyond the more suspect places, Mithridates thought he must engage the remaining Egyptians. The ground was more open, but the men of that region, whose settlement was called the Army of the Jews, were stronger. He fought so vigorously that he put himself in headlong danger and would almost have been killed had Antipater not seen the whole right wing, where Mithridates was, hard pressed by the enemy and enclosed on another side by the river, with no escape for the men. From the left wing Antipater rushed upon those pursuing the retreating Mithridates and pursued them until the entire body of the enemy was destroyed. In that battle Antipater lost only eighty of his men, Mithridates more than eight hundred; his own escape was beyond expectation. This disaster befell in a single moment. Antipater received many wounds in his body and won outstanding testimony to his valour before Caesar, particularly from Mithridates, who not only gave an account of his deliverance but proclaimed Antipater’s courage.Compare with Bellum [I.24.3] Greatly delighted by these things, Caesar received Antipater with honour among his friends, as was fitting. Then, after arranging what needed to be settled in Egypt and advancing into Syria, he bestowed on him honours of the Roman state. He also granted exemption from taxes and imparted other pledges of his favour, as to a man he had found worthy. At Antipater’s recommendation, he also willingly confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood.Compare with Bellum [I.25.1] Antigonus too met Caesar in Syria. It would have been fitting for him to lament either the misfortune of his father, who had been killed by poison at the hands of Pompey’s friends, or the execution of his brother, whom Scipio, with the utmost cruelty, had struck down with the axe as though he were a criminal. Instead, he acted from envy rather than grief. With the most vehement complaints he piled up accusations that Hyrcanus and Antipater were occupying the possessions of others, which had been criminally wrested from himself and his brothers. He had been made an exile from his father’s dwelling; the land where he was born was denied him. Yet the wrongs done to him seemed more tolerable: far more bitter were those Hyrcanus and Antipater inflicted upon the whole nation of the Jewish people. They claimed favour for their successes in Egypt, although no diligence arising from an innate goodwill towards Caesar had prompted their service in helping Mithridates. Rather, fear arising from the consciousness of their alliance with Pompey had wrung it from them, to provide a shield against offence.Compare with Bellum [I.25.2] Against these charges Antipater offered not words in return but the proof of deeds. He tore his clothing and, bare of garments but covered in wounds, displayed the signs of his proven valour to the eyes of those around him, his cloak ripped open. “Look,” he said, “let these testimonies to my ill will towards Caesar defend the accused: they shine like lights of the soul. These scars, Caesar, I offer you as hostages for my inward intentions. These are the pledges of my faithfulness I deposit; I bear the written characters of my heart. If citizens are not believed, let the enemies be asked for whose sake I received those wounds. What else were they attacking in me but the faithfulness I showed you? Yet he reproaches me with Pompey’s favour. I confess, Caesar, that I was a friend not to a man but to the Roman name, and made it my particular endeavour to devote my services to your republic. Thus I served not one man but all. Let Pompey have been dear to me: he began to be my friend before he was Caesar’s enemy. He was your son-in-law, and you his father-in-law. When he was in the regions of Judaea, I helped him as a Roman commander; yet I did not receive for him the wounds I received for you. For you I have staked my life and borne the blows of enemy weapons. What wonder if a captive does not know the glory of wounds, and a fugitive does not know what faithfulness is? What can a perpetual enemy bring against me except your friendship? It certainly seems strange that Antigonus should approach the Romans to accuse anyone, when he is accustomed to assail them in war, and should complain before them that he has been stripped of rule. He desired its exercise and business not for his own power or his family’s distinction, but to challenge Roman arms and avenge his father’s and brother’s deaths. Ungrateful for his safety, he does not fear the Roman tribunal but dares attack it of his own accord, knowing that his partner in rebellion paid the penalty there.”Compare with Bellum [I.25.3] When Antipater finished speaking, Caesar pronounced Hyrcanus more worthy of the priesthood, but offered Antipater his choice of power. Antipater asked that same man to be the arbiter and regulator of his honour, leaving the measure of the honour to the man who bestowed the honour. Quite shrewdly, he gained both the credit of modesty and an increase of power: he was made procurator of all Judaea. He did, however, ask to rebuild the walls of Judaea that had been destroyed in the war. Confident in the assurance given him, he both requested and obtained so great an undertaking. As was customary for Roman commanders, the distinctions Caesar judged should be conferred on Antipater were recorded at his discretion on the Capitol, so that testimony both to his own justice and to the man’s services would remain for posterity’s knowledge as well.Compare with Bellum [I.25.4] After escorting Caesar, Antipater turned his course from Syria to Judaea. First he restored to its former state the wall Pompey had destroyed. Then he suppressed disturbances, addressing each man with a father’s affection, now with milder warnings, now with threats. They should choose the ways of peace rather than war, and not exasperate the king’s mind: if he remained unoffended, he would show himself a fellow citizen; if he were roused, a tyrant. Although Hyrcanus was gentle by nature, they should take care not to embitter him by insult. For his own part, Antipater too was eager to provide for the common good out of devoted concern, not an assertion of power. But if they attempted any changes, he would not lack the will to punish. They should experience the Romans’ friendship rather than their domination. For who could doubt that the Romans would turn from friendship to arms if they learned that the man whose kingdom they themselves had confirmed had been stripped of it? At the same time, Antipater knew that Hyrcanus’s mild temperament made him slow in attending to the demands of public duties. He thought that the care of protecting the region should be divided between his sons, since Hyrcanus was unequal to so great a burden and command. He therefore put Phasael, the elder of his children, at the head of Jerusalem and in command of its army. Herod too, younger and still very young, he placed over Galilee with equal honour. As soon as he gained power, Herod, naturally more vigorous in attending to affairs, at once found scope for his temperament.Compare with Bellum [I.26.1] For Syria was suffering from the incursions of the bandit Hezekiah, who, as leader of a band of raiders, harassed the whole province and appeared as an enemy everywhere. Herod seized him and ordered his throat cut, and killed many of the raiders. This won him the greatest glory for valour and abundant favour among the Syrians. Hence he was celebrated by the voices of singers in cities and villages, as a man who had restored peace and public quiet after a long interval. This acclaim, amid the people’s favourable talk, stirred Phasael to seek praise like his brother’s in a spirit of devoted emulation: he would equal in kindness of mind his younger brother, whom he could not equal in valour. He selected for leading positions men outstanding in goodwill, who would temper severity with favour. Thus the greatest honour was paid to Antipater as a father of the community; he himself nevertheless changed nothing of the goodwill and faithfulness with which he had been accustomed to attend upon Hyrcanus.Compare with Bellum [I.26.2] But it is difficult to be free of envy in prosperity. At first Hyrcanus was silently stung by the young men’s praises. The reports of Herod’s outstanding deeds nevertheless embittered him more violently: he saw that Herod had advanced beyond the laws of the Jews and the bounds of a private person, to claim all power for himself, his brother and his father, and to strip the king of every honour. Nothing remained to the king but a name which, devoid of power, presented an empty appearance. Indeed, very many had been put to death without consulting him and killed without royal orders, men whom the ancestral law did not permit to be put to death. Hence many said that Herod ought to be called to account, to explain why he had violated the law that forbade putting men to death unheard. Hyrcanus ought to rouse himself and test, at least by this means, whether Herod was acting as a king or a private person. If he failed to appear when summoned to judgement, it would be clear what his great insolence had aspired to.Compare with Bellum [I.26.3] Through these and similar words of the king’s attendants, Hyrcanus was gradually set ablaze with envy. They pressed home the shame of his cowardice: he had relinquished his right to conduct royal affairs and transferred power to Antipater and his children, making them masters while diminishing his own freedom to rule. Roused by them, he resolved that Herod should appear before his judgement to clear himself of the alleged usurpations contrary to law. Though indignant at being summoned to judgement, Herod nevertheless came, whether through his father’s warnings or a calmer decision of his own, having first secured the fortifications in Galilee. He came neither with a force that would arouse resentment and seem to threaten war, nor with protection so insecure that he would betray his safety. He was also supported by the favour of Sextus Caesar. Fearing that a plot might be laid against the young man, Sextus had given Hyrcanus stern written orders to spare him the danger of a severe judgement. Herod therefore attributed his acquittal more to Sextus than to Hyrcanus’s goodwill, although Hyrcanus, despite yielding to the accusers in calling him to account, had acquitted him willingly: he preferred to preserve Herod rather than pursue him.Compare with Bellum [I.26.4] But Herod, smarting at the affront in the heat of youth and ungrateful for his acquittal, went to Sextus with the settled intention of disobeying if he were summoned again, and gave his detractors grounds for accusation. Although Hyrcanus did not rise to seek vengeance, seeing that Herod was stronger, Herod was nevertheless roused by the recollection of his injury, which is nourished by dwelling upon it. Gathering an army, he made for Jerusalem to abolish all Hyrcanus’s power. He would almost have succeeded had his brother and father not broken his impulse and worn it down. They begged him to think it enough that he had risen up and to set the limit at threatening vengeance, but refrain from destroying the ruler under whom he had gained no small favour and attained such great power. He seemed to have been injured by his summons to judgement, but in turn he had received favour in being acquitted. It was excessively harsh to pursue an injury and be ungrateful for his safety. Moreover, the outcome of wars was doubtful and uncertain, and the burden of odium heavy when he took up arms against his own ruler, a man who had cherished him with a father’s affection, often helped him and never injured him, except when, following bad counsellors, he had raised a shadow of injustice by which Herod thought himself injured.Compare with Bellum [I.27.1] With these and similar arguments they broke the young man’s impulse. Civil war was removed from Judaea, but transferred to the slaughter of the Romans and turned against them. For Sextus Caesar was treacherously killed by Caecilius Bassus, and afterwards Julius Caesar, having held perpetual power for three years and seven months, paid a heavy penalty in the senate because he had exceeded the condition of a private person. Cassius and Brutus were the instigators. Then Julius, the adopted son, gathered forces and, with Antony joined to him, resolved to avenge his father’s death. Since Herod was thought to have helped with the greatest part of the war by sending auxiliaries, he was entrusted with responsibility for governing all Syria. This became the cause of Antipater’s fatal end.Compare with Bellum [I.28.1] For Malichus feared Antipater’s power, which Herod’s valour was increasing. He bribed one of the royal servants and prepared poison for Antipater. Having drunk it, Antipater died immediately after the banquet: a man of tireless spirit in other matters, and above all vigorous in seeking and establishing Hyrcanus’s rule.Compare with Bellum [I.28.2] Herod took his father’s death hard. Calling his army to action, he promised to act as avenger. But his brother’s advice restrained him, lest Judaea be afflicted by civil war between Herod and Malichus. Malichus was prepared to resist and, above all, concealed his complicity in Antipater’s death. Herod was easily brought to another form of vengeance: accepting an assurance that Antipater had not died through any deceit of Malichus, he invited Hyrcanus and Malichus to dinner.Compare with Bellum [I.28.3] With the approval of Cassius, who had also entrusted the affair to his own men sent to exact vengeance, the centurions and officers of the Roman army were ready. They met Hyrcanus and Malichus together on the shore and, drawing their swords, surrounded both. Malichus alone they stabbed with many wounds, slashed and slaughtered. Overwhelmed by the terror, Hyrcanus lost consciousness and collapsed, all vigour of mind and body gone. When he had recovered a little, he asked Herod who had ordered Malichus to be killed. Learning from the officers that he had been killed on the orders of Cassius, the Roman commander, he immediately replied: “Cassius, then, has saved both me and my homeland by killing the man who plotted against us both.” But whether Hyrcanus said this out of fear or really thought it is not clearly apparent and cannot be determined by our judgement.Compare with Bellum [I.28.4] Elichus had risen up, wishing through the bond of brotherhood to avenge Malichus’s death. But since he did not dare provoke Herod, he thought he should attack Herod’s brother Phasael. Learning this, Herod wished to set out but was held back by bodily weakness. Meanwhile Elichus had occupied several fortifications, especially Masada, and installed garrisons in them.Compare with Bellum [I.28.5] But when Herod’s vigour and health returned, he recovered everything and let Elichus himself go from the fortress of Masada at his entreaty. Antigonus, Aristobulus’s son, had challenged his power with the support of his father-in-law Ptolemy. Herod routed them in battle and, having expelled Antigonus, returned victorious to Jerusalem. He also enjoyed great favour for his recent triumph, and especially for his new marriage. First Dosis had been joined to him as his wife, and by her he had a son, Antipater. Afterwards, in a second marriage, he had taken Mariamne, born to Alexander, Aristobulus’s son, a close relative of Hyrcanus and thus endowed with royal nobility.Compare with Bellum [I.28.6] Yet he did not escape the odium of having aspired to snatch the kingdom from Hyrcanus. For when Caesar and Antony had overwhelmed Cassius and the Bruti in the Macedonian war, one of the victors hastened to return to Italy, while the other thought he should hurry to Syria. Amid the many embassies flocking in, the leading Jews came to meet Antony and proceeded into Bithynia, accusing Herod and his brother Phasael. They had violently seized control of all affairs, leaving Hyrcanus only the name as an appearance of honour. But Herod’s presence and favour prevailed: he had bound Antony’s mind to himself not with a little money but with lavish gifts. Hence, without receiving even a word of censure from Antony, he nullified the odium raised against him by the embassy.Compare with Bellum [I.28.7] Again, nearly a hundred Jewish men travelled as far as Antioch with no less spirit to bring accusations. At Daphne they found Antony, already wholly given over to Cleopatra’s love and serving her lust, and there began to denounce the brothers’ intolerable power. Messalla argued against them, with Hyrcanus present, and denounced the insolence of the nation: roused by a faction of a few, it rejected its own and sought outsiders, making Hyrcanus’s injury a pretext when Hyrcanus had preferred what was advantageous to the citizens. After hearing the arguments of both sides, Antony asked Hyrcanus whom he considered better fitted to preside. Hyrcanus’s preference was for Herod and his brother. Finding the answer in accord with his own wish, Antony was greatly delighted, for he was joined to the brothers by a bond of hospitality through their father: when he had come into Judaea with Gabinius, Antipater had received him most warmly as a guest and honoured him with many services. He appointed Herod and Phasael tetrarchs and ordered them to undertake the administration of all Judaea.Compare with Bellum [I.28.8] From this too the number of complainants increased. Although some of the envoys had been imprisoned and others insulted, a thousand envoys were later ordered, after sedition arose in Jerusalem, to go to Antony, who was staying in the city of Tyre. They did not fail their fellow citizens’ will. Although the protesters had been harshly punished, they dared raise their clamour again. Antony sent the governor of the Tyrians to rebuke those guilty of insolence. The governor, together with Herod and Hyrcanus, sought to prevent them from bringing the heaviest punishments upon themselves, and disturbances and causes of war upon their homeland.Compare with Bellum [I.28.9] When nothing was achieved and everything began to fall into confusion through irrational strife, Antony sent armed men. Some were killed by them, and many were gravely wounded. From Hyrcanus, however, the dead received the benefit of burial, and those who had managed to escape the benefit of medical care. They thus furnished an occasion for a twofold display of humanity, through which his goodwill towards his fellow citizens became manifest. The others who had escaped so exasperated Antony by keeping the city in turmoil that he ordered the execution even of those whom he was holding in chains.Compare with Bellum [I.29.1] Insolence had yielded to severity, but when almost two years had passed, a Parthian army poured into Syria, with Pacorus, the king’s son, and Barzaphranes, the Persian satrap, leading the barbarian host. Lysanias, Ptolemy’s son, joined them as an instigator. After the death of his father, whose surname was Mennaeus, he had already been stripped of power. Through the satrap just mentioned, he solicited Pacorus with a promise of a thousand talents of silver and five hundred women, to give Antigonus the kingdom and dissolve Hyrcanus’s priesthood. Pacorus gave part of the cavalry to a royal servant to cross into Judaea, act on Antigonus’s behalf and support his endeavour, since he himself was detained by rebellions within Syria.Compare with Bellum [I.29.2] But this too would have made little progress had it not been proposed, on Antigonus’s advice, that the Jews should receive Pacorus as a mediator of peace, while they were fighting one another under Herod and Phasael on one side and Antigonus on the other. Phasael, in his easy-going disposition, approved this at the time, despite Herod’s opposition. Soon, finding it ruinous to himself, he learnt that barbarians were unfaithful by nature.Compare with Bellum [I.29.3] For he was sent to Barzaphranes as though to an agent of peace, and, setting out with Hyrcanus, met the satrap, who was cunningly concealing his ambush beneath an appearance of kindness. Indeed, he gave them gifts as they prepared to leave, and made his arrangements for their entrapment. Men accompanied them more to keep them under guard than to share their dangers. Reports arrived that the Parthian had been bought for a thousand talents to destroy the men just mentioned.Compare with Bellum [I.29.4] Ofellius too urged flight, since he had learnt from Saramalla, the wealthiest of the Syrians, that a plot had been prepared against them. Yet even so Phasael was not persuaded to abandon Hyrcanus and look to his own safety. Instead, he assailed the satrap with bitter abuse for betraying trust for a price and valuing money more than justice: he himself would give more for their safety than Antigonus was paying for the kingdom. But the Persian tried by perjury to win back the trust he had betrayed and dispel suspicion, and not long afterwards carried out the deception. For when he had departed to Pacorus, those to whom they had entrusted this business seized Phasael and Hyrcanus. Since the captives could now do nothing else, they sought by curses to avenge the barbarians’ perjuries and the faithlessness of their betrayal.Compare with Bellum [I.29.5] The cupbearer sent into Judaea had likewise laid out his deceptions to capture Herod. But Herod had long suspected the barbarians’ ambushes, and grave concern kept him on his guard; he remained within the fortifications. Nor did he think he should leave the walls and entrust himself to conversations with the enemy in response to feigned instructions from Pacorus, by which the cupbearer would approach Phasael’s brother about Phasael and his insolence.Compare with Bellum [I.29.6] When he learnt that his brother and Hyrcanus were being held, he sent his people ahead into Idumaea at night, and himself with his servants routed the barbarians in pursuit. After killing many, he hastened to Masada, finding the Jews who had pressed upon him in flight more troublesome than the Parthians. Having avenged himself upon his pursuers, he settled his people within the fortifications. He himself left a garrison to protect his mother and younger brothers, and made for Petra in Arabia.Compare with Bellum [I.29.7] The Persians poured into Jerusalem, breaking into the houses of those who fled. Everything was turned to plunder, war and tumult. The outrage went so far that the kingdom was handed over to Antigonus, and Phasael and Hyrcanus too were delivered into his power, to undergo whatever he pleased. He could restrain himself no longer, but immediately attacked Hyrcanus and bit off his ears with his own teeth, so that no change of circumstances should ever open the way for his return to the priesthood. For the high priest must be unmutilated, and it is clear that the law does not permit anyone with a mutilated body to perform the supreme office of the priesthood.Compare with Bellum [I.29.8] Phasael forestalled humiliation by swiftly bringing death upon himself, dashing his head against some rocks that happened to be at hand. He disdained to be preserved for mockery or to die at another’s command, when, even with his hands bound and denied a sword, he could find a way out of life. Yet another account of him also circulated, that Antigonus brought a doctor to the wounded man to pour poison into the wound as though it were medicine. Whichever of these endings occurred, it had its beginning in a defiant spirit. It is alleged that in his last moments, when he was already breathing out his life, on learning that Herod was alive and had escaped the ambush prepared for him by flight, he added that he died with gratitude, leaving alive someone who would bring him vengeance.Compare with Bellum [I.29.9] Herod, meanwhile, hastened into Arabia, hoping to obtain money, which he believed was the only means of bending barbarian greed, to ransom his brother from captivity. If he found the Arab either forgetful of his father’s affection or too tight-fisted to repay his gifts, he would ask for a loan to pay the ransom, pledging in return the son of the man to be ransomed, a boy of seven whom he had brought with him for this purpose. But Phasael’s death forestalled the endeavour of devoted brotherhood, and Herod was carrying out his brotherly duty with such diligence, all in vain. Yet before he learnt of his brother’s death, he found Bocchus, king of Arabia, hostile, though he had believed him a friend. For Bocchus changed his faithfulness with the times, and forbade Herod to enter when he was already approaching Arabia’s borders. He fabricated a story that Parthian envoys had warned him not to think of receiving their fugitive into the kingdom of Arabia and bringing a most grievous war upon himself.Compare with Bellum [I.29.10] Offended at this, Herod at once replied with the words that the pain of his just indignation brought forth, and turned from there towards Egypt. Soon, however, Bocchus regretted the violation of their friendship and sent men to recall him, but Herod had gone on ahead. When he entered the regions inhabited by the Rhinocorites, reliable reports made known to him his brother’s death and the captivity of Hyrcanus, who had been taken in chains into Parthyene. He took on as much grief as he laid aside anxiety, and prepared for flight instead of war. He hastened with all eagerness to Alexandria, where Cleopatra received him with honour, thinking that a man of such renown should be sought as a commander for her side. Disregarding the queen’s requests, he sailed from there for Rome. He judged the storms of winter and the disturbances he knew of in Italy less serious than the waves he dreaded in Cleopatra’s inconstancy, more grievous than any shipwreck.Compare with Bellum [I.29.11] Setting out without waiting for the winds, he encountered danger around Pamphylia, but escaped. Changing ships, he reached Brundisium first, and from there Rome. There, with the advantage of his father’s friendship, he approached Antony. He lamented his own misfortunes and those of his family, who were under siege and for whom he had come to Rome to plead, and moved Antony to pity at so great a reversal of circumstances. A king until recently most powerful, who had often brought aid to the Roman state, had suddenly changed his home for exile, like a shipwrecked man destitute of everything and lacking the help he begged for his people in danger.Compare with Bellum [I.30.1] Although Antony was strongly inclined towards him by the bond of hospitality he had shared with his father Antipater, and especially because, in making him tetrarch, he had left him destined for kingship, Caesar was still more generous in his natural goodwill. He cherished all the more Antipater’s service in Egypt in all his father Caesar’s battles and their bond of hospitality, as though the pledges of favour had been renewed. Yet he regarded with suspicion the king’s cunning disposition, perversely intent on the advantage of his own affairs rather than on what was fair and good. Herod was granted access to the senate. Before it, Messalla and Atratinus set forth his father’s good deeds and Herod’s own services to the Roman state. By the senators’ authority it was decreed that Herod’s kingship appeared advantageous to Roman rule, since, as Antony supported the proposal, it would be useful in waging war against the Parthians for the Romans to gain the alliance of the king just mentioned. When the senate was dismissed, Caesar, Antony and Herod left the senate house together and were escorted by the magistrates’ attendants. On the first day that kingship was conferred upon Herod by the senate’s decree, Antony prepared a banquet and invited the king.Compare with Bellum [I.30.2] At about the same time, Josephus, Herod’s brother, had arranged to flee at night because of a shortage of water. But suddenly so great a rain flooded the land that it filled all the water channels. Abandoning the escape he was preparing to the Arab nation, he routed the forces of Antigonus, who was besieging him, partly by ambushes and partly by engagements and open battle. Yet he too often withdrew into the fortress after an adverse outcome.Compare with Bellum [I.30.3] And now Herod had arrived unexpectedly from Italy at Ptolemais, a city of Syria. Disembarking swiftly, he advanced against Antigonus with a great force of citizens and foreigners. Ventidius and Silo, commanders of the Roman army whom Antony had ordered to assist in escorting Herod, came to meet him. Dellius, sent by Antony for this purpose, had persuaded them to come from nearby to meet him, at least for appearance’s sake, though their sympathies were opposed, since Antigonus had bought them both off. Ventidius was staying in the neighbouring cities to suppress the disturbances of the Parthian war; Silo, stationed within Judaea, was making money in open alliance with Antigonus. Yet Herod did not need help: all the Galilaeans except a few had joined him. His purpose was to rescue his people from the siege at Masada as soon as possible, and he took Joppa by fighting. It lay on the way and was full of enemy troops, whom he did not wish to leave behind him as he advanced further. Although Antigonus wanted to obstruct his march, he recovered Masada without difficulty and rescued his people from danger.Compare with Bellum [I.30.4] Then he went to Jerusalem. He did everything to avoid the necessity of fighting, declaring that he had undertaken war on behalf of his fellow citizens against rebellion, not against his own people. When Antigonus’s supporters provoked him with arrows and lighter missiles, he forced those assailing him from the wall to flee.Compare with Bellum [I.30.5] There would have been no delay in victory had Silo, commander of the Roman force, not suborned soldiers to complain of shortages. They alleged that everything around the walls was devastated, that supplies were difficult to obtain and food scarce, and that the time had now come when they should withdraw to winter quarters. They threatened to disobey orders unless their demands were accepted. The mutiny would already have gained strength had Herod not placed himself among the centurions and Roman soldiers alike and begged them not to abandon the man whom Caesar, Antony and the senate had entrusted to their protection, especially since he promised that nothing they needed would be lacking. When he had finished speaking, he went out into the countryside and suddenly had an abundance of everything supplied to the army, leaving Silo no excuse.Compare with Bellum [I.30.6] With everyone’s spirits thus raised, he recovered Idumaea with two thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry, while the Roman force was now at rest in winter quarters. Josephus was chosen to lead the undertaking, a lighter task, so that he would not think he should attempt anything against Antigonus at greater risk.Compare with Bellum [I.30.7] Herod himself transferred his people from Masada and settled them in Samaria, providing what he believed would serve for their protection and use. In the icy winter, when all the country was covered with snow, he arrived ahead of the report of his coming and entered without a battle the place called by its ancient name Sepphoris, which they later named Diocaesarea. He thought it suitable for restoring those wearied by the winter frosts and journeys made harsher by ice, for there was also an abundance of food there. When his soldiers had recovered there with food and a spell in camp, he decided to undertake battle against the brigands who ranged throughout the country and wore down its inhabitants no less than an invasion in war. He therefore first sent a detachment of cavalry and infantry ahead to the village of Arbela, and himself arrived with the remaining force forty days later. The brigands were not frightened by the sight of the army, but thought they should meet it in arms, displaying military discipline and the audacity of brigands. When battle was joined, Herod’s left wing gave way, but he quickly restored it, brought up reinforcements and steadied his men, struck the pursuers and broke the attacks of thoseCompare with Bellum [I.30.8] who could not withstand Herod fighting at close quarters. He pursued them as they turned away, as far as the Jordan, and put them to death. All the rest were scattered beyond the river, so that Galilee was freed from all fear of raids. Only those who concealed themselves in hiding places and, as it were, buried themselves in caves remained, delaying victory.Compare with Bellum [I.30.9] On the steep mountain slopes, in the hollow recesses of the rocks, there were fearsome caves among rugged crags, inaccessible from every side and impossible to approach except for the inhabitants of the place. They used cross-paths and narrow tracks, the only usual approaches, and their familiarity with danger made them safer against the danger of being caught. Within were the dark recesses of the caves. In front of them a rock projected like a continuous ridge down to the deep bodies of water, excluding any hope of approach, with slippery ground on every side, water falling from the mountain brow and the crashing course of streams. The rush of the falling waters and the rock overhanging the ravines thus made the precipice more terrifying. For some time the king hesitated in uncertainty, unable to discover how to overcome nature. Later he used the following contrivance: he enclosed his strongest men in protective structures fashioned like chests and lowered them, armed, by ropes to the very mouths of the caves. They easily began to slaughter the unarmed and kill them with all their kin and offspring, and to burn alive any who dared resist by casting fire upon them. There was no place for pity. Indeed, even when Herod wished to rescue many from death and give them confidence to take refuge with him, he drove them further away. No one joined Herod voluntarily, and those compelled by force preferred death to captivity. One of the older men, who had seven sons and a wife with him and could have provided for their safety, killed them all in the following way. Ordering each one to come forward in turn, he stood at the entrance and killed each of his sons as he emerged. Seeing so grievous and pitiable a deed, Herod was gripped by the bond of fatherhood. He tried to stop him with his hand and begged him in words to spare his children, promising immunity. But the man was not moved at all by these words. He even abused the king, killed his wife as well as his sons, and, after throwing his sons’ bodies down from the height, finally hurled himself headlong into the depths.Compare with Bellum [I.30.10] Antigonus was terrified that Herod had so easily overcome the multitude of brigands and the difficulties of the terrain. He avoided his presence, but turned against Ptolemy, whom Herod had placed over part of the army. A man most adept at the stealthy devices of war, he used those accustomed to disturbing Galilee to have Ptolemy killed in a sudden attack.Compare with Bellum [I.30.11] He also destroyed Josephus, Herod’s brother, while his brother was occupied in other regions. Josephus resisted vigorously with the Roman soldiers who had come to his aid, hastily assembled.Compare with Bellum [I.30.12] Not content with so great a triumph, he added to his victory a grievous insult to the dead man, leaving him with his head cut off. Pheroras, the slain man’s brother, offered fifty talents for it, but did not obtain it. This victory again turned the sympathies of many in Galilee towards Antigonus, and the business of war was renewed.Compare with Bellum [I.30.13] Herod had made for Antioch and was resting there in the very pleasant place called Daphne. On receiving news of his brother’s killing, he groaned briefly at his suffering, deferred his grief and prepared vengeance. Antigonus could not face his raging sorrow, but hid himself within the fortifications.Compare with Bellum [I.30.14] Herod burst in to pursue the authors of so great a crime, and easily drove back the forces that met him. Very many were killed. The roads were blocked with the bodies of the fallen, so that the very routes were filled with the corpses of the slain. The battle would have been finished, with everyone put to flight, had Herod thought he should march straight to Jerusalem. Antigonus had cast away his spears and dreaded the final punishment.Compare with Bellum [I.30.15] All were so confounded by fear that, when the harsh winter had recalled Herod from pursuit and he laid aside his arms and entered a bath accompanied by a single servant, three men with drawn swords met him, and then more, who had fled the battle and were seeking hiding places. On seeing the king, they were thrown into confusion by fear, passed him and hurried to the exit of the bath to escape, although they could have killed the king and ended the war. Indeed, there was no one to seize them as they fled. Inferring from this how great the enemy’s fear was, Herod pressed on with the fighting and killed Pappus, the very commander of the opposing force, and ordered his head to be cut off, because he had killed Josephus, the king’s brother.Compare with Bellum [I.31.1] Meanwhile Antigonus, who had prepared to flee, delayed. As he lingered, Herod surrounded him with his army and besieged him, pressing upon the side in front of the temple, where Pompey too had broken into the city. The king was now so confident of victory that, after beginning the siege, he turned aside to take Alexander’s daughter as his wife, exchanging the battle trumpet for wedding songs and mingling marriage with war. Having gained the opportunity for the union from the occasion of battle, he returned from the festivities to the war.Compare with Bellum [I.31.2] Sossius too arrived, sent by Antony to aid the king. Their forces were thus united. Although the Romans excelled in experience of war and military discipline, and strove eagerly to please the king, the city was only broken into in the fifth month, when Herod’s men dared to climb the wall and the Roman centurions burst in. Then there was countless slaughter, and everything around the temple was devastated. Some were cut down as they fled to the temple, others gathered inside their houses. There was no pity for old age, none for infancy or women’s weakness. Antigonus presented himself and, forgetful of his position, threw himself at Sossius’s feet. Sossius, whom so great a reversal of circumstances ought to have reminded of pity, abused the prostrate man and called him Antigone. Yet he did not spare him as a woman, but cast him bound into custody.Compare with Bellum [I.31.3] Herod wavered over how to rescue his homeland from Roman hands, how to preserve the temple undefiled by the gentiles. For the Romans hurried to inspect the inner mysteries and profane the holy of holies. The king drove them away one by one, now with pleas, now with threats, judging victory worse than flight if any of the sacred mysteries were divulged. The Romans pressed on towards plunder; Herod resisted, lest they leave him an empty city and nothing of his kingdom but a desert. Sossius, on the other hand, claimed the plunder of the captured city for the soldiers. But the king promised to give the soldiers money from his own resources, and thus bought back with money what remained of his homeland. To fulfil his promise, he received the soldiers most hospitably, treated the commanders as befitted them, and rewarded Sossius himself with royal generosity. No one left ungrateful. Sossius offered a crown to God and departed, taking Antigonus with him to Antony, who had him struck with an axe as a man of ignoble spirit.Compare with Bellum [I.32.1] Herod also bestowed very many gifts upon his own people. He gave very many to Antony and his friends, yet could not buy his own security from Antony. For Antony, mortgaged to his love for Cleopatra, was already her servant and, enslaved to her lust, attended upon her. Yet he could not overcome the greed of a woman, especially one practised in killing her relatives: once they were dead, she had added their possessions to her own as spoils. With the same avarice and cruelty, she had any Syrians she heard were particularly wealthy put to death. With Antony already enslaved to her desires, she thought that the kingdoms of Judaea and Arabia too could be added to her avarice, once the rulers of both nations had been killed.Compare with Bellum [I.32.2] But although drunk with lust and heavy with sleep, Antony came to his senses in this matter and refused to destroy such men and most powerful kings at the command of a most wanton woman. Yet, so as not to let them go unscathed, he struck down their friends, took away the greatest part of their possessions, especially the land that produced balsam, and awarded all the cities on this side of the river Eleutherus, except Tyre and Sidon, to Cleopatra’s greed. Appeased towards her husband by such a payment, she accompanied Antony as far as the Euphrates when he set out against the Parthians, and returned through Judaea. There Herod did not neglect to win the queen’s goodwill towards himself, especially with gifts and presents. Success increased her arrogance, so that her womanly lack of restraint exalted itself beyond measure. Indeed, not long afterwards Artabazes, king of the Parthians and son of the most powerful King Tigranes, was given to her as a gift. Antony held him captive with all the Persian plunder and spoils. Though owed to a triumph, he was assigned to a woman like a worthless slave, so that the more glorious the victory had been, the more shameful was the gift that dishonoured kings with such mockery.Compare with Bellum [I.32.3] Yet the man who did not know how to use success did not enjoy it for long: through a woman’s insolence, he roused Augustus against himself. Thus the Actian war was being prepared with great movements on both sides. The king was most eager to enter the war with Antony, since Judaea was free from hostile disturbance and he had recovered Hyrcania, long held by Antigonus’s sister. Yet in this too Herod was most fortunate, being begrudged a share in others’ dangers. Cleopatra therefore wished to estrange Antony’s mind from the kings and turn it away. She persuaded her husband that Herod should wage war against the Arabs, so that, if he prevailed, Arabia would fall to the queen, and, if he was defeated, Cleopatra’s dominion would extend into Judaea.Compare with Bellum [I.32.4] Whichever won would destroy the other. This plan inclined in Herod’s favour in its outcome, rather than its intention. As soon as he began battle, his superior cavalry drove the enemy back, but in the end he was overcome by the enemy’s multitude and surrounded by their numbers. His adversaries’ forces had gathered at Canatha, and he wished to draw up his line closely against them. But his men’s spirits were elated by their earlier success, and for that reason they rushed out against the enemy, leaving him unsupported. Above all, this came through the treachery of Athenion, whom Cleopatra had attached to the commander to abandon Herod at the very moment of need, not to help him. The Arabs then attacked his abandoned army in rocky and inaccessible places, struck it down in grievous slaughter and routed it, pursuing the fugitives to their places of refuge and destroying them.Compare with Bellum [I.32.5] Herod arrived, later indeed than the need demanded, but nevertheless avenged the disaster. In subsequent battles he so afflicted the Arabs that they repeatedly lamented that single victory of theirs. Added to this was a grievous loss of heart caused by an earthquake, in which very many livestock and about thirty thousand people perished. Yet the entire military force remained unharmed, since it lived in the open air. This too raised the enemy’s spirits: they thought they could more easily invade a deserted Judaea and afflict those stricken by such portents. Herod therefore thought that his men must be roused to their own defence, especially because he had learnt that the envoys he had sent into Arabia had been treacherously killed. He addressed them in their fear with these words:Compare with Bellum [I.32.6] “After so many successful battles on our side, the enemy’s fortunes have been broken, even by their own admission: driven by frenzied grief, like defeated men, they murdered our envoys. It therefore seems strange to me that an irrational fear has so shaken you that you set the accidents of the elements above the known successes of valour. There has been no encounter in which the Arabs did not immediately give way and turn to flight, thinking they must retreat. As is the way with the stealthy devices of war, they sought remedies in deceit and ambushes, not to win themselves, but to delay our victory. In place of the confidence this should have brought, agitation has arisen, as though the war were terrifying, because the earth shook, although the very men who wage war were alone unharmed. Or, if we wish to consider whom it harmed, we shall judge it to be the Arabs rather, whom it brought back to war so that they should not escape stronger men by fleeing. For I see that they have returned to the battle line relying not on their arms and strength but on the loss of our livestock. Yet frail is the hope that depends not on confidence in one’s own valour but on another’s misery, since nothing on earth is so changeable as prosperity or adversity. For the state of human affairs is renewed by slight turns; prosperity does not endure, nor does hardship persist. Thus neither misery nor its contrary is perpetual: fortunes frequently alternate and vary even for the same people. Indeed, we may take an example from events. In the earlier clash we had the advantage, but as the battle advanced our fortune changed, and we were defeated by those we had defeated. We too therefore have grounds to hope that those who defeated us will be defeated by us. For excessive confidence is always incautious and careless of itself. Fear, however, warns us to look ahead and teaches diligence. In prosperity, audacity steals upon us, and unthinking rashness does not know how to await the commander’s counsel. Indeed, it was when you advanced against my judgement that Athenion’s wickedness found an opportunity to do harm. Now your trembling pledges me the first claim to victory. Raise your spirits, then, and exalt the Jews’ ancient greatness of soul. Do not let the disturbances of insensible things terrify you, nor think that movements of the earth indicate some other disaster. The disturbances of the elements have their own harm: fear nothing other than the injury that lies in them. For an earthquake and the destruction of living creatures are not signs of dangers, but the dangers themselves.
