There is therefore no reason for us to fear as though we were about to suffer grievous things, when we have already suffered the most grievous. He who has exacted punishment can now be favourable, and gentler than if he had not exacted it. What remains after earthquake and pestilence except mercy, since we have paid for twofold sins? Yet we have intact what is useful for war. For pestilence carried off those outside the war, while our victory took from the enemy those they had chosen as fit for war. Moreover, our livestock have died, but their judgement has died: they thought the envoys we sent should have their throats cut against human and divine law. They have transgressed the law of all human beings, even of the barbarians themselves. Even among those who know nothing of humanity, envoys are held inviolable, through dread of heavenly vengeance and fear of God as the avenger of so great a crime. Our adversaries have therefore committed what neither human nor divine laws leave unavenged. Let us go out, then, to fight not for territory or spoils, but for an injury to God. Let us be roused to war not by love of wife or children, but by our confidence in God’s protection. We carry out not our own decisions, but the sacred precepts of divine law, to exact vengeance for those whom religion requires to be inviolable. Amid hostile arms, an embassy alone mediates peace; one who serves as an envoy lays aside the character of an enemy. Their blood now cries out to God and demands vengeance. Let us hasten to battle, then, while we have God as avenger, vindicator of the slain. They fight better on our behalf and, surrounded by legions of angels, stand before us in the battle line.”Compare with Bellum [I.32.7] Having exhorted his soldiers with such words, he rushed upon the enemy, seeking every opportunity to fight. The Arabs were superior in number but inferior in spirit, and when battle was joined about five thousand of them fell. The rest withdrew into a fortification and were wearied by a shortage of water, so that they sent an embassy to ask for peace at a price. But when they saw that they were being put off and thirst burned still more fiercely as the water ran out, many came out and offered themselves voluntarily to the enemy, preferring to perish by the sword rather than by thirst. Herod kept them bound, lest there be any ambush. Thus in five days about four thousand were received; when others came out to fight, about seven thousand men were again killed. Humbled by the king through this blow, the Arabs were as superior in judgement as they were inferior in valour: they asked for the very man they had as an adversary to be their defender and helper.Compare with Bellum [I.33.1] But greater anxiety struck him in victory. Having subjected something to himself, he now dreaded imminent danger not to his territory but to his entire kingdom, for Antony, whom faithful friendship had bound to him, had been defeated. Indeed, Augustus Caesar, victor in the Actian contest, did not yet think Antony overcome while Herod survived the victory. When the anxious king learnt from a reliable report that Caesar had reached Rhodes, he sailed to him, lest rumour outstrip his journey by land. On arrival, he laid aside his diadem and presented himself in the dress of a private man, but with a king’s spirit. Withholding nothing of the truth, he maintained his firmness and preserved his authority. “I confess, Augustus,” he said, “that I was Antony’s faithful ally, since I received my kingdom from him and still do not deny that I am his debtor. I would have proved this by arms had Cleopatra not begrudged it and the Arabs not prevented it. It was through that necessity that I did not bear arms against you, not as one who deserted a friend or feared battle, but as one occupied with affairs at home. Yet Antony did not find me ungrateful to him: although absent, I sent him reinforcements for his army and countless supplies of grain. Nor would you, Caesar, have judged me ungrateful for his benefits had I taken part in the Actian war. See how I withhold nothing. I am more afraid of appearing before you ungrateful to your enemy than an enemy to you. Your judgement weighs more heavily upon me than war, for before you it is crimes that are put in jeopardy, not the deserts of excellence. I too prefer to plead my case before you for faithfulness rather than faithlessness. See, Caesar, how I did not desert Antony when he was unharmed: I did not flee from him when defeated. You defeated Antony, Caesar, with your greatest legions; you defeated him with your counsels; you defeated him with the strength of the Roman dominion, which he abandoned and which he disowned. He was truly defeated by your excellence, but more by his own conduct. His wife Cleopatra defeated him; Egyptian love defeated him; Canopic luxury defeated him. It defeated him because he preferred to be defeated with Cleopatra rather than win without her. A woman more hostile to her own people than to her adversaries defeated him. I had advised the woman’s death, if he wished to look to his own interests. I had promised help to restore him in his affliction, promised forces to protect him in flight, and offered myself as a partner in war; but his mind had been blocked by his desires for Cleopatra. He was defeated because he would not listen to me. I too was defeated with Antony, yet with less disgrace, because Cleopatra defeated him, Antony me. He did not abandon a barbarian woman, I a friend. With him I laid aside my diadem, but I have come to you retaining the credit of a faithful friend. I have put away the insignia of kingship, but have not cast aside the consciousness of excellence. Judge as you will; yet, whatever the outcome of your judgement, I shall take this away with me: what sort of friend I have been will be recognised.”Compare with Bellum [I.34.1] Caesar answered these words. “Greetings,” he said, “and now enjoy your kingdom all the more, for we do not envy excellence but delight in it. You deserve to rule over more people, since you so defend friendship that you neither disown a man in adversity nor blush to acknowledge him as your friend. But undertake to attach yourself to the more fortunate, and to preserve in prosperity the faithfulness you have amply proved in adversity. Antony may have defeated you, but I shall not consider defeated a man whom friendship has made equal to the victors. We seek you for this reason, that no outcome of war changed you, since you did not desert Antony: Antony deserted you first, trusting himself to Cleopatra rather than to you. His folly gained you for us, because he chose the woman most ruinous to him and rejected a faithful man. Nor is it strange if Antony, defeated, clings to Cleopatra, by whom he was captured in victory. Why are you surprised that Cleopatra made Antony break with you, when she parted him from me and made an enemy out of a partner in rule? You too, therefore, were rejected with us, and so reign with us. Nor is it without benefit that, while we were occupied in civil wars, you subjected the untamed Arab nation, for we count the enemies of the Jews as our own. Those who assail you bear arms against us. You therefore served us as a soldier when you won for yourself, and so we reward you, that your kingdom may be confirmed by our gift. For now, our favour is to have diminished nothing; for the future, we shall endeavour to ensure that you do not miss Antony. For it is not fitting that we should fail to surpass in goodwill the man whom we surpassed in war.”Compare with Bellum [I.34.2] When he had said this, he placed the diadem on Herod’s head, adding attentiveness to his gift. Encouraged by this mark of Caesar’s regard, Herod wished to rescue Alexas, one of Antony’s friends and a man at whom Caesar was most indignant, from disfavour. He lamented with many pleas, but Caesar’s excessive indignation left no room for pardon. When Caesar departed from there for Egypt, Herod accompanied his journey, supplying everything that would be useful to him or his army. By winning the greatest favour for himself, he secured the commander’s affection, especially because, in the more arid places as far as Pelusium, his royal foresight provided an abundant supply of water. Through these services he inspired such love for himself in everyone that he was judged to have deserved more than he had received, and the power of his kingdom to be less than the generosity of his hospitality. Hence, after events in Egypt had gone as he wished and Antony and Cleopatra were dead, Caesar not only restored what had been taken from Herod, but, besides what Cleopatra had diverted, granted him Gadara, Hippos and Samaria. He also gave him the coastal cities of Gaza, Anthedon, Joppa and Strato’s Tower together. He granted the king four hundred bodyguards from Gaul, surrounded by whom Cleopatra used to walk, to guard his person, and many other things. But the king valued above all these gifts that Caesar loved him more than anyone except Agrippa, and Agrippa loved him more than anyone except Caesar.Compare with Bellum [I.35.1] In the fifteenth year of his reign, then, to respond to his good fortune and favour, uplifted by so great a course of successes, he turned his attention to devotion. To show himself grateful for the heavenly benefits flowing upon him beyond measure, he adorned the temple. He surrounded the whole circuit of ground around the temple with a wall and enclosed a doubled area, with immense expenditure on building and exquisite beauty. The great porticoes around the sanctuary, which he erected from their foundations, bore witness to this. His concern to protect it was no less than his concern to adorn it: he fortified the stronghold facing north, which he called Antonia on account of Antony’s favour, inferior to none of the earlier palaces. Within the citadel itself he also added two dwellings for the royal house, of the greatest extent and marvellous beauty, with whose charm you would think nothing could compare. One was named Caesarium, the other Agrippium, so that the lasting memory of such great friends might be celebrated in his own buildings.Compare with Bellum [I.35.2] He also not only built up the city of Sebaste but filled it with inhabitants. Not to pursue every detail, he scarcely passed over any site of an ancient city without renewing what was falling into decay or adorning it by adding the buildings it seemed to lack. Extending his generosity even to the five-yearly contests, he enriched that worthless class of men by pouring out his wealth.Compare with Bellum [I.35.3] He also built a temple of white marble to Caesar at the sources of the Jordan, so forgetful of religion that he dedicated a temple to a man and introduced the practice of the nations into Judaea. The place is named Panium. There a mountain of lofty height stretches aloft with its highest summit, and in its side a shadowy cavern opens, through which the depth of a foul-smelling chasm exhales a fierce stench. Within was a body of water, a great mass utterly still, so that its profound depth could not be estimated. Outside, however, springs gush out around the roots of the mountain itself. Hence many have thought that the Jordan rises there; yet we think that what the truth holds should be disclosed later.Compare with Bellum [I.35.4] On the coast there was a city called Strato’s Tower, already worn out by frequent wars and inclining towards ruin through age itself, but outstanding in the convenience and charm of its site. He renewed it in white stone and adorned it with palatial buildings, expressing in it the strength of his greatness of soul and the elegance of his work. For it lies midway between two coastal cities, Dora and Joppa, and on either side is hemmed in by a shore without harbours, so that all who wish to sail from Egypt past Phoenicia are tossed on the open sea. For the sea there is often roused by winds, especially the blast of the south-west wind. Even when it blows more moderately, a wave rises; striking the projecting rocks and rebounding with its force broken, it makes the wild sea rougher as it retreats. Thus the king, setting no limit to expense, overcame nature by greatness of soul and established a harbour larger than Piraeus. Within it, penetrating the vast mass of rock, he made safe anchorages.Compare with Bellum [I.35.5] He also measured out a space suited to the size of the harbour and cast enormous rocks into the sea, many of them fifty feet in height, others even taller. He marked out the harbour itself with very great towers, one of which he called Drusion, to weave the name of Drusus, who was among Caesar’s ancestors, into his own conspicuous works.Compare with Bellum [I.35.6] He also inserted shorter flights of steps at more frequented places, by which ships could be hauled up without great labour, and embellished the whole charm of the harbour with three enormous colossi. Again he founded a temple to Caesar on a higher site, and in the middle of the temple set a colossus bearing Augustus’s name, as his image, no smaller in size than the image of Olympian Jupiter or Argive Juno. You would not know whether to think that beauty amid such great difficulties excelled more, or the strength and protection of the work amid such great splendour, since the work remains indestructible against both sea and age. Thus manifold benefits came together in a single work: a very great city was added to the province, a harbour for sailors, and honour for Caesar, from whose name it is called Caesarea to this day.Compare with Bellum [I.36.1] The pursuit of marriage to a single woman brought low this royal power, which abounded in prosperous successes, and broke it with bitter sorrows, from the time when, contrary to law and right, he thought marriage should be measured by rank of birth rather than love, in a certain royal fashion. He had as his partner a woman of Jerusalem named Dosis, who had been joined to him earlier when he was a private man. She should have been all the dearer because she had brought her husband good fortune: it was with her that he had attained the heights of kingship. But, forgetful of his debt of gratitude, he cast Dosis aside and married Mariamne, Aristobulus’s granddaughter and Alexander’s daughter. Thus, in pursuing noble birth, he fell into turmoil: his own household would not be at one with him, although the manifold people of different provinces obeyed him. Antipater—for that was the name of the young man born to Dosis—was expelled not only from his father’s house but from the whole city, lest the sight of him in the house offend the new bride in her stepmotherly hatred. He made way for the ill-fated marriage, which his father celebrated with the exile of his only son, and was scarcely summoned even for the celebrations on feast days. Seeing her husband comply with her wishes even when it brought his family devotion into disrepute, the woman turned to arrogance. A further cause was added that justly inflamed her spirit: she had learnt that her grandfather Hyrcanus had been killed through her husband’s plots, falsely suspected of desiring the kingdom. He is the man we mentioned above, whom Barzaphranes, who commanded the Persians, had carried off captive when he occupied Syria. He had first been detained in Parthia; then, pitying his fallen lot, Barzaphranes had handed him over at the request of the Jews who lived beyond the Euphrates. If only, just as he had been granted to those who entreated for him, he had also trusted those who warned him not to let the power of his relatives tempt him, in the manner of human nature, to go over to Herod. That power would endanger him, since a man eager to preserve his kingdom harassed none more than those closest to him and guarded against his relatives. But, weary of living abroad and longing for his own people, he crossed the Euphrates and returned to Judaea. This sank deeper into Herod’s heart than anyone had thought, not because Hyrcanus had aspired to the kingdom, but because it was thought uncertain whether a man of royal birth, with the privilege of power long exercised, could refrain from it. His granddaughter’s marriage was therefore the snare of death for Hyrcanus. For its sake he hastened to Herod, unaware that captives lived more safely with an enemy than relatives with a king. Thus, without even a slight suspicion that he sought to reign, he was killed for this reason alone: the kingdom seemed to belong to him.Compare with Bellum [I.36.2] Meanwhile he loved Mariamne with lavish love and did not wish her to be offended. Her many children had increased his favour towards her. For she had borne him five children, but the youngest of the three males had died in Rome while being instructed in the liberal arts. The other two were honoured with royal splendour beyond the measure of private men. The young men were supported by their mother’s noble birth and their own birth into kingship, since they had been born when their father was already reigning. Above all, however, they were supported by his love for Mariamne, which inflamed the king more and more each day. Although his wife repaid him with no love in return, he nevertheless took care not to sadden her spirit in anything. The woman’s hatred and the man’s love contended against one another in an evenly balanced scale. Yet Mariamne had better cause to hate the husband who loved her than Herod had to love Mariamne, who did not love him. The woman drew hatred from his crime, confidence from his love: she recoiled from the one with a granddaughter’s grief, while the other exalted her through her lover’s submission. She therefore did not refrain even from reproaching him with his crimes: he had wickedly robbed her of her grandfather Hyrcanus and her brother Jonathan. The one was his grandfather by marriage, the other his brother-in-law; the former should have been spared because of the frailty of old age, the latter at least because of his youth. It was an unworthy deed: he had entrusted the high priesthood to a young man of seventeen, and immediately upon conferring honour on him he inflicted death, for no other reason, as we have learnt, than that the people suddenly burst into tears when he first approached the altars on a sacred feast day, clad in priestly robes. Herod found this so suspicious that he believed the people had wept for joy and thereby betrayed their affection for the youth. Those tears revealed their wish; the people’s enthusiasm endangered him, since they had shown from their inmost hearts what enthusiasm they felt for the young man’s dignity. That noble grandson of a king, son of an unrestrained woman, brother of a most insolent queen who disdained her royal husband, would burst forth into power unless he were removed all the sooner. He possessed beauty and the charm of comeliness, so that he was thought rightly to deserve preference over everyone. Herod therefore resolved to kill the young man. The young man’s mother troubled him: most keen in investigation and most vehement in vengeance, she allowed nothing to remain hidden or unavenged. For that reason he considered drawing back and restraining himself. Yet the daily increase in everyone’s love for the young man and the danger to his kingdom troubled him in turn. Hence, roused by headlong fury, he resolved to look to his own interests by whatever means.Compare with Bellum [I.37.1] The young man was sent by night to the city of Jericho. There, where he was accustomed to delight in swimming, many gathered as though for play; submerged beyond all measure, he was killed in the pool.Compare with Bellum [I.37.2] His sister did not bear this in silence. Out of affection for her brother, she made it known in reproaches and repeatedly charged her husband with having her brother taken from her at his command. She had been bereft of everyone; her husband’s house was a house of mourning for her, for he had first taken her grandfather from her and afterwards killed her brother. Wretched woman that she was, she had brought destruction upon her own people. She called down dreadful curses upon her husband, her mother-in-law and the king’s sister: the crime was common to them all. She called upon God as avenger, that so great a deed should not be left unpunished. Herod bore this, captive to love and devoted to her every nod, but the women raged. They could not bear her curses as she reviled them or her arrogance in indignation, especially since Herod, overcome by his admiration for her, could not rise against the woman he loved. Thus, to arouse him all the more in his love, a scene of adultery was devised and a charge of this kind was fabricated against the woman: she had sent her portrait to Antony in Egypt. What lack of restraint she had shown, offering her beauty for sale to an absent man prone to lust and, moreover, powerful, one who used power as his right, auctioning off her beauty! In the commerce of this novel auction she had prostituted herself, whether through the force of love or hatred of her husband, whose peril she had demanded as the price of adultery. Through this invention of the women, therefore, Mariamne was assailed before Herod all the more grievously the more she was loved. Yet the accusation itself, although made by indignant women, was not wholly alien to truth. It was nearer the truth to believe that her mother Alexandra, furious that another was being preferred to her son Aristobulus for the priesthood—for she preferred her son Jonathan to be called by this name, to recall that her grandfather had been king—had asked Antony to grant her son the priesthood through a certain musician who acted as intermediary for the letters; and then that, when Antony’s friend Gellius came to Judaea, the young man, upon becoming known to him, had aroused his admiration through the charm of his exceptional comeliness. Mariamne had done so no less: the more illustrious her rank, the more brilliant her reputation. Perhaps he had come to know her through a certain habit of human nature, by which men too wish to show how dear they are to their more intimate friends by allowing them to share a hospitable table with their relatives also present.Compare with Bellum [I.37.3] There too, Alexandra was said to have been given an opportunity to speak with Sossius, although, as a widow rather free in her conduct, she could not have lacked another opportunity to become acquainted with the guest, especially since she sought occasions and people of this kind. Then, after consulting together, they had decided that portraits of both should be sent to Antony. Dazzled by the splendour of the portraits, and especially by Sossius’s testimony, Antony had written to Herod to send Aristobulus to him without delay. Sossius, acting as a pander to excite Antony’s far from sober desires, had declared that he had never seen anything like them on earth and that their charm was divine, not human. He had passed over Mariamne because she was married to Herod, not because he was accustomed to conceal his lust even for women living with their husbands: he could enjoy them without danger and commit disgrace without shame. Rather, he guarded against Cleopatra’s indignation. She took offence at a rival of either sex, but more so if she discovered a woman attached to Antony, since she thought herself more beautiful than all other women. Upon reading the letter, Herod had therefore excused himself on the grounds that he could not tear the noble young man away from his people without their rising in sedition and the whole nation being thrown into turmoil. To satisfy Alexandra, he had promised Aristobulus the priesthood. But, thinking the promises were being delayed and that she was being cunningly deceived, Alexandra had prepared a ship. While she was making ready to flee, her plan had become known through Sabbion and she had been brought back with her son. Moved by these things, Herod had concealed the affront for a time and hastened the grant of the priesthood to Aristobulus, so as to veil the odium of the murder he had prepared beneath the appearance of honour.Compare with Bellum [I.37.4] Once the murder had been carried out, as we have said, he was shaken as though struck by lightning, and at the same time by the charge fabricated by his own people that she had sought an adulterous lover. He knew that Antony was prone to lust and, because of his very great power, inflamed his unconcealed desires for every kind of love affair. He also knew that Cleopatra’s implacable resentment, especially of rivalry, and her savagery had killed very many men whom she had found too slow to restrain their wives’ lack of restraint. He shuddered at the danger not only of losing his wife but of facing death as well. He therefore resolved to go himself to Egypt to sway Antony or Cleopatra, whom he feared most. Others report that he went there after being summoned by Antony’s letter to give an account of the young man’s killing.Compare with Bellum [I.37.5] Before setting out, however, he privately disclosed to his brother-in-law Josephus, whom the king’s sister Salome had married, that he feared being killed because of desire for his wife’s beauty, which the woman was accused of having made known by sending an image of her comeliness. He entrusted this task to him as his brother-in-law: if he himself were killed by Antony, he was to kill Mariamne, so that no reward for the disgrace should survive. Josephus, by no means, I think, from a desire to betray him, but to soothe the woman’s complaints against her husband, in which she said that in her affliction she burned with hatred for him, revealed the instruction. He interpreted it as a lover’s affection: not even in death would Herod allow himself to be separated from his union with his wife. But, far differently from what Josephus had supposed, the woman took it as proof of his still unappeased cruelty towards her. He had charged his own brother-in-law with carrying it out even after his death. He wronged her in his hostility: he did not test his suspicions against any evidence of truth but pressed them through to the destruction of headlong death. There would be no end to hatred that extended beyond the very end of life and safety. But Josephus, forgetful of trouble at home, inflamed his own wife’s suspicions against him while seeking to reconcile another man’s wife to her husband. She thought that her own husband’s conversations with Mariamne and his lingering in the royal palace should not be taken lightly. Indeed, when her brother returned, she did not delay her accusation, adding her own injury to the insults against the king: Mariamne had taken her husband from her too. But Herod, although shaken, was at first by no means greatly moved. He did not show himself hostile to his wife; indeed, broken by the force of love, one day he began to swear to the woman that he loved her with such affection that he had never burned with desire for another woman. He had cast them all from his mind so as to remain faithful to his wife. But she said: “You showed your love for me well enough in the instructions you gave Josephus, ordering him to kill me. How can a man love who can kill?”Compare with Bellum [I.37.6] The king immediately lost his senses when he heard that his secret had been betrayed. He therefore began to think that Josephus would never have betrayed him unless, captive to love for the woman, he had sought in illicit intercourse the reward for betrayal. What had long been hidden was now revealed; the crime was in the open, the debauchery beyond doubt. His sister had not been roused without reason, for she had detected the injury to her household before anyone else. Thus, raging with excessive indignation and beside himself, he leapt from the bed, fleeing the contamination of shameful debauchery, and the palace could not contain his fury. His sister heard him shouting and at once seized the moment for an accusation, an opportunity to do harm, and confirmed his angry suspicions. Impelled by the pain of the injury and his sister’s accusation, he therefore ordered both to be killed.Compare with Bellum [I.37.7] Not long afterwards, remorse for his deeds followed. When anger fell away, love succeeded it and passion was revived. Such a heat of desire blazed up that he did not believe she was dead and, out of his mind, spoke to her as though she were alive. He sent servants to her as to a living woman, asking her to lay aside their quarrels, come to him and restore herself to their conjugal affection. Only after much time and instruction did he finally believe that she had died. In his love, he had thought that a woman of such immortal beauty could not die. So great was his affection for the dead woman. Indeed, he is said afterwards to have grown savage and, embittered by hatred of those around him, to have killed many, and to have suffered not only from sickness of mind but also from a grave illness of the body, which they said he had contracted also from the pestilential air. For the corrupted atmosphere brought pestilence upon very many. Hence, after consulting those skilled in medicine, he withdrew into the seclusion of the woods. As his vigour gradually returned, hunting restored both his bodily health and his sobriety of mind.Compare with Bellum [I.38.1] These things too he added to the wonders with which he revered the dead woman’s charm: he had paid the penalty for his unjust crime, and the destruction of such beauty had been expiated by the sickness of the elements. The death of one woman had been avenged by the world’s ruin and a plague upon peoples, yet with an unequal recompense, as the earth refused its fruits and famine increased the pestilence. [I.38.2] Mariamne met this end with composure, chaste towards her husband but insolent in her awareness of her beauty. She had magnanimity in excess but lacked attentiveness, so that she disdained her husband’s caresses, confident that she could suffer no destruction at the hands of one who loved her beyond measure. [I.38.3] She not only found vengeance for the present but also transmitted hereditary hatred into the future. Her sons succeeded her as executors of their mother’s grief, with an affection indeed devoted to their mother but impious towards their father, although the right of nature should have been discharged towards both parents with equal service. Grief did not find them untrained. For, educated for a long time in Rome in Latin and Greek letters alike, they had acquired no small cunning. On learning of their mother’s death while absent, they were embittered by the many who incited them to hatred of their father. Even upon their return, reverence for their father’s presence had not instilled attentiveness in them; malice grew with age. Marriage added to their presumption: Salome’s daughter, Herod’s niece, had been joined in lawful wedlock to one, and the daughter of Archelaus, who held the kingdom of Cappadocia, to the other. The nobility of these unions had lent authority to their hatred. Herod therefore took offence even at his sons’ unspoken disposition, more agitated than a father’s family devotion could bear, which is often wounded even by a look. Further provocations were added by those who repeatedly warned him, as though out of concern, to guard against his sons’ plots, asserting that they were arming their hands to avenge their mother’s death.Compare with Bellum [I.38.4] Terrified by these warnings, Herod began to prefer Antipater, Dosis’s son, to his brothers and, with more abundant affection, to draw him into his favour. The royal palace began to burn with greater hatred and to be shaken by rivalry between the brothers, as the others resented a private woman’s son being preferred to them, who had been born into kingship. Cunning in flattery, the lower he saw his maternal standing to be, the more eagerly Antipater commended himself to his father. He did not cease assailing his brothers with fabricated accusations until, by himself and through others he had attached to him, he excluded them from their father’s affection. Indeed, he took away all their hope of reigning, so that in a publicly drawn-up will he alone was designated successor to the rule. Sent to Caesar in Rome, he was supported with every royal adornment and splendour except the distinction of the diadem. Returning from there to Judaea with increased favour from Caesar and very many illustrious men, he gained so much influence in a very short time that he even restored his mother to marriage with his father. With the twin weapons of skill in flattery and cunning in accusation, he began to press his brothers so hard before their father that their father prepared death for his sons.Compare with Bellum [I.38.5] Indeed, beside himself with fury, he went to Rome, dragging Alexander with him, and arraigned him before Caesar on a charge of magic directed against him. Given the opportunity to lament his misfortune and all his afflictions, Alexander saw that he had the support of so great a judge, who could neither be swayed through favour by Herod nor deceived by Antipater. Thinking nothing should be passed over, he touched upon his father’s crimes with a certain restraint, so as neither to appear to press them as an accuser nor allow them to remain hidden, since it would greatly help his case if he showed that his father’s hatred assailed him because of his grief at his mother’s murder. For in trials of this kind nothing weighs more heavily upon children than nature’s family devotion and the authority of that devotion. If these are discredited by some crime, the prejudgement is diminished and the privileged claim removed. When he came to his father’s charges, however, he refuted them with powerful assertions and first showed that his brother had no part in the crime. He shared his dangers, and Alexander groaned that an innocent man was being accused. The force of his pleading and his skill in speaking supported his clear conscience. He lamented most bitterly that no honour remained to himself and his brother: everything had been taken away through their brother’s wickedness and their father’s pliancy. Death was being inflicted upon him, and his father so eagerly awaited it that he added a charge and attached a crime. With these words he brought everyone to tears and turned the course of the trial so that Caesar rejected the accusation and his father embraced reconciliation. It was most pleasing and distinguished for the Roman ruler not only to have given a kingdom to an illustrious king but also to have restored his children. It was therefore determined after a just examination that reverence for the father’s right should remain inviolate and the sons’ innocence safe. The children were to obey their father, as was fitting, and he was to show his sons the unimpaired affection of nature; nevertheless, he could leave the kingdom to whom he wished.Compare with Bellum [I.38.6] Alexander returned from the city of Rome with his father, acquitted at trial more than cleared of suspicion. For Antipater did not allow Herod’s mind to be free of hatred for his sons. He himself was the very material of that hatred; yet, out of regard for the reconciler, he restrained his purpose so as not to betray the scene he had staged against his brothers and expose his plots. When they reached Cilicia and put in at Eliusa on their voyage, Archelaus received them with a sumptuous banquet, giving thanks on behalf of his son-in-law Alexander, whom Herod had considered worthy of reconciliation as well as rescue from danger. He himself had also asked his friends, in letters sent through his own people, to assist his son-in-law’s defence. At Herod’s departure he offered thirty talents as gifts of hospitality and accompanied the king as far as Zephyrium.Compare with Bellum [I.38.7] Upon returning home, the king immediately summoned the people and addressed them in this manner.Compare with Bellum [I.39.1] “Hebrew citizens, my reason for going to Rome proved both useful and fruitful: Caesar was to judge my sons, so that I, who was angry, should not hear the case alone. I went to Caesar so that the man who had restored my kingdom might pronounce upon my successor. He added to his benefits by doing what was difficult: restoring almost lost sons to their father, and restoring to brothers concord, which stands above kingship. I therefore return richer than when I set out. I have learnt to be a better father, because my sons have learnt to be better children, through Caesar’s benefit. For he determined that my sons’ succession should depend upon my decision: lest the privilege of succession engender arrogance, I myself should appoint as my successor the man I chose, the man who had deserved it, the man who had honoured his father more. I shall imitate Caesar, for by acquitting my younger sons he made them equal to my elder son. Thus today I appoint my three children kings together. Age supports the one, noble birth the others. Let their number trouble no one: the greatness of the kingdom is abundant enough for even more. Let God first judge my decision; then you too should join in. Honour fittingly those whom Caesar has united and their father appointed, so that their honour is neither excessive nor too low. The one inflates, the other exasperates. Let each be granted what is appropriate to his share. For a man does not so much please the person he honours beyond measure as wound the person to whom he denies his due. Often both are offended where flattery shows preference. I am certainly father to them all: honour paid to my sons is surely a favour to their father. Yet if anyone honours my children beyond measure, he is answerable to me also on my children’s behalf, for he brings about their downfall. Excessive honour supplies the means for audacity. Do I envy my children? Far from it. But I prefer them to have less power with goodwill than very great power with sedition. What belongs to arrogance or rapacity soon slips away; what belongs to goodwill is held for a long time. I shall therefore take care to attach relatives and friends to my children as guarantors of concord, through whose exhortation they may clothe themselves in mutual affection. For, while every evil utterance readily infects the hearer’s mind, continual conversations and prolonged familiarity especially tend to pour a plague into minds, which soon passes, as by contagion, into the conduct of those living together. Even if their conduct is tranquil, just as a pool, though calm, can rise in surges when stirred by winds, so a good nature is tossed by wicked advisers. I therefore think that each man ought to place his greatest hope for himself in me, for what accrues to my children is not lost to me. Each tribune or soldier should show greater reverence to the father of his commanders. I am the one, I am the one who will repay you all even for what you have bestowed upon my sons. If I observe upright efforts, I shall reward them in deeds. Ill will will receive its price, losing its reward even with the man it thought it should flatter. But you, good sons, consider first the sacred obligation of nature, whose affection binds even beasts and compels even wild creatures to love their kin. Mutual love remains among untamed animals, and beasts redeem their own by endangering themselves. Revere Caesar too, who has made you friends instead of enemies; and thirdly myself, who prefer to ask when I can command. Remain brothers; do not cast off what you were born. I give you the dress and splendour of rulers, but more precious is the inviolate seal of your love that I urge upon you. If family devotion remains, kingship delights; if affection is absent, rule is worthless and often harmful. Thus, while I put you to the test, for the present you have the honour of kingship, not the kingdom. If you love your father, the right will follow. Yet demonstrate your love for me among yourselves: as rulers you will enjoy everything by which kingship usually delights, while the burdens of rule and the mass of affairs will await me alone, even if I am unwilling. It is therefore to your advantage to wish what I wish, since I both wish for what is yours and consider it mine.” With these words he kissed his sons, so as to bind them to one another with a single kiss of love. Having done so, he dismissed the assembly.Compare with Bellum [I.40.1] Many departed happy, pleased by the concord between the brothers, but discord returned with the brothers, all the graver because their greater rank aroused more envy and supplied greater power to do harm. Mariamne’s sons resented being placed on an equal footing with the son of a private woman whose lineage knew nothing of kingship. Antipater, on the other hand, disdained having the hope of kingship divided between himself and his brothers, and envied his brothers, for whom even a lower place was scarcely reserved instead of the first. But he concealed and veiled himself, covering his hatred with a show of favour, while their every design lay open in their speech even to those who did not seek it, their tongue too ready and lavish with secrets. Whatever they had said reached Antipater at once; much that they had not said was also fabricated. The messenger added a great deal by way of amplification. Antipater was the architect of everything by which his brothers were assailed. His life was nothing other than a meeting place of cunning devices, a stage of wickedness, a plot of crimes, a mystery of disgraceful deeds. He planted informers, suborned witnesses and feigned a defence, carrying about the mask of a brother as though in a theatre, so as to shake off the lighter charges and yield to the graver ones, thereby deceiving his father more and stirring him more violently against his brothers. Above all, he skilfully aggravated the odium of a plan to kill their father and seize the kingdom, matters more suspicious to kings through fear of danger. Yet, lest the charges seem less credible to the king without anyone to rebut them, he first attempted to refute them himself and then wished to appear constrained by manifest evidence of the facts. With the case pleaded on both sides, as though nothing had been lacking in the trial, their father would be roused all the more against his sons as men convicted. For nothing lent greater credibility to the assertions than that Antipater was thought to be his brothers’ defender. Through this fraud he courted the favour of very many and inclined even his father’s mind towards himself.Compare with Bellum [I.40.2] Whatever was daily taken from his brothers’ share of their father’s affection was transferred to him. He drew away the king’s friends and relatives, and especially estranged the king’s brother Pheroras and his sister Salome from their nephews, so that they not only failed to defend them but also assailed and hated them. Alexander’s wife Glaphyra added material for hatred. With womanly insolence in her present circumstances, she had begun to exalt herself in proud disdain because she surpassed everyone in the distinction of her lineage. Thus she set herself above everyone in the royal palace as though their mistress, habitually boasting that her father and grandfather were kings, and especially that Darius Hystaspes was the summit of her maternal line. She insulted the king’s sister Salome and his wife Dosis for their low birth, which caused them grief and brought hatred upon herself. She similarly exasperated the other women joined to the king for their beauty rather than the nobility of their birth. For Herod delighted in very many women, not only according to royal custom but also by the practice of the Jews, as though with a certain licence for error: they use the figures of their ancestors as a cover for their own vices. Alexander was therefore burdened by his wife’s insolence.Compare with Bellum [I.40.3] Aristobulus too assailed his wife with the same words as Glaphyra: she was of lowly standing, could not be compared with royal offspring and was unequal to Glaphyra. It was a reproach to him that his brother enjoyed marriage to a woman of royal birth, while he himself had fallen below his birth by cohabiting with a private woman. Madman, to disturb his own bonds of kinship with abuse! Stung by these insults, Aristobulus’s wife reported them to her mother in tears. Salome in turn reported to King Herod what she had learnt through her daughter.Compare with Bellum [I.40.4] But he, thinking it better to warn his sons than destroy them, summoned them. In part he terrified them with a commander’s authority, in part he urged them with a father’s affection to love their brother and not be divided as enemies, forgiving past offences and threatening correction for future ones. Lamenting that they were assailed by many fabricated accusations, they pleaded and at the same time promised that henceforth their very deeds would lend credibility to their defence, if only their father would look at what was done and not rashly believe what he heard. For wicked informers would not be lacking so long as a credulous listener was available.Compare with Bellum [I.40.5] With these and similar words they softened their father. Although for the moment they drove away the fear that threatened them, they nevertheless increased their sorrow, seeing themselves pressed by Pheroras and Salome: the one their paternal uncle, the other their father’s sister, plotting against those whom they should have defended. For a grave fear was added by their very great influence with their brother. Except for the diadem, Herod had shared almost the whole power of the kingdom with his brother, and had bestowed no small wealth upon them both, especially Pheroras. Indeed, he put away a hundred talents each year, apart from the region situated beyond the Euphrates that multiplied his abundant revenues. He had also been appointed tetrarch by Caesar at Herod’s request and granted kinship with the king’s wife, since he had taken the queen’s sister in marriage. After her death, with the king’s elder daughter betrothed to him, he would have gained the favour of a son-in-law had he not, captive to love for a young slave woman, declined marriage to the royal girl. Exasperated by this affront, Herod gave his daughter to a man who later died in the Parthian war.Compare with Bellum [I.40.6] Nevertheless, when Pheroras was accused before him of having assailed his brother’s life with poison—a suspicion from which he had not been free even while his wife was alive—Herod willingly acquitted him after an interrogation first of very many people and finally of his friends had found him innocent of the deed of which he was accused. He also pardoned his planned flight: the confessions of his household disclosed his intention to carry off the slave woman he loved and flee to the Parthians. Alexander had breathed a little more freely while Pheroras was being assailed and Pheroras himself was assailing Salome for having promised to marry Syllaeus, Obodas’s man, who was the king of Arabia’s procurator and most hostile to Herod.Compare with Bellum [I.40.7] But when both were pardoned their offence, the storm of the household settled upon Alexander and enveloped him in grave danger. For Antipater, the savage plague and tempest of the whole palace, raged, bearing down upon his brother by every means and even through the concerted action of his relatives. His father’s sober state of mind was so disturbed that he loudly declared Alexander was standing over him with a sword. A scene of this kind had been brought forward: Alexander had enticed three eunuchs with more lavish gifts into his favour and participation in a shameful deed. One of them habitually served the king’s drinks, another brought in the dishes at dinner, and the third watched over the royal bed and never went away once Herod had lain down. When this was revealed, the eunuchs were compelled by torture to disclose the degrading acts of obscene lust. Unable to conceal the amorous promises either, they disclosed the words with which they had been solicited and the reward for illicit intercourse, so that a plan to murder his father might be believed beneath the disgrace. Through the charm of youth he possessed beauty of form and the strength of his years, whereas Herod was weak and already burdened by old age, dyeing his hair lest he reveal his years. Alexander could transfer the right to reign from Herod to himself whenever he wished. He promised immense rewards, and so they should place their hope in a young man, not in a decrepit old man whose end nature itself was hastening.Compare with Bellum [I.40.8] These things moved Herod deeply, but above all the eunuchs’ disclosure that had informed him that a body of soldiers, commanders of the army and centurions were conspiring with Alexander. Indeed, he was so agitated that he thought no kind of cruelty should be passed over, trusted no one and suspected everyone. Punishments were swifter than the investigation of crimes, and the death of the accused preceded judgement. Everywhere those assailed by any suspicion were seized for punishment. False accusations raged. Many, wishing to please the king, denounced the accused; but immediately the very men who had denounced others were themselves denounced and led to the place of punishment with those they had accused. Thus Herod had grown savage towards everyone, so that anyone left alive was suspect, the king thinking himself safe only if the human race should fail. He was irreconcilable towards the accused, distrustful of friends, arrogant towards his household, pitiless towards those on trial, fearful of everything, so that he frequently changed his quarters and spent sleepless nights. Exasperated by all these things, he suddenly bound Alexander in chains, surrounded him with guards and summoned his friends for interrogation. Those who denied the charges died under torture; those who remained silent in turn were torn with wounds to the very end of life because they confessed nothing that agreed with the suspicions. Yet some, overcome by the bitterness of the tortures and punishments, asserted that the young men had resolved to kill their father while he was intent upon hunting and to go to the city of Rome without delay, so as to evade punishment by flight. Although this was supported by no evidence, their father turned it to the consolation of his savage purpose, wishing to have just grounds for his son’s chains.Compare with Bellum [I.40.9] Alexander therefore considered that his father’s ears were barred against every defence of him, and that matters could in no way be brought to the point where Alexander could rely on his own innocence, assailed as he was by so great a mass of false accusations. He thought he should meet the most wicked informers with similar skill, deceiving the fraudulent fabricators of false accusations by cunning and arraigning on a false charge those by whose false accusations he believed himself oppressed. He therefore wrote four booklets in which he confessed the invented crime of having assailed his father’s life, and named as accomplices in plots of this kind many of those by whom he himself was assailed. In the same booklets he named Pheroras and Salome especially: she too had broken into the young man’s bedroom in the dead of night, enticed him against his will and compelled him, despite his resistance, to commit incest. He sent the booklets to the king as though disclosures of his own crimes, implicating in them all the king’s most powerful companions and friends. Archelaus arrived hastily in Judaea at the right moment to bring his son-in-law and daughter whatever help and support he could. But, foreseeing that access to a lawful defence was barred before the most hostile father, he restrained his agitation by cunning. For as soon as he entered the royal palace, already within Herod’s sight and hearing, he began shouting loudly as though beside himself with fury: “Is that sorcerer, my son-in-law, still alive, still enjoying this light? Where is he, I ask? Where shall I find that murderous creature who plotted against his father, so that I may tear him apart with my own hands? A kinsman must kill the man who wished to kill his kin. What will he do to his father-in-law if he has not spared his father? Who will point him out? I shall first tear out the scoundrel’s entrails, then add my daughter to her fine bridegroom. Even if she was not an accomplice in the crime, she is not free from its contamination, since she enjoyed marriage to a would-be murderer of his father. I do not acknowledge a daughter who failed to detect her husband’s devices and failed to show herself such a daughter-in-law to her father-in-law as to make his son subject to him. I joined her to him not to serve crime but to share marriage, so that she should show herself a coheir of favour, not a helper in crime. I am surprised at you, Herod, if that Alexander, who plotted against his father, still lives. I thought he had already paid the just penalty and should not have been put off: why should a man who has confessed to attempting his father’s murder be kept alive any longer? But perhaps this too belonged to divine providence, that the judgement of both parents should condemn the man who, in you, violated the family devotion of both. I shall not refuse to act as avenger, though I was preparing to proclaim the vengeance already exacted. Nor do I except my daughter, whom I myself betrothed in that ill-fated marriage, relying upon you as guarantor. For I entrusted her not to her husband’s character but to your faithfulness. Let her give an account of why she disregarded her guarantor and loved her husband. We must now judge them both. If you are resolute in exacting satisfaction for so great a grief, gird yourself. Father, set family devotion aside: it is indeed no task for fathers to wish for, but neither one to disregard. If family devotion softens you and nature bends you, let us exchange roles, so that I may act upon your son and you upon my child in the execution of this mutual service.”Compare with Bellum [I.40.10] Blustering in this manner, Archelaus swayed Herod and gradually softened his furious resolve, so that Herod entrusted himself to Archelaus as one who shared his suffering and his mind, and gave him the booklets Alexander had written to read. Attending to each detail, Archelaus understood that they had been piled together from grief rather than founded on truth. With deep calculation he began gradually to diminish the odium of the attempted murder of a father and to transfer responsibility for the charges to those named, especially Pheroras. Thus, when he perceived that the king was not averse to his opinion, he said: “We must consider whether the young man has perhaps been assailed before you by the plots of so many wicked men, rather than you by the young man. For what reason had he to assail your life, when you had granted him the honour of kingship and reserved for him the right to reign and the hope of succession? Why should he seek what he already had, or how could he be ungrateful for such great gifts? What else would he achieve by your death but seek his own danger, which he could not fear while you lived but would fear once you were dead, from those very men by whom, even while under his father’s protection, he dreaded the destruction of his own life? That age lies open to deceit: it is readily deceived and circumvented by the plots of fraudulent men. Old age scarcely withstands cunning, and yet often even the prudence of the old is ensnared by the devices of deceivers. Therefore, if more mature experience has often been assailed, what wonder if a less mature age could not come to its own aid when it was pressed by throngs of conspirators?” Those men, then, were the disturbers of the royal house, the inciters of the young men, the sowers of discord. They had brought the young man to despair of his safety, so that he had indulged his anger, aimed at vengeance rather than acquittal, and yielded something to his agitation.Compare with Bellum [I.40.11] With these words Herod had begun gradually to relent and soften his indignation towards Alexander, but to be moved more violently against Pheroras, since the four booklets portrayed him as the agent of every crime and architect of the whole scene. Seeing that the king had inclined his mind towards Archelaus and bestowed upon him above all others the favour of intimate friendship, Pheroras went to him, begging him to restore the king’s mind to reconciliation with him. But Archelaus said that he was entangled in very many bonds of crime, by which he was clearly proved to have plotted against the king and assailed the young man. There was no room for pardon unless, laying aside the cunning of denial, he did not hesitate to confess the charges to the brother who loved him and ask his forgiveness. Archelaus would not fail such a course with whatever efforts he could make.Compare with Bellum [I.40.12] So, changing his clothes and bathed in tears, a pitiable sight, he clung to his brother’s feet, begged pardon and confessed his wickedness. He did not deny anything of which he was accused but acknowledged it all: madness had caused so great a fall, since excessive fury of love for the woman he cherished had blazed up within him. With Pheroras thus established as both accuser and witness of his own crimes, Archelaus, as though in reward for the fabrication of an argument that would serve his own purposes, entreated Herod to soften his anger out of regard for nature and forgive his brother, setting the right of nature above vengeance. Nor was it strange if, in very great kingdoms as in great bodies, some part often became inflamed: it should be treated with gentler medicines, not cut away. His own brother too had laid much graver plots against him, but for the sake of kinship he had remitted what was owed to his grief. The more he lightened the ungrateful man’s punishment, the more he aggravated his case.Compare with Bellum [I.40.13] By adding these and similar arguments, he did indeed soften Herod into forgiving his brother, but himself remained seemingly implacable towards his son-in-law. Indeed, he threatened to tear his daughter away from him and raged with such violent indignation that Herod himself thought his son’s offence against him sufficiently expiated. He begged the avenger of his injuries and himself intervened for his own accused son before his father-in-law, asking him to renew the marriage afresh. Archelaus persisted: Herod could join his daughter-in-law to anyone else he wished except Alexander, on whose account even his wife was discredited. By this device he impelled Herod much further, so that he thought his son would be restored to him if his marriage were not dissolved. Alexander dearly loved his wife, by whom he had also had children, sweet to their grandfather and dear to their parents. This would be the gift of a son restored to him, since to no small extent a good wife restrained her husband’s errors or compensated by her attentiveness for the odium of his crimes. If she were torn away from him, her husband would have no remedy to keep him from rushing headlong into every wickedness. For criminal audacity was usually softened when checked by affection at home. At length, with difficulty, Archelaus relented, was himself reconciled to his son-in-law and reconciled his father to him. By this design he rescued his son-in-law from death, receiving his acquittal as a reward while pretending to condemn rather than intervene. Had he thought to plead for him, he would undoubtedly have obtained nothing. Archelaus added that Alexander ought to go to Rome to clear himself of what his father had suspected in him, since Archelaus himself had written everything to Caesar. I think this too was contrived, so that in this way, when Alexander had cleared himself, he might be commended to Caesar and the plots Antipater had prepared against his brothers might be exposed.Compare with Bellum [I.41.1] By this design the faction was dissolved and there was a change to joy. A banquet was renewed as a sign of the reconciliation achieved. Archelaus, its author, was presented with seventy talents, a golden seat adorned with gems and chosen eunuchs, with royal magnificence. A concubine named Pannychis was also given and accepted as a gift. At the king’s prompting, his relatives likewise bestowed most splendid gifts upon Archelaus. Nor did any of his companions go without a gift: Herod bestowed very much upon all these men of his, according to each man’s deserts. As Archelaus returned to his kingdom, Herod also accompanied him with his powerful men as far as the most splendid city in Syria, named Antioch.Compare with Bellum [I.41.2] Alexander would have escaped had a man far more practised in devices than Archelaus not thrust himself into Judaea: a Laconian by birth named Eurycles, excessively greedy for wealth yet ready to disdain it as business required whenever the hope of gaining more shone forth. Indeed, not content with the resources of Laconia, he had set his mind on royal lavishness. Skilled in the hunt, he approached Herod with rich gifts, preparing the way for the most ample repayment. Although he obtained far more than he had offered, he was still not satisfied unless he became bloodstained and bought the king’s favour through impious intrigues. Thus, in a manner and practice familiar to Greeks, by flattering the king and praising everything about him—not only what had no claim to praise but even what was entangled in vice—he soon attained his most intimate friendship, so as to be chosen among the foremost confidants of his secrets. The privilege of his homeland also supported him, since the Jews regard the Spartans as brothers, joined to them by kinship of descent.Compare with Bellum [I.41.3] Once he knew the vices of the royal house, the father’s suspicious mind and the brothers’ hatred of one another, he used novel devices to pretend he was dear to everyone and was regarded as faithful to each. But he shaped his efforts according to the king’s disposition or the value of gifts, so as to be more closely attached to Antipater and circumvent Alexander by cunning and plots. With a show of friendship he exasperated both: the kingdom was owed to the one by the privilege of age, while the other, endowed with the nobility of his maternal line, was rightly superior and had no equal partnership with the offspring of the vilest debauchery. Captivated by these words as a younger man, delighting in what was said to him without weighing what in turn was being fabricated about him before Antipater, Alexander poured himself out to Antipater’s hireling and his own betrayer. With an unsteady disposition and incautious affection, he opened his mind, complaining that his father was the author of his troubles. He had taken his mother from him and dishonoured the kingdom, which he wished to divert from Alexander although it was owed to him through his grandfather and the distinctions of his ancient lineage. The legitimate sons were being defrauded of their right of succession, and a bastard preferred as the reward for illicit intercourse. But God’s judgements would not long remain still: the man who had killed an innocent wife would himself soon be deprived of the rule he had gained through his wife. The Laconian conveyed these things to Antipater without delay, having also deceived Aristobulus into being caught in the snares of the same complaint. For a price, he brought them before the king in an accumulated heap, saying that he could not keep silent about so monstrous a deed and that, in return for the gift of hospitality, he was repaying the benefit of the light of life, which the sons were proceeding to take away. Had he himself not called them back by pretending to offer more faithful counsel, their father would long since have been killed by Alexander’s sword and the kingdom left vacant for unworthy heirs. Nor did Alexander feel a religious scruple about the atrocity of killing his father, since he considered it the greatest crime that they still held their grandfather’s and mother’s deaths unavenged. The complaints of the slain confronted and pressed him, demanding that they avenge so terrible a deed: funeral offerings for the slain were required of him; blood was demanded. Their succession ought not to be contaminated by his receiving the kingdom from the man who had killed their forebears. He would renew the proceedings before Caesar, not with the same reverence as before, but so that Caesar himself might learn all the king’s secrets: wealth acquired through blood and a province undermined. He would recall his grandfather from the underworld and set forth his mother’s most bitter murder, so that an outsider might be appointed successor to the kingdom.Compare with Bellum [I.41.4] Eurycles had roused the king, but Antipater, thinking little of one man’s report, also suborned other accusers against his brothers. They were to say that a conversation had taken place with Jucundus and Tyrannus, former commanders of the cavalry, and that plots had been laid against the king out of grief at their removal: danger was at his neck unless he took precautions quickly. Herod did not delay: he had them seized at once and interrogated them severely, but they were found to have confessed nothing of the charges. Since such grave things could be fabricated with impunity before a man who professed himself an avenger of crimes but disregarded false accusations, there was no lack of people to devise plots of this kind, believing they would be more acceptable to the father. For a letter was also produced as though sent by Alexander and Aristobulus to the commander of a fortress, asking him to allow them to take refuge there after the king had been killed, until they could defend themselves with arms against their pursuers and prepare protection with other resources. The fortress commander was tortured and confessed nothing.Compare with Bellum [I.41.5] Nevertheless, although no evidence of the intended crime existed, Alexander and Aristobulus were placed in custody as though guilty. Eurycles was rewarded with fifty talents and regarded as the author of the king’s safety and life.Compare with Bellum [I.41.6] It is fitting not to pass over the Coan either. He had crossed to Judaea in Eurycles’s time and was one of Alexander’s most faithful friends. Thinking that he knew of Alexander’s attempts, the king considered that he should be questioned about whether what the Spartan had disclosed about the young men agreed with the truth. But, pledging an oath, he gave assurance that he knew nothing of the kind about them; yet it did the young men no good. Herod put an end to the questioning, lest the man, if questioned more severely, diminish the odium of the denunciation and undo Eurycles’s deceit by denying it. Thus he was excluded by Herod as though unworthy of belief. For the good father gladly heard his sons accused but did not allow them to be defended; he delighted when they were assailed and took offence when they were cleared. The Spartan, however, enriched by royal rewards, paid the price of his false accusations once he reached Achaea.Compare with Bellum [I.41.7] Salome could not clear herself of having agreed to marry Syllaeus the Arab. But when she betrayed her son-in-law’s confidential warning to look to her own safety and escape her brother’s agitation, since she was being accused on suspicion of reporting the king’s plans to the Arab in the hope of their future union, she obtained pardon for her offence and turned the entire storm of royal savagery upon the young men. Submerged in that final and inescapable shipwreck, they paid the penalty. They were therefore bound, and, what was harder for them than chains, the brothers were separated from one another. Volumnius, master of the soldiers, and Olympus, a man among the king’s friends, were sent to accuse them before Caesar. Although offended that a father sought the punishment of his sons, Caesar nevertheless thought a father should not be denied authority over his children and granted him licence. But he added advice: it would be better to assemble a council of the king’s relatives and the provincial governors, and for the inquiry to proceed by their common judgement as to whether the sons had laid any plots against their father. If they were proved to have attempted their father’s murder, they should be put to death; but if accused of flight or lighter offences, the punishment should be more moderate.Compare with Bellum [I.41.8] Granted this power to kill his own children, but on condition of a trial and with an admonition to moderation, Herod immediately hastened to the city of Berytus, which Caesar had prescribed for holding the trial. The provincial governors assembled in accordance with the instructions sent to them by the Roman ruler Caesar. Saturninus and the legates took their seats, among them the procurator Volumnius, followed by the king’s relatives and friends, Salome and Pheroras too, and the leading men of Syria. Archelaus alone, king of Cappadocia, was excluded, charged with suspect favour towards his son-in-law, while the young men’s accusers and those who plotted against them constituted the court. But what semblance of a trial was there, when the accused were not allowed to appear for themselves and were accused in their absence? For Herod perceived that if they were merely seen, they would be acquitted, human nature being inclined to pity, especially where there was a privileged claim upon natural affection. Moreover, if Alexander were allowed any opportunity of defence, he would easily demolish the charges.Compare with Bellum [I.41.9] Thus, with them banished to a village of the Sidonians, the accusation was directed against them as though present. Their father charged them with plots laid against him; no proof was offered, no evidence of attempts. The accuser faltered, although no one contradicted him. Unsupported on every side, he gathered together kinds of insult to arouse odium, so that those who sat in judgement might consider them graver than death. But no one discussed them, no one dared examine what was alleged by a father and commanded by a king. The appearance of family devotion prejudged the case; the right of power terrified them. He asked their opinions, confident of victory, unaware that in a trial of this kind the victor was more wretched than those so bitterly condemned. Saturninus condemned the young men because nothing else was permitted, but moderated his sentence, declaring that care should be taken lest, if two of the three brothers were killed, the death of the two be attributed to the third. Timidly, indeed, but he had stated the cause: that brother was the author of his brothers’ danger. A few out of many followed him. Volumnius, however, muttered a deadly judgement, and after him everyone, weighing what the king wanted with such a man to lead them, pronounced a sentence of death, with differing feelings indeed but the same outcome. Flattery had extorted it from some, hatred instilled it in others: either they sought the king’s favour, or they wished the cruelty of a murderer of his own children to be visited with a graver punishment, since in his victory he would have won so bitter a triumph over himself. Yet no one recoiled as at an actual deed and pronounced judgement as though moved by it. For it was the semblance of a stage, not the discipline of a court, to condemn absent men, to condemn without witness or informer, solely by the privilege of nature, which was usually directed towards safety rather than danger. All Syria and all Judaea were stunned, and with minds aghast awaited the end of so great a tragedy. For, although Herod’s cruelty was known, no one could believe that he would persist to the point of killing his own children. But in him the savage force of his mind was restrained by neither sea nor land. Thus, as though celebrating a triumph, he dragged his sons from place to place, going to the illustrious city of Tyre and from there crossing by ship to Caesarea, carrying about the wretched spectacle of the murder of his own children, until some pretext could be found for their most bitter death.Compare with Bellum [I.41.10] The whole army was moved, but fear restrained their indignation. There was in the royal army a man of long service named Tiro, who had a son attached to Alexander. He was a most indulgent father and for that reason dear to his child, since family devotion has a certain universal charm and especially draws one’s own people to love. He was also more inclined in his attachment to the king’s young sons because they loved his son. Overcome by indignation beyond measure and troubled in mind, he began to cry out that justice was being oppressed, truth excluded, religion abolished, the rights of kinship confounded and natural affection overwhelmed by injustices. At last, advancing into the king’s very presence, he charged him to his face with being wretched for thinking that the most wicked men should be believed against his sons. Pheroras and Salome were chosen as counsellors: what faithfulness could come from those who knew that they had very often been condemned to death by the king? What else were they doing but looking to vengeance, so that, bereft of suitable successors, he would incline towards the one weaker than the others, who could easily be removed? The royal army itself would pursue with hatred the man to whom the death of his two brothers had been paid. There was no one untouched by pity for innocent youth. Moreover, many of the commanders were no longer restraining their indignation but making it known.Compare with Bellum [I.41.11] After giving their names, he finished speaking. They were immediately seized with Tiro. Tryphon, one of the servants of the royal palace, who possessed the skill and practice of a barber, suddenly made a disclosure against himself through some foolish impulse. He asserted that Tiro had devised a plan and persuaded him to press his razor into Herod’s throat until he killed him while shaving his beard as usual. It would bring him a very great reward, which Tiro promised from Alexander’s gifts. Tiro was brought forward with his son, and the informer was interrogated at the same time. They denied the charge, while the informer offered nothing further. Since there was no manifest assurance of the facts, no supporting argument and no indication to serve as proof, Tiro was ordered to be tortured more violently. Then his son, pitying his father’s sufferings, promised to disclose everything if his father’s safety were granted him. When the king promised pardon, he declared that his father had prepared the king’s murder at Alexander’s instigation. Many thought this had been contrived for the occasion to save Tiro through such a disclosure by his child; others said it had been given as the truth. But Herod adjudged the doubtful as certain, as though afraid that the opportunity to murder his own children might escape him.Compare with Bellum [I.41.12] He therefore summoned the people and assembled the commanders, poured forth his complaint about the plots discovered with the gravest agitation, and roused the populace to kill them. There Tiro, his son and the barber were killed with stones and clubs.Compare with Bellum [I.42.1] Alexander and Aristobulus too were sent to the city of Sebaste, which was not far from the city of Caesarea, and strangled at the king’s command. Such was the end of Mariamne’s sons.Compare with Bellum [I.42.2] Antipater did not rejoice long in their death. With them removed, he flattered himself that his succession was beyond doubt; but the grave hatred of the whole nation soon blazed against him, since it was plain to everyone that his brothers had fallen through his intrigue. No small fear also followed as he considered how numerous the offspring of the slain grew day by day. Alexander had left his sons Tigranes and Alexander, born to him by Glaphyra; Aristobulus was survived by Herod, Agrippa and Aristobulus, born of Berenice, Salome’s daughter. Herodias too survived, and Mariamne’s daughters, whom their sex would not hinder and desire for the kingdom would stir. Terrified by these things, Antipater placed his hope in fraud and cunning and tried to bind each man to himself more and more with gifts and presents, even attempting to buy the favour of Caesar’s friends and household. But, on the contrary, even affairs at home turned against him. For, with the passage of time, the king gradually softened towards his grandchildren born to Alexander and Aristobulus and displayed remorse for his deed, pitying those whose parents he had killed.Compare with Bellum [I.42.3] Indeed, one day he gathered his friends and relatives and, his face bathed in tears, said to them: “I see my years advancing, and I cannot look without tears upon these little ones, the offspring of unhappy fathers, whose grief I have caused. Let me not leave them in a worse condition than that in which I took away their parents. Some affliction robbed me of their fathers, but nature and pity commend these children to me more and more: the one because they are my grandchildren, the other because they are bereft of their parents. My sons may have wronged their father: what have my grandchildren done to their grandfather? I have been an unhappy enough father; I ought to be a more attentive grandfather. I shall try to provide for my grandchildren after my death. If only I had also provided for myself in my sons! But the deceit of our common enemy and adversary may have crept upon them. We must take care that their perils do not involve these children too, and that I have not at one stroke both lost my sons and struck down my grandchildren. Let us provide defenders for those from whom we took them away. I shall therefore betroth your daughter, Pheroras, to the elder of Alexander’s sons, and appoint you as his father; and Aristobulus’s daughter to your son, Antipater, so that in this way you may become a father to the orphan girl. Her sister too shall marry my Herod, born to me by Mariamme, Hyrcanus’s daughter. This,” he said, “is my decision: that the successive generations of my posterity should be joined to one another by marriage, so that none may be suspect to another and I myself may look upon my grandchildren with more tranquil eyes than I looked upon their parents.”Compare with Bellum [I.42.4] With these words he joined the right hands of those mentioned and, kissing each, burst into tears. While the others rejoiced, Antipater took this so hard that he immediately betrayed his grief even in his face. No small anxiety gripped him as he saw that Alexander’s sons had stronger support than the others, backed as they were by King Archelaus and Pheroras, who held the tetrarchy. He perceived that hatred of himself was growing, while pity supported the grandchildren.Compare with Bellum [I.42.5] Nor could he receive Aristobulus’s daughter into his house, lest the continual sight of her, evidence of his crime, offend him. He did not dare approach his father, lest he provoke a man susceptible to every suspicion by suggesting that the bonds of the agreed marriages should be dissolved. Yet he subtly ventured to beg his father to look to his interests, so that he should not be exposed, powerless, with the bare name of kingship, against the resources of two powerful men, a king and a tetrarch.
