He should at least support the honour he thought fit to confer upon his son, so that the appearance of kingship should not pass to Antipater and its strength to them. Nor did he suspect only the sons of Alexander and Aristobulus: he thought everyone stood in his way who, born of Herod’s different wives, seemed even in silence to lay claim to the succession to the kingdom. They were numerous. For nine women enjoyed marriage to the king, of whom only two were childless; the others had offspring. Antipater raised up his mother Dosis, Herod his mother Mariamme. Antipas and Archelaus were the sons of Malthace, a Samaritan woman, and she also had a daughter, Olympias, who was joined to Josephus in lawful marriage. Cleopatra of Jerusalem too had borne Herod and Philip to Herod, and Pallas had borne Phasael. The king also had other daughters, Roxane and Salome, whose mothers were respectively Phaedra and Elpis. The full sisters of Alexander and Aristobulus, whom Mariamne had borne to Herod, also survived, as we mentioned above.Compare with Bellum [I.42.6] Fearing Herod’s numerous offspring, therefore, Antipater finally succeeded, though with difficulty, in having Aristobulus’s daughter joined to himself and his own son to the daughter of his paternal uncle Pheroras. At his first attempts the king had been greatly moved that he should begrudge the marriage alliances arranged for the grandchildren bereft of their father’s help. Such was his influence through flattery that he dissolved the agreed marriages.Compare with Bellum [I.42.7] Salome, by contrast, when she wished to marry Syllaeus, could not obtain this from her brother even with the support of Livia, Caesar’s wife, but was unwillingly married to a certain Alexander, one of the king’s friends.Compare with Bellum [I.42.8] With the king’s arrangements overturned, therefore, Antipater exulted in spirit as a man who had provided for himself as he wished, and surpassed everyone in cunning. Yet he could in no way suppress the hatred against him; instead he inflamed it, since he sought to secure protection for himself through terror.Compare with Bellum [I.42.9] He had attached his father’s brother Pheroras to himself as a fellow worker in his intrigues. Not long afterwards Herod expelled Pheroras from his house when he refused to be torn from his own wife, towards whom Herod was particularly hostile because of the injuries that woman had inflicted upon his wife Dosis. Pheroras, however, embraced the affront and withdrew to his own territory, over which he presided as tetrarch, firmly resolved never to return to Herod while Herod lived. Indeed, even when he learnt that Herod was afflicted by a grave illness and repeatedly begging him to come, since the king thought he had certain things to entrust to him as a dying man, Pheroras did not think him worth visiting. Although struck by this injury, when the king recovered from his illness against expectation, he nevertheless came to Pheroras with a brother’s affection on learning that he was ill. He shared his suffering attentively, and, when he died, conveyed him to Jerusalem and conducted his funeral with much weeping and splendid pomp. Yet these signs of attentive love did not dispel the opinion that he had attacked him with poison. Such was his cruelty even towards his own family. Nor was it difficult to believe that a man who had killed his sons could have killed his brother.Compare with Bellum [I.43.1] Thus one of the killers of Alexander and Aristobulus found this end to his wickedness. Beginning with him, punishment passed to Antipater, the author of the crime. For Herod was stirred by the complaints of the freedmen, who asserted that their patron had been killed with poison. In his more diligent inquiries he learnt that Pheroras had received from his wife a drink made from Arabian juices, thought to be a love potion, and that it had been poison, supplied through Syllaeus’s efforts and immediately turned to destruction. He therefore proceeded to interrogate very many people.Compare with Bellum [I.43.2] Hence one of the slave girls cried out under torture that almighty God should transfer every torment to Antipater’s mother, the director of all the crimes. Through her, Antipater and Pheroras had held secret meetings day and night and drunk to intoxication, so that on returning from the king’s banquet they drank the whole night through.Compare with Bellum [I.43.3] It was rightly suspected that this was neither idle nor free from an attempt at conspiracy, especially since the slaves and servants had been sent away. Such prolonged gatherings were a great bond of association and an indication of conspiracy, all the more suspicious to kings in the secrecy of solitude and silence of night. There it had been arranged that Antipater should go to Rome and Pheroras to Perea. They were revealed to have been accustomed to discuss this frequently with one another, because after Alexander and Aristobulus Herod would turn to killing them. Wretched men that they were to have thought Herod hated his sons’ designs against their father: he was pursuing heirs to the kingdom. Those removed were not rivals for power but partners in misery; all the danger and hatred had passed to themselves. He would not spare even women’s sex, since he had not spared his beloved Mariamne or the children born of her. They had no remedy except to withdraw somewhere further away, so as to escape the fury of so great a beast at least by flight. Frequent complaints by Antipater to his mother were added: he lamented that he burned under the odium of the royal succession, since the savagery of kingship had fallen chiefly upon himself, so that he could no longer endure it. Devoted to the most abject services, he was pressed by the utmost dangers. Not only had the right to reign been lost to him, but the course of the years of his life had also run out. He was of more mature age, his head already grey, while his father grew young again. It was vain to hope for the inheritance of a man who might perhaps be preserved long enough even to outlive him. What advantage would the succession bring him as an aged heir, when the numerous offspring of Alexander and Aristobulus sprang up before him like a hydra whose severed heads grew again? His father’s will had deprived him even of the common right: given the appearance of kingship, which he would hold temporarily as a deputy, he could appoint none of his sons to succeed to his rule but would be obliged to hand the kingdom over to Herod, Mariamme’s son. Thus he had been given the appearance of kingship to endanger him, not to benefit him, making him suspect to his predecessor and burdensome to his successor. Finally, the king himself, vigorous in his prolonged old age and intent upon slaughtering his own family, was the executor of his own will, so that no one should survive who could succeed. He was borne by grave hatred against his sons and no less against his brother: he had given Antipater a hundred talents not to speak with his uncle. Pheroras had replied: “For in what have we injured him? Am I too a successor?” Antipater was said to have answered that Herod had no grounds for offence but fabricated them himself. He was a savage beast, not sated even by deaths, who could not endure any love remaining between relatives. “If only, with everything lost, we could escape him stripped of everything but our lives! But that is impossible.” Therefore they needed secret conversations for the present. A time would come when they would employ manly vigour of mind and alertness of judgement, and the service of an avenging right hand.Compare with Bellum [I.43.4] These answers were given by slaves under torture, and Herod believed them, especially because he had spoken of the hundred talents to Antipater alone and no intermediary had been present at their conversation. Ablaze with indignation, he therefore dragged very many, including the innocent, to torture, lest any of the guilty be left behind.Compare with Bellum [I.43.5] Antipater the Samaritan was summoned for torture because he was Antipater’s procurator, and was tormented in various ways. The interrogation revealed that poison had been sent from Egypt through a certain Antiphilus, a companion, and that he had given it to Antipater’s friend Theudion, through whom it was delivered to Pheroras. The king’s son Antipater had entrusted Pheroras with carrying out the deed: while he himself was in the city of Rome, his father Herod was to be killed, so that at that time no suspicion of the murder would fall upon the absent man. But Pheroras had entrusted the poison he received to his own wife for the time being. A second accusation of poisoning thus returned against Pheroras’s wife. The king immediately ordered her to come and bring the poison. The woman went out as though to bring what was requested, and threw herself from the top of the buildings to escape the burden of the double charge and forestall disclosure of the matter and the bitterness of interrogation by her death. But since deadly vengeance for the intended murder of his father was being hastened for Antipater, she did not fall on the crown of her head, which would readily have killed her, but landed on another part of her body, so that death was postponed. Nevertheless, the woman was unconscious and stunned, since she had fallen from a high place. Herod ordered that she be given a little time to recover until she came to herself, and promised pardon if she would disclose the sequence of events plainly. It was not for nothing that she had thrown herself down: conscious of a great crime, she had sought a shorter way through punishment. If she confessed, all her crimes would go unpunished; if she denied them, torments would be heaped upon her and even burial denied.Compare with Bellum [I.43.6] When she had recovered a little, she said: “For whose sake should I still keep silent about these secrets, now that Pheroras is dead? To him I owed faithfulness in keeping silent, and for his sake I would not have refused torments had they been necessary. But he is now free from torture, and, if correction of an error may win pardon, free from guilt. What, then, compels me to wrap truth in lies? Or should I do so to comply with Antipater’s wishes? Am I to spare him and not myself? A fine reward indeed we owe the man who has brought us all to these torments through his crimes! Hear me, king, with God presiding, who alone is the judge of my truthfulness, for I have resolved to conceal nothing. Hear me, I say, but first recall how you sat weeping beside your brother in his peril and fulfilled every duty of devoted brotherhood towards Pheroras. Moved by these things, as soon as you departed he called me back to him and said: ‘Woman, I have strayed no little distance from affection and concern for my brother. I hated one who loved me so, and wished to kill one so unable to bear grief at my peril. He cannot bear a death that comes by chance, though I was pressing an undeserved death upon him. I was deceived, I confess, by Antipater’s cunning, but I shall pay the price of his design. Quickly bring the poison you have, which he left for me, and pour it out before my eyes, so that at least I may not carry a murderous intention against my kin to the underworld. Let repentance be a correction of what it was criminal to prepare. Quickly, I say, woman, so that I may at least forestall death, since I could not forestall guilt.’ Then I brought the poison and emptied it before him. Yet I kept a little of it for myself, since I feared you, so that, if it were disclosed, there would be a remedy: poison prepared for that use.”Compare with Bellum [I.43.7] With these words she produced the box containing the poison that remained. Antiphilus’s mother and his brother were subjected to interrogation. They confessed that Antiphilus had brought the box full of poison from Egypt, having received it from his brother, who was living in Alexandria as a physician. Mariamme too was discovered to have known of the plots being prepared against her husband, and this was made plain by her brothers’ confessions under torture. Hence the younger Herod paid the price of his mother’s audacity: his father, who had appointed him to follow Antipater in the succession to the kingdom, thought he should be erased from the will. This was indeed no small error on the elder Herod’s part, to punish one person for another’s discovered crime; yet the younger Herod’s punishment was not unjust either. For it seems that divine foresight provided for his exclusion from kingship, not yet as deserved by his deed but as the price of his future wickedness. For who could have endured him as king, when as tetrarch he was so insolent as to be intolerable?Compare with Bellum [I.43.8] Another kind of poison was also added, which Antipater’s freedman Bathyllus brought to Pheroras and his wife, compounded from the juices of serpents and the venom of asps, so that if the first had not proved strong enough to kill Herod, they could use the second.Compare with Bellum [I.44.1] Letters fabricated against his brothers Archelaus and Philip were also found. These were sons of the king being educated in Rome. Antipater assailed them especially because he saw that they possessed no small wisdom and that the king’s fatherly affection inclined towards them; indeed, he had summoned them by letter to return home sooner. Antipater therefore thought that they stood in the way of his interests and pressed upon his devices, so that the hope placed in the young men would overshadow all the feigned efforts of his intrigue. He therefore composed letters in the names of powerful men whom he had drawn into his friendship while in Rome, and also paid others to write that the young men were assailing their father with hostile hatred and lamenting the deaths of Alexander and Aristobulus with excessive complaint.Compare with Bellum [I.44.2] As he secretly put letters of this kind before his father through the courtiers who served his crime, he used the same cunning as before to pretend to plead for his brothers, so as to weave the impious murder of his kin beneath the pretended protection of family devotion. When all these things were brought forward, the interrogations revealed most clearly that his father’s life had been assailed, and the letters that his brothers’ deaths had been sought. It was therefore decided to exact punishment from the author, whose later false accusation had betrayed that he pursued his brothers as rivals for the lawful succession, not as would-be murderers of their father: he was not defending his father but preventing anyone from sharing his kingdom. Meanwhile, although seven months elapsed between the evidence of his crimes and Antipater’s return, no indication of events became known to him, so fiercely did everyone’s hatred burn against him. Thus, knowing nothing of it all, he wrote from the city of Rome that he would soon be there and had been dismissed by Caesar with the highest honour.Compare with Bellum [I.44.3] Herod replied to this letter that he ought to hasten back, assured of his father’s affection. Not only had it diminished in no way through his absence, but so much favour had been added that for his sake his mother’s offence would be lessened. For, after discovering her complicity in her son’s devices, he had again expelled her from his house, stripped of the gains of royal generosity. He wrote as though he would relent in his indignation towards her, fearing that Antipater, on learning of his mother’s expulsion, would grow suspicious and take precautions. On reaching Tarentum, Antipater first learnt of Pheroras’s death and there mourned greatly. Some attributed this to family devotion, thinking he could not bear the grief of his uncle’s death. But he was groaning at the loss of the agent of his attempted murder of his father. Not only had the preparation of the crime failed; the poison had also remained, and this terrified him, lest it somehow come to the king’s knowledge and Herod expose the scene of the crime. He therefore crossed to the harbour of Caesarea, by no means free from graver care and anxiety, since his mother’s expulsion gave no small prejudgement against her condemned offspring. But his friends urged him on, thinking that whatever served Antipater’s interests should take second place to their longing for their homeland. Having also observed his disposition, by which he had been accustomed readily to sway his father through his counsels even when estranged from favour towards him, they urged him to present himself all the sooner to his father and the kingdom destined for him. No one would dare oppose him when he was present; only the opportunity of his absence had smiled upon them, so that they thought the king’s mind could be turned away from him. He should therefore forestall this quickly, lest by delaying he either offend a father who longed for him or further embitter a suspicious one by betraying his own lack of confidence. Thus he believed those who advised what he wanted rather than what he needed.Compare with Bellum [I.44.4] But when he entered the harbour and looked about without seeing anyone coming to meet him, he sensed that his presence was being shunned like a plague: amid the greatest throng there was the greatest solitude. No one dared meet him, some through fear, others through aversion, for by then hatred too had gained the authority to cease concealing itself. He began to reckon his crimes within himself and to be troubled by the goads of conscience. No place of flight or means of escape remained to him; surrounded as though by nets, he was held captive. He drew all his confidence from shamelessness, concealing everything so as to present himself unexpectedly to his father, rush into his embrace and discharge the duties of family devotion.Compare with Bellum [I.44.5] But his father stretched out his hands to push him away as he pressed forward and turned his head aside lest he be touched by the kiss of a would-be murderer of his father. He exclaimed that this too belonged to the madness of such a man: “To seek an embrace when you know yourself to be hated, to fill your father with horror of you and wrench away the sweetness of life by contact with your guilty body! Do not therefore touch or taint the man you have criminally assailed. First at least clear yourself, if you can; refute what has been discovered. I shall not shun a trial or allow you to be denied a hearing, nor shall I take upon myself the examination of your case, lest I leave you an opportunity for argument. Varus is conveniently here: prepare your defence before him. There is no room for delay. Tomorrow, though endowed with cunning and fraud, you have the opportunity to clear yourself.” Stupefied by fear of so great an outburst, Antipater dared answer nothing, nor could he. He went outside and wavered in spirit, since he had learnt nothing at all of what had happened and been disclosed before the king. His mother and wife later came to him and revealed everything. On learning it, he began to collect himself and prepare in his mind the means by which he would meet the accusation and lessen the offences.Compare with Bellum [I.44.6] The next day all the relatives assembled, and Antipater’s friends were present at the examination. Everyone who had made various disclosures about Antipater was ordered to be brought in. Letters from his mother were also read, in which she had written to her son to let him know that the scene of their crimes had been betrayed to his father. He should by no means come unless some force were summoned from Caesar to surround him with its protection. Assailed by the confessions of so many, he should not entrust himself to judgement but secure himself with arms. With these things added to the earlier evidence, Antipater entered, threw himself at his father’s feet and begged him not to regard him as condemned in advance. He was confident that, if granted a hearing, he would be free of the charge, if his father wished it.Compare with Bellum [I.44.7] His father ordered him to be silent and spoke before him in this manner: “I am certain enough that Antipater’s wickedness can seem pardonable to no just man, but I think I am all the more burdened before you, Varus. For I fear that you may hate me too for having fathered sons who would murder their father, whom not even their father could spare, although in this too I deserve pity rather, because I loved them even as they were. But I shall say nothing of those whom I myself exasperated and whose just allegations against this man I rejected. For they had no grounds for grief against me except that Antipater was preferred to them and received the privilege of sharing kingship, although he had not been born into it. I thought, however, that I was taking an elder son to protect the younger ones, but I brought in an enemy who would envy the nobler, provoke the young, deceive the weak and betray the unwary. I do not deny that they fell, but they should have been excused rather than pressed. Antipater took them from me too; this man compelled them too to plot against me. I grieved, I confess, that those to whom I had given the hope of kingship and reserved the succession devised wicked things against me. But in me they hated Antipater, not their father. Thus they died to their father’s grief and Antipater’s profit. Do you ask, Varus, who killed them? Learn whom their death benefited. The house was emptied for a stepmother’s son; the palace, which had had many successors, lay open for one man to succeed. Nor were his bloodstained spirit and impious mind satisfied by his brothers’ deaths. When he no longer had brothers to hate, he pursued his father. I reflect within myself: I, who had secured his inheritance, seemed myself to live too long to a man disgusted with his predecessor. I taught him what to want. Having removed his rivals for the succession, I was not tolerated when I delayed him. He would not wait for the kingdom but must obtain it by his father’s murder. He repaid me for taking him in when he had been cast out and preferring him to men of nobler birth. For upon which of them did I confer as much as upon him? While still alive, I yielded power to him and openly designated him heir in my will, something usually ruinous to kings: that someone should know he will succeed. I granted him fifty talents in revenues, gave him three hundred when he left for Rome, commended him to Caesar as though my only son, and kept nothing for myself for which I should fear a son who would murder his father. But this armed him all the more for his father’s murder, that he saw himself superior. What crime so great had his brothers committed, whom he drove to death? What evidence of this kind was discovered against them, comparable to what is found against him? Yet the would-be murderer of his father dares interrupt and clamour, and tries to wrap the truth in cunning. Beware, Varus, I warn you, beware his feigned tears and groans artfully contrived, wrung from no grief. This is the man who robbed me of the affection of family devotion, warning me in fabricated fear to guard against Alexander. He asserted that very many minds agreed with Alexander’s and that I should not rashly entrust my presence to everyone. He pretended to look about at everything, to escort me to bed, to investigate and examine each man. This was the dispenser of my sleep, the minister of my security, in whom I placed my consolation and through whose services I lightened my grief for the slain. I thought he would restore them to me too, remove my sorrow and hold family devotion before me. This was my protector, to whom I entrusted the guarding of my aged body. I do not know how I am alive, how I escaped so great a conspirator, with what allurements he deceived me, with what frauds he held me bound, so that I trusted myself to the one man against whom alone I should have guarded. It is incredible to me that I escaped. I do not seem to myself to be alive; I think it a dream. For who would believe either that he could become so ungrateful, when I had entrusted him with every power over me, or that I could escape if Antipater were unwilling? Yet I thought favour had made me safer. But what accursed misfortune is mine, that it makes those I have loved more rise against me! I lament the affliction of my house, Varus, I weep for its solitude, I groan at the force of so great a grief. Yet such is the bitterness of the crime of murdering a father that I shall allow no one to escape me who has thirsted for my blood, even if evidence of intended murder of their father is brought forth against all my sons.”Compare with Bellum [I.44.8] As he said these things, indignation and grief together cut off his voice. Antipater immediately raised his head, for he lay at his father’s feet as though struck and pierced by a grave wound. Not thinking to rise, he said: “You indeed accuse me in anger, father, but I have no greater defence than the testimony of your accusation: I have always guarded your safety. In your desire to accuse, therefore, you have supplied a defence for me. For how am I a would-be murderer of my father when you yourself acknowledge me as your protector? Or how am I circumspect and cunning if, as you allege, I devised my father’s murder, when it is the utmost folly to have contemplated what both is execrable among human beings and cannot go unpunished before God? At least my brothers’ example could have taught me that there would be no escape from so great a crime, since a crime of this kind finds no hiding place and evades no punishment: they too paid the penalty for such great ill will towards you. But some envy, as you say, may have impelled them to murder their father, because they saw me preferred to themselves. The nobility of their maternal line gave them the spirit to claim the kingdom as owed to them by succession from their mother and demand it back as though taken from them by you. What like this was there in me, who knew only to hope for the kingdom from you, seek your judgement and please you alone? What was there to impel me to dare anything against your life? Desire for the kingdom? But I was reigning. Suspicion of hatred? But I was loved. Grief at an injury? But I was preferred. If only fear of my preferment armed them to murder their father, I am acquitted, since those preferred know to hate the murder of a father, not to contemplate it. Unless perhaps some fear of you compelled me; yet, as your voice testifies for me, I knew only to fear for you. For what should I fear for myself, who was the minister of your security and dispenser of your rest? Or did lack of money and poverty compel me, as they commonly persuade the needy to brigandage? But you had given enough to abound not only for the present but for all time, and had sent me rich to Rome, so that the kings of kings declared that pre-eminence in rule lay with them, not pre-eminence in wealth. Indeed, I won for you that Fabatus, a director of Roman affairs and an intimate of Caesar. Though Syllaeus had courted him with immense sums to attack you, I changed him so that he became your defender and the betrayer of the man soliciting him. Through whom else, father, were those plotting against your life discovered? How then am I a would-be murderer of my father, who discovered your bodyguard Corinthus in hiding, removed him as he plotted and brought him from denial to confession? I could have avoided contemplating my father’s murder and yet enjoyed its fruits, had I kept silent. But even if I had the savagery of beasts and the fury of ferocious wild creatures, I could nevertheless have been tamed by such great benefits from you, so as to place no help except in the support of your safety. For everything you gave, I could at least repay you with love alone, protect you with my body and, if it were possible, enclose you within my inmost entrails. You had preferred me, less noble in maternal descent, to sons of nobler birth; you had also recalled my mother, an exile from the kingdom, into the kingdom, and now held me as a partner in your rule rather than a successor. Wretched man that I am, upon whom your generosity poured so many good things as to kindle envy! Most foolish man that I am, to have left you, father, if an opportunity was given to envy and power to conspirators! For, while I lingered long for your safety, I betrayed my own, and yet I have nothing to impute to myself. You ordered me to depart, father. For you I was abroad, father, lest Syllaeus deceive your old age, strip you of the kingdom while you lived and assail your safety before Caesar. Rome is my witness to family devotion; Caesar too, guardian of the world, censor of all and judge of my heart, was accustomed to call me a lover of my father. Bear witness, Caesar, to what I said of my father before you, before whom alone I could have harmed him. Bear witness for me, I say, you who had pronounced upon others and thought the murder of a father should be investigated, not disregarded. If only your presence would favour me! But you are absent and far away, and without you I am condemned by my father. Yet though absent, you are present in your letters. I offer your writings, which would-be murderers of their fathers usually fear; I carry your letter, which those who wish such murder not to remain hidden usually produce. Receive Caesar’s letter, father: let the man who recently avenged you instruct you himself. Receive Caesar’s writings, stronger than every argument. You recently used them for vengeance: use them now for safety. I bring these written characters as witnesses to my innocence. That right hand never deceived you; that right hand of Caesar placed the diadem upon you, it did not take it away. That mind of Caesar restored to you the kingdom you had cast aside. Caesar could have hated me first if he had found me like my brothers, but he examined me and pronounced me an interpreter of family devotion. Had I not been in Rome, Syllaeus would have won. To him I am condemned today; to him I, wretched man, pay the penalty. Remember, father, that I did not sail willingly. I already saw the pit of the conspirators being prepared for me, yet I preferred, father, that I should be endangered rather than you. Nor do I shudder at the danger to my life, but I grieve, father, to be endangered before you as though your enemy. Yet I am endangered if even Caesar’s testimonies are endangered before you: these, then, are the proofs I use in my defence. I do not appeal to Caesar as a man awaiting a hearing, but implore him as one already acquitted. If you think a trial must be held, here I am, father: I came to you after Caesar; I hastened to you from Caesar. If only I had never gone anywhere away from you! But you, father, unknowingly exposed me to dangers by ordering me to go. I am here, father, and I do not think the truth about your safety should be sought lightly from witnesses of lower standing. Let neither those who can fear torments nor those who can despise them prejudge the case. Scripture says, ‘Every human being is a liar.’ I offer the incorruptible testimonies of the elements. I come to you over seas and lands, never having suffered anything. Had I been guilty of attempting my father’s murder, I ought not to have escaped. Let heaven, which did not strike me with lightning, acquit me before you, father; the sea, which did not drown me; the earth, which did not swallow me. Through these I come to you safe, father, although even those who are not would-be murderers of their fathers often fail to escape them. The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram in its yawning chasm, yet they had not assailed the father who begot them. The earth suspended Absalom as he fled in the branches of its tree, lest he reach his father; had he reached him, he would have escaped. I have come to you and am still endangered. David avenged the son who would have murdered him because he could not save him. I do not ask to be avenged upon my enemies and false accusers by summoning them to torture. Let them escape the penalty for false accusation. I ask one thing, father: do not trust other people’s torments; inquire from me myself against myself. Hang up your accused: let the interrogation of truth proceed into my entrails, let the cords of interrogation descend into my body and its inner chambers, let the blood flow that is accustomed to cry out against the murder of a father, let fires be brought upon the guilty limbs. Why hesitate, father? If you spare me, you pronounce me innocent; if you refrain from torture, you acquit me of the crime. A man thought worthy of a simple death is no murderer of his father. Or if you spare me as your son and pity limbs begotten from yourself, those limbs are not yours that are instruments of cruelty.” Having said this, he ended his speech with much weeping and lamentable groaning, and with the greatest wailing moved Varus and everyone to pity. Herod alone was moved by no tears and himself refrained from weeping, implacable towards pardon, pressing for interrogation and seeking vengeance.Compare with Bellum [I.45.1] At the king’s command Nicolaus followed Antipater’s speech, to answer his cunning skilfully and draw those who had been moved back from pity by turning upon Antipater the odium of his brothers’ murder. He argued that, if anyone was moved by pity, they ought to pity those who had been killed by his fraud and demanded vengeance. If they acquitted one man, the whole royal house would be brought into danger: brothers, relatives by marriage, parents, the king himself, whose life he had not spared. Turning therefore to the cunning of orators, as though in a kind of peroration he summoned from the underworld the souls of the slain to fill the court benches with their pitiful complaint: they had died innocent, weighed down by suborned witnesses, fabricated letters and fraudulent words. Their father had been deceived into trusting a son whom he did not think capable of lying about his brothers. Now this man offered himself for torture, although he had not believed his brothers’ torments; he had weighed them down with chains and bound them so that they could not attend the hearing. Sentence had been passed against absent men; they had been killed far away, lest their father pity them. No one would therefore be left if this man escaped, trained to pour poison for the murder of kin into his own kin’s entrails and change men’s minds. He had even roused Pheroras, who had always loved his brother Herod so greatly, to kill him in a deadly murder of kin.Compare with Bellum [I.45.2] Nicolaus added very many other things to these to stir emotion. When he had finished his speech, Varus asked Antipater whether he wished to reply. He answered nothing except: “God is my witness that I have done no harm.” Then Varus ordered the poison to be brought forward and given to one of those already condemned to death. He drank it and died immediately. This was reported to Caesar, and Antipater was led away in chains at his father’s command.Compare with Bellum [I.45.3] Yet he was not free from plots. For at that very time he was trying by deceit to endanger Salome. Antipater had sent letters composed in Salome’s name, full of insults against the king, and had ordered them to be conveyed through Antiphilus’s slave to Acme, the slave girl of Julia, who was Caesar’s wife, so that Acme would forward the letters delivered to her to the king. The fraud nearly succeeded in destroying the woman, but a letter from Acme to Antipater was found that exposed the deceit. It was written in this manner: “As you wished, I have written to your father and sent those letters, and I do not doubt that the king will rise to endanger his sister.Compare with Bellum [I.45.4] You, having obtained the outcome you desired, repay the service.” When these letters were intercepted, the king was led to suspect that Alexander too had been assailed by letters fabricated by his brother with the same art, and, exasperated by excessive agitation, he contracted a grave illness. Seeing himself pressed by this danger, he named one of his sons, Antipas, as heir to his rule in his will, preferring him to his elder children Archelaus and Philip, since Antipater’s deceit and falsehoods had also made them suspect to their father. He bequeathed a thousand talents to Caesar, with gifts and presents added, and allotted five hundred to Caesar’s wife and children, freedmen and friends. Nor did he leave his sister Salome without a share in his gifts.Compare with Bellum [I.45.5] The illness grew worse and became more severe with the passage of time, while the disabilities of feeble old age aggravated it daily. For he bore a body weighed down by no fewer than seventy years and afflicted also by frequent grief of mind, wounded by so many murders of kin, which it was the utmost misery either to have discovered in his sons or to have inflicted. Yet the illness burned incurably because Antipater, still alive, was feared.Compare with Bellum [I.45.6] He also became more contemptible day by day: images of Caesar and likenesses of animals placed upon the temple contrary to the law were being torn down. The chief instigators were Judas and Matthias, teachers of the young, who told those conspiring with them that the time had come to avenge the wrong done by violation of the law. The sacrilegious man was paying the penalty: he thought that whatever power permitted was right, and, not bowed by religion but exalted by pride, had exercised his desire to do whatever he wished in the temple’s inner sanctuary as though it were a right. Although divine force was hastening vengeance, it nevertheless seemed noble that those consecrated to the temple should also demonstrate their freedom by defending the observances of their ancestral rite. No one ought to be deterred by fear of danger, since even to die for the ancestral law was a mark of immortality.Compare with Bellum [I.45.7] They were the first to attempt to tear down the golden eagle fixed above the top of the gate. They were seized and brought before the king, and when asked whom they wished to obey in attempting so great a deed, they answered: “The ancestral law.” When he asked again what they trusted in, that they appeared so cheerful when summoned to the danger of death, they replied that they trusted in the rewards of devotion and dedication, the recompense for which would be paid to those who sought death for the ancestral rite.Compare with Bellum [I.45.8] He could no longer bear the firmness of the reply. Raised above his illness by indignation, so that he overcame his weakness, he went out into the assembly of the people. There, bringing them before the people as guilty of sacrilege, he began to accuse them on the grounds that graver things were suspected from such deeds. Even if these were not proved, everyone nevertheless feared for himself and pleaded that the instigators who had been seized should pay with punishment and that proceedings should not be extended to the rest, lest the interrogation trouble more people, including those uninvolved and innocent. Thus entreated, he passed sentence upon those present, that they should be burnt alive.Compare with Bellum [I.45.9] His infirmity increased from this, and the force of a graver illness consumed his whole body with various sufferings. His fever was violent, his itching intolerable; there were continual pains in his inner entrails without any interruption, and he was tormented by colic in his middle. Dropsy weighed down his feet, his private parts swarmed with worms, and spasms of the whole body, heavy breathing and deadly gasps were signs to anyone that he was being made to pay the penalty for the unjust murder of his kin and the sacrilegious sentence. Yet he did not yield in spirit, and in his desire to live struggled against his sufferings. The hot waters of Callirrhoe, which he sought across the Jordan, had done him no good. At Lake Asphaltites, healing for very many, he lay ill without any improvement. There, while he was being soothed with copious oil, his body relaxed and lost its strength; he turned up his eyes in the manner of the dying, his voice failed and he lost consciousness. But, roused by the noise of those crying out, he recovered.Compare with Bellum [I.45.10] Wishing to return to his own lands, when he reached the region of the place called Jericho he devised a monstrous deed, driven by black bile and in a manner threatening death itself, so that peoples might be sent as funeral offerings to him. For he had already ordered the nobler men to be gathered from all Judaea, so that they should assemble from each village in one place. When his command was obeyed, he ordered them to be shut inside the hippodrome. He summoned Salome and her husband Alexas and entrusted to them a legacy of blood. He asserted that his death would bring joy to the peoples of the Jewish nation, and that he had therefore devised a way for his funeral commemoration to be celebrated most splendidly. He demanded of his family that, when he had breathed his last, they should immediately order all those confined there to be killed. Thus there would be no one in all Judaea or in any house for whom his death would be unmourned, since he would have left everyone an inheritance of mourning at home. As they bewailed the murder of their own kin, they would seem to be paying the king his funeral dues, and thus the joy of public wishes would be hindered by private griefs. Lest the wicked commands fail to be carried out, he ordered fifty drachmas to be given to each soldier, so that, with such a reward for crime set before them, the soldiers would not refuse the deadly service, offsetting the horror of carrying it out with the gain of the reward.Compare with Bellum [I.45.11] He was already almost yielding to the torments of so great an infirmity, but he awaited the replies brought by the deadly embassy. It reported that Acme had been put to death in response to Herod’s complaint, and that Antipater too had been convicted of attempting his father’s murder and condemned to death. Yet, if his father wished to grant him the opportunity to flee, expelled from his homeland and kingdom, Caesar would give the order, passing sentence upon the crime but leaving the decision to family devotion. Nature had removed the necessity of killing kin. For, briefly revived by the power granted him to act as he wished, while he considered the manner of death, he was racked by pains and had desired to forestall the day of his own death. He therefore asked for an apple and a sword together, to take some refreshment by cutting the fruit with it as he was accustomed to do. Raising himself a little and leaning upon his elbow, he lifted his right hand, wishing to strike himself. But Achiabus rushed up and prevented the blow. The whole house rang with mourning, so that outside it was thought that Herod had died. Antipater exulted at the sound of lamentation and asked the guards to release him from his chains. But the man in charge of that duty not only refused the request but also reported it to the king. Exclaiming that he was being mocked while still alive, Herod sent assassins to kill Antipater and ordered him to be buried in Hyrcania after his death. He changed his will again and appointed Archelaus, the elder of the brothers, king, leaving Antipas as tetrarch.Compare with Bellum [I.45.12] Thus he survived Antipater by five days and died, having held the kingdom for thirty-seven years from the time when the Romans ordered him to rule. From the time when he removed Antigonus, his rival for the kingdom, he spent thirty-four years in power. If only he had been as happy in life at home as in his public successes! For abroad prosperity favoured him so much that he was raised from private station to kingship and, after enjoying it for a great many years, died with his power intact, a difficult thing, leaving his children a succession to rule that he himself had not received from his own family. But within his house he was most unhappy and filled it with the bitter bloodshed and mourning of his own family. Yet he found no one to carry out his final cruelty. In this one act Salome effaced the disgrace of her earlier crimes: she released all those whom the king had ordered to be killed, saying that the king had afterwards repented of the deadly command, revoked his earlier instructions and ordered that they should all be sent home.Compare with Bellum [I.46.1] Then, after the soldiers and the rest of the people had assembled in the amphitheatre, the king’s death was announced. Ptolemy came forward, a man who had remained one of the king’s most faithful friends to the very end. Bearing the ring he had drawn from the dead man’s finger, he praised the king and urged the people to remain calm. He opened a letter in which the king appealed to the soldiers most faithful to him and exhorted them to show goodwill and favour to his successor. The tablets of the will were also opened and read: Philip was named heir to the region of Trachonitis and neighbouring places, Antipas tetrarch, and Archelaus king, on condition, however, that his ring should be conveyed to Caesar and that the judgement and confirmation of all his arrangements should be reserved to him. His will was to be valid only if Caesar approved it. He ordered the remaining provisions to be observed according to his earlier wills.Compare with Bellum [I.46.2] At once the soldiers acclaimed and applauded Archelaus. He was immediately surrounded by a ring of guards; they promised goodwill and pledged allegiance. After this the funeral was fittingly and magnificently arranged, with the whole display of royal wealth sent ahead and the splendour of a funeral procession. The bier was adorned entirely with gold and gems, its covering shone with purple dye, and the body was covered by a double purple robe fastened with a clasp glittering with precious stones. A diadem clung to his head with a golden crown above it, and a sceptre was in his right hand, so that one might think him alive. A band of Thracians went before him, and the Germans and Gauls, the royal guards, kept military order. Armed alike as though going out to war, they followed with sorrowful faces, as if grieving. The rest of the force went ahead in their usual equipment and accustomed dress, their commanders and centurions accompanying them. Fifty slaves and freedmen of the royal household also sprinkled spices, so that the whole road was fragrant with a sweet scent. The king’s sons and a very great crowd of relatives surrounded the bier. He was buried in Herodium, as he himself had commanded, two hundred stades from the place where his life had ended. Over so great a distance everyone escorted him with great ceremony, but not with equal affection from all. For fear had wrung out duty, not willing service; grief at least kept its judgement free within itself. Such was Herod’s end.Compare with Bellum

PROLOGVS [Prol.1] Quattuor libros Regnorum quos scriptura complexa est sacra, etiam ipse stilo persecutus usque ad captiuitatem Iudaeorum murique excidium et Babylonis triumphos historiae in morem composui. Macchabaeorum quoque res gestas propheticus sermo paucis absoluit; reliquorum usque ad incendium templi et manubias Titi Caesaris relator egregius historico stilo Iosephus, utinam tam religioni et ueritati attentus quam rerum indagini et sermonum sobrietati. Consortem se enim perfidiae Iudaeorum etiam in ipso sermone exhibuit, quem de eorum supplicio manifestauit, et quorum arma deseruit eorum tamen sacrilegia non dereliquit: deplorauit flebiliter aerumnam, sed ipsius causam aerumnae non intellexit. [Prol.2] Vnde nobis curae fuit non ingenii ope fretis sed fidei intentione in historia Iudaeorum ultra scripturae seriem sacrae paulisper introrsum pergere, ut, tamquam in spinis rosam quaerentes, inter saeua impiorum facinora, quae digno impietatis pretio soluta sunt, eruamus aliqua uel de reuerentia sacrae legis uel de sanctae constitutionis miraculo, quae malis licet heredibus uel in aduersis obtentui fuerint uel honori in prosperis; simul, quod est indicium domesticae improbitatis, liqueat uniuersis quod ipsi sibi propriae cladis auctores fuere, primum quod alia curantes Romanos in se conuerterint et ad cognitionem regni sui inuitauerint, quibus ignorari satius fuit, rogauerint amicitiam fidem non seruaturi, pacem uiolauerint uirtute impares, postremo bellum intulerint quibus spes omnis in moenibus non in uiribus erat, cum sit omnium miserabile claudi obsidione, quae etiam si bene procedit, augere saepius quam minuere pericula solet. [Prol.3] Ac ne quis uacuum fidei et superfluum putet nos suscepisse negotium, ideo per principes ductum Hebraeorum genus omne consideremus, ut liquido clareat, utrum a femoribus Iudae nusquam generationis eius successio claudicauerit, an uero offenderit in principum serie, sed manserit in eo cui reposita manebant omnia et ipse erat spes gentium. Hinc igitur sumam exordium. LIBER PRIMVS [I.1.1] Bello Parthico, quod inter Macchabaeos duces gentemque Medorum diuturnum ac frequens uariaque uictoria fuit, incentiuum dedit sacrilegii dolor, quia rex Antiochus cui nomen Illustris, Antiochi regis filius, ubi Aegyptum quoque suo imperio adiunxit, in superbiam elatus, quod ei incerta bellorum prosperauissent, ritus Hebraeorum neglegi mysteriaque eorum profanari iusserat, idque postulantibus plerisque Iudaeis statuere ausus. Compare with Bellum [I.1.2] Quod factum Matthathias sacerdos perpeti nequiuit, nec solum ipse temperauit a sacrilegio regalique edicto non obtemperauit, uerum etiam immolantem simulacris hostias de popularibus suis nanctus gladio transuerberauit. Et congregata manu atque Asidaeis in societatem adscitis ipse cum filiis suis temerantes usum patrium et iustitias legis alios necauit, plerosque expulit bellique sabbato adoriendi auctor fuit, ne simili arte ipsi quoque deciperentur, sicut iam plerique eorum, dum sabbato bellum suscipere detrectant, inruentibus in se hostibus inulti occubuere. Potentiam prosperi actus dederunt, et perseuerauit in uiro usque ad exitum uitae studium defensionis et pietatis uigor. Sed cum sibi supremum diem adesse intellegeret, uocatis ciuibus atque adsistentibus liberis hortatus est, ut tuerentur patriam templique religionem, ducemque his Iudam Macchabaeum curae ac sollicitudinis suae successorem reliquit. Compare with Bellum [I.1.3] Qui bello strenuus, consilio bonus ac prae ceteris fide promtus quam frequenter innumeras hostium copias parua manu fuderit, persequi non est negotii praesentis. Quod tamen breui colligere datur, saepe prosperis usus successibus excitauit in se magnam hostium multitudinem, qua circumfusus undique, dum cedere pudori existimat, refugientibus sociis in proelium ruit. Caesisque quos aduersum ierat, a latere circumuentus sed tamen ultus propriam mortem occiditur. Compare with Bellum [I.1.4] Huic successit Ionatha non minus uirtutis similitudine par quam naturae germanitate. Qui post multa in bellicis rebus opera, in rebus sacris officia, quae circa templi purificationem spectata ac probata sunt, praetenta per dolum amicitiae fide intra urbem hostium clausus nec longo post interuallo necatus est. Iohannes etiam senior natu frater et Eleazar iunior ceteris pro religione mortem non recusarunt. Compare with Bellum [I.1.5] Post hos rei summam Simon recepit, ad quam non rudis sed iam probatus fraternae societatis triumphis adpropinquauit, utinam et ipse tam perspicax ad fraudes cauendas quam manu ualidus bellandique artibus satis spectatus. Etenim cum uirtutis ope Romanorum ducibus regibusque gentium amicitiam foederauisset, Ptolomaei dolo generi sui rogatus ad conuiuium inter mensas et pocula cum duobus filiis qui aderant circumuentus atque exutus armis impiae neci traditur. Compare with Bellum [I.1.6] Sane praeuenit insidias Iohannes ortus ex Simone cui nomen Hyrcanus et properauit ad uicinae urbis moenia, ubi a populo propter egregia patris merita, odio quoque hostilis sceleris expectabatur. Vix denique ingressus urbem est, et iam Ptolomaeus aderat. Sed cum per aliam portam ingredi uellet, repulsus multitudini cedendum existimauit. Adsumsit ilico Ionathes paterni sacerdotii munus et a cultu rerum diuinarum profectus statim pietatis officia curamque seruandae necessitudinis exsequebatur, matrem cupiens fratresque periculo auferre. Compare with Bellum [I.1.7] Congressuque superior factus iustae passionis adfectu superabatur, quominus castro potiretur, in quo clausi adtinebantur. Nam Ptolomaeus ubi se urgueri uidebat, matrem eius atque germanos in muris locabat praecipitandos ilico, nisi Ionathes bello quod inferebat desisteret. Vincebatur iuuenis pietatis metu, qui uincebat fortitudinis adsumtione, et iracundiam excitatam in hostem reuocabat suorum misericordia. Mater tamen parata ad tormenta tendebat manus obsecrans non salutis auxilium sed ultionis solatium. Verebatur enim ne filius plus matri metueret quam paternae uindictae impenderet. Sibi mortem illam loco immortalitatis futuram, qua maritus uindicaretur et gener impius pro scelere immani poenam exsolueret. Sed iuuenis plus intra ipsum se quam in hostem proeliabatur; nam quotiens patrem cogitabat, accendebatur, rursus cum matrem uerberari atque ad necem aptari uideret, molliebatur. Reuocabat impetum, referebat gradum, quia retrahebat passio. Inter obsidionis moras feriatus ex lege superuenit annus qui erat septimus. Cessit pietas religioni, soluta obsidio. Sed eo magis Ptolomaei excitata immanitas, ut quorum obiectu pestem euaserat eos iugulari iuberet. Qui continuo se ultioni exemit ad Zenonem, cui nomen Cotylae, Philadelfiae regem confugiens, ut eius ope sese tueretur. Compare with Bellum [I.1.8] Nec Antiochus quieuit qui Simoni patri Ionathae ludibrio suos fuisse exercitus indignabatur, cupiensque adsurgentes adhuc Ionathae primitias extinguere, cum magna ueniens manu, Hierosolyma Hyrcanumque obsedit. Reppulit Hyrcanus auro, quem ferro nequibat, reseratoque, ut Iosephus auctor est, Dauid sepulchro tria milia auri talenta eruit, ex quibus trecenta adnumerauit Antiocho, ut obsidionem relinqueret, pretio emtus abiret. Atque ut facti inuidiam leuaret, fertur ea pecunia Hyrcanus instituisse primus xenodochia, quibus aduentum susciperet pauperum peregrinorum. Compare with Bellum [I.1.9] Aucupatus etiam Antiochi necessitatem, qua Medis bellum inferebat, ultus dispendium plurimasque urbes Syriae sibi adiunxit. Samariam quoque, ubi postea Sebastia condita est, circumdedit munitionibus, cuius expugnationem Aristobolo et Antigono filiis suis mandauit, quorum lenta obsidio usque ad diram famem et tetra alimenta humanorum cadauerum clausos coegit. Qua impulsi necessitate opem ab Antiocho, cui nomen Aspondius, petendam arbitrati ferentem adiumenta aerumnae societate implicauere. Victus enim a fratribus proelio fuga sese eripuit neci. Samaritani autem repentina obsidione captaque et euersa urbe seruitio dati. Quo rerum secundarum processu exciti Aristobolus atque Antigonus impetum non refrigebant, sed adiungere sibi finitimos bello coactos hautquaquam dissimulandum arbitrabantur : donec inuidia oborta bellum immane exarsit conspirantibus locorum incolis et coacta ualida manu. Quae tamen uicta profundam in reliquum tranquillitatem Iohanni exhibuit et sibi otium. Compare with Bellum [I.1.10] Hyrcanus trigesimo et primo anno longae quietis gratia functus diem clausit quinque liberis superstitibus, quod a plerisque beatitudini datur. Moderator egregius et pulchre sobrius, qui nihil umquam uel fortuitis euentibus dereliquerit, in quo actus eius offuscaretur, uxori summae rei commisit negotia, ipsam consultius ratus rebus publicis moderaturam, filios praescientia quadam animi tenens non diuturnos fore. Compare with Bellum [I.2.1] Nec fefellit opinio, siquidem Aristobolus, cui inter fratres aetas prouectior, mens praeruptior, principatum sacerdotii ad regni potentiam uertit et diadema primus imponere sibi usurpauit post quadringentos septuaginta quinque annos triumque curricula mensuum, ex quo de Babylone remeans Israhel seruitio exutus in suam terram sese recepit. Superbe itaque nec partem ponere ceteris contentus fratribus solum Antigonum honoris specie, quia uidebatur diligere, mulcebat; matrem, quia potestatis exsortem et iudicio uiri fraudatam se expostulauerat, alligauit uinculis et usque eo processit immanitatis parricidali spiritu ferox, ut et ipsam et fratres suos simili modo uinctos arta custodia detineret, quo prope usque ad mortem supremam fame compellerentur, ni maturius Aristobolus scelesti parricidii merita soluisset. Ac primum in ipsum Antigonum ferus animus exasperatur et de amore in odia conuertitur, ut eum ante omnes necaret, quem solum sibi consortem imperii pollicebatur. Adeo apud improbos affectus uilis, ut cito prauis suggestionibus extorqueatur. Compare with Bellum [I.3.1] Dignum igitur ut crudelitatis eius seriem non praetereamus, quo iudicium Iohannis etiam post mortem probetur, qui summam publicae rei committendam seniori filio hautquaquam existimauerit, quem tanto declinaturum furore a pietatis lege et norma iustitiae praeuidebat, haut scio morumne eius contuitu an insita gratia sacerdotum principibus, ut his aliqua quae futura erant etiam minus dignis infunderentur. Facinus miserabile, fuisse qui fratribus inuiderent amorem naturae. Inde mali prima oborta est labes, inuidiam commenta secuta huiusmodi sunt. [I.4.1] Composuerant primo alia, quibus fidem Aristobolus non detulit, et obtrectationem molliuit caritatis gratia inuidiae tribuens delationis amaritudinem. Ideo falsa ueris admiscuere, ut ex his quae ad speciem ueri adsumserant renitentem circumuenirent. Compare with Bellum [I.5.1] Scenopegia Iudaeorum in terris ex lege celebrabantur, dies uidelicet festus et plenus reuerentiae, quo sacrificium sollemne deferebatur. Eo die clarus militiae gestis Antigonus domum reuertit et accidit ut fratrem adueniens inaequalem offenderet. Ilico ad templum — quid enim praeferret religioni? — ut erat succinctus ornatu bellico et circumfusus comitatu pari tendit, multus ibi pro fratris salute domini precator, et inde ad fratrem sedulus properat. Hinc calumnia componitur acerbo felle et acerbiore paratur exitu. Compare with Bellum [I.6.1] Continuo enim regem adeunt improbissimi homines et inuidiam excitant, quod pompam armatorum celebratiorem quam priuatis mos est direxerit ostentui uulgo futuram, ne quis conatibus eius obuiare auderet; tanto adparatu non aliud nisi necem regis et usurpandi imperii potentiam affectatam. Haut difficile aeger animus inualido fessus corpore impulsus est, ut credibile duceret quod pro uero adserebatur, maxime cum dies sacratus religioni mendacii suspicionem excluderet, pompa excitaret inuidiam, infirmitas metum adderet armatorumque cohors fidem patrandi sceleris impleret. Compare with Bellum [I.6.2] Itaque priusquam sibi probaretur temtamentum aliquod flagitii parricidalis, stipatores suos cum armis iubet in hypogeo obscuro locari, qui aduenientem Antigonum deloricarent, nec expectarent imperium regis sed ipsi extinguerent, sane mandato per nuntios praemisso ut inermis ueniret. Eius indicii qualitatem nupta Aristobolo in aduersum mutauit, ut per illos coniuratos sibi insinuari faceret Antigono, fratrem eius delectatum esse armorum decore, quibus proxime accinctus adfuerat, sed per aegritudinem intentius non considerasse, nunc petere ut omnem illum ornatum bellicum quem sibi composuit ad fratrem deferat; gratum hoc regi futurum si armatus adesset. Compare with Bellum [I.6.3] Antigonus dolum non praeuidit, dicto paruit eo studiosius quo placere regi pariter et fratri desiderabat. Decumbebat Aristobolus in castro, cui nomen primo Baris, postea Antonia fuit, ab Antonio uidelicet triumuiro donata appellatione cum urbis dignitate. Eo postquam Antigonus appropinquauit atque accessit ad illum obscurum transitum, conspicientes armatum uenisse regii stipatores adorsi repente iuuenem praecepto satisfaciunt atque imprudentem opprimunt. Compare with Bellum [I.6.4] Is locus Stratonis turris appellabatur, quo deceptum uocabulo Iudam qui erat Essaeus genere opinio est frequens, quem siue probitate uitae siue mystica obseruatione saepe quae futura erant adnuntiasse historia uetus prodidit. Compare with Bellum [I.7.1] Is, ut accepimus, cum uidisset Antigonum praetereuntem ut fratrem reuiseret, dicit ad eos qui numero discipulorum eius adnectebantur: ‘Papae, nunc mihi bonum est mori, quando mihi mortua ueritas est. Viuit Antigonus quem necesse est hodie interfici, locus autem eius neci decretus Stratonis turris qui sexcentis hinc stadiis abest. Hora iam diei quarta est. Tempore itaque excluditur praedestinatae mortis fides.’ Haec ubi dixit, intentius secum ipse conferre coepit quomodo fefellisset opinio. Nec multo post indicium defertur, interfectum esse Antigonum in hypogeo ad Stratonis turrem, qui locus simili uocabulo aeque ut ille qui erat in maritimis Caesareae nuncupari solebat. Compare with Bellum [I.7.2] Quo facinore patrato Aristobolus secum ipse reputans quid sceleris admiserit in morbum incidit. Erat in oculis parricidium, perturbatio in animo, nec ullum interuallum dissimulationi dabat. Defigebatur imis uisceribus dolor, inuidia in miserationem uersa est, quod innocentem peremisset contra ius germanitatis; tanti sceleris immanitas mentem exulcerabat, non somnus oculis, non animo requies dabatur. Serpebat caeco uulnus dolore, coquebant aegra praecordia curae ac sollicitudines, sauciabant inualidos artus et crebro gemitu pulsabant alta nimis suspiria. Compare with Bellum [I.8.1] Itaque immoderata maestitudine eo prorupit morbi uis, ut conuulsis uisceribus sanguinem uomitu oris reiecerit. Quem puer aulicus regiis usibus exhibens ministerium foras extulit atque imprudens facti, quod casu potius quam industria gerebatur, ad eum locum peruenit, in quo Antigonus fuerat extinctus. Illic supra rorantes adhuc fraterni sanguinis maculas percussoris sanguinem effudit. Clamor subito factus et gemitus intuentium eo, quod profunda quadam dispositione domini libatus peremto scelestissimi parricidae sanguis uideretur. Sono excitus causam quaesiuit; cum sileretur, elicuit studio quaerendi et motu indignationis. Cuius accepto indicio suffusus oculos lacrimis et quantum erat in eo uirtutis ingemescens ait: ‘Rependitur meritis meis congrua uicissitudo. Neque enim dei oculum tam impii machinator sceleris praeterire poteram. Matura flagitio ultio subest et digno iam conuenior parricidii mei pretio. Vale, corpus. Quousque animam fratri matrique condemnatam detines? Quid per partes eis libo meum sanguinem? In me omnes, si qua est pietas, contorqueant manus spicula, me omnes filii germanique ultore pietatis gladio transfigant. Mactetur hostia parricidalis atque immoletur uiolatae necessitudini, totum simul caro noxia sanguinem euomat. Non uiscerum meorum cruciatibus et lenta tabe daemonium exsaturetur, quod me in tam nefarios ausus saeui facinoris impegit.̓ His dictis finem imperio uitaeque dedit uix anno functus potestate regia, propter quam parricidium non refugerat. Compare with Bellum [I.9.1] Soluit ilico mulier atque exuit uinculis fratres defuncti, regem constituit Alexandrum, cui et processa aetas et moderatio suffragari aestimabatur. Qui ut regnum adeptus est, fratrem quem aduerterat regni cupidiorem statim interemit. Reliquum qui supererat ex fratribus, uitae ac saluti potius quam regno intentum, reseruauit uacuum negotiorum. Compare with Bellum [I.9.2] Continuoque, ut se habet inquietudo morum, bello pacem mutauit congressuque habito aduersus Laturum Ptolomaeum plurimos quidem hostium interfecit, sed ad Laturum uictoria deflexit. Cui tamen fructum uictoriae ademit Cleopatra mater coacto in Aegyptum concedere, ut matrem sibi imminentem euaderet. Eius absentiam Alexander aucupatus, dum regni eius partes inuadere cupit, etiam Theodorum in se conuertit, quoniam potissima quaeque de eius possessionibus sibi adsociauerat. Improuiso itaque impetu Theodorus regias opes occupauit, decem milia quoque Iudaeorum proelio fudit, sed super plagam factus Alexander plura adhuc de hostium partibus suo imperio adiunxit captarumque urbium populos seruitio subegit. Compare with Bellum [I.9.3] Hos bellandi successus domestica seditio interpolauit, et orta de conuiuiis usque ad bellum contentio processit familiari peste huiusmodi Iudaeorum uiris, ut de epulari ludo sese in arma excitent. Ac nisi peregrina auxilia regi praesto fuissent, seditio praeualuerat, sed aduentitia manu aegre licet compressa est tamen octo milibus ferme Iudaeorum interemtis. Inde in Arabiam iter direxit, ac nonnullae eius urbes subactae, tributa quoque Moabitis et Galaditis iure uictoriae adscripta. Vnde regressus in Amathun, Theodoro tantis eius successibus stupefacto, uacuum defensoribus castellum inueniens sine mora expugnauit. Compare with Bellum [I.9.4] Non usquequaque tamen otiosus Obodeas rex Arabum fuit, nec inulta diu regni sui passus dispendia. Nam insidiis oportune locatis omnem eius exercitum deleuit conclusum uallis profundo et multo camelorum agmine adtritum. Euasit tamen Alexander. Effugiens de proelio Hierosolymitanae urbis receptacula petit, inuisus suis, quoniam recruduerant in odia aerumnae eius occasione, qui ante metu potentiae premebantur. Nec silentio tegebatur animorum discordia aut uerbis tantummodo exercebatur: proelio non uno sed plurimis decertatum, quibus extincta fere quinquaginta Iudaeorum milia quos Alexander interemit, suis quam hostibus perniciosior et maiore uictor detrimento, quoniam regni sui uires uincendo adtriuerat. Vnde ne ipse quidem iam suis uictoriis delectabatur auersusque a proelio arte tractabat sibi subditos, ut iam non armis premeret, sed uerbis urgueret ac solis sermonibus offensionum genera dissolueret. Nihil tamen proficiebat ad colligendam sibi gratiam, quoniam fictis facinora praeponderabant atque ipsa repentina conuersio ad paenitentiam morumque inaequalitas saeua passis suspecta habebatur. Compare with Bellum [I.10.1] Denique cum simulata eius placiditate se circumueniri arbitrarentur, Demetrium regem sibi auxilio futurum aduersus Alexandrum in bellum excitauerunt. Pugna in manibus nec comperendinata, quamuis uni aduersum duos exercitus numero inferiore certandum foret. Mille enim comitatus equitibus et sex milia peditum, quos mercede sibi adsociauerat, decem milia quoque Iudaeorum sibi conspirantium in bellum arcessens iuxta urbem Sicimam occurrit hostibus, quibus tria milia equitum erant et peditum quadraginta milia. Temtatoque utrimque agmine ubi neque Demetrius pecunia conductos desciscere a fide uidit, neque Alexander de Iudaeis aliquos, quibus se Demetrius adiunxerat, deposuisse erga se odia cognouit, armis decernendum aestimauerunt. Compare with Bellum [I.10.2] Superior bello Demetrius factus plurimo tamen suorum sanguine. Namque ab his qui e diuerso mercede conducti uenerant egregie bellatum, ita ut usque ad mortem uirtute ac fide certauerint. Destitutum itaque sese Alexander uidens caesis suorum cateruis in montes concessit. Sed praeter utriusque spem ad alterum eorum species uictoriae peruenit, fructus alteri partus, quia et Demetrius nudatus est discessu Hebraeorum, qui eundem ad societatem rogauerant, et Alexandro ex ipsis sex milia sese adiunxerant more quodam humani ingenii adstipulantibus ad misericordiam rebus aduersis. Cessit itaque Demetrius ei quem bello uicerat, uidens illum affluentibus paulatim Hebraeis iam pugnae idoneum seseque cum paucis relictum. Compare with Bellum [I.10.3] Cuius uictoria libertate adsuetis dominationis metum mouebat. Redit Alexandro saeuitia cum securitate regnumque in suos et usus belli reformatur. Quaerenti ab his quidnam faciens animos sibi plebis conciliaret responsum est, si moreretur; uix enim forte cum mortuo tam grauia perpessi in gratiam reuerterentur, ut odia aduersus defunctum deponerent. Quibus excitatus rebellandique adsuetudine multis necatis reliquos coegit in urbem cui nomen Bemeselel. Cuius expugnatio acerbiorem solito pestem inuexit tam saeuo crudelitatis processu, ut ex eo numero octingentos in media ciuitate crucifigeret, quorum in conspectu coniuges eorum filiosque iugulare iussit. Compare with Bellum [I.11.1] Haec spectabat accubans in medio concubinarum, laetus inter uina et pocula sed magis sanguine quam uino inebriatus. Hoc solo facto amplius populum quam bello terruit, ita ut proxima nocte Iudaeorum octo milia ultra Iudaeam discederent, quibus fugae finis mors Alexandri foret, tantique horror mali quietem regno attulit. Compare with Bellum [I.11.2] Sed ubi a domesticis feriatum proeliis, exorta est ei causa inquietudinis Antiochi aduersum Arabas expeditio, quam sibi terribilem et periculo futuram arbitrabatur. Hic est Antiochus qui etiam Dionisius appellatus, Demetrii frater, a Seleuco ultimus. Cui transitum negare cupiens Alexander inter urbem Antipatridem et Iopes litora foueis ingentibus ductis muroque altissimo, turribus quoque e ligno impositis, lusit operam magno suorum labore, nullo hostis impedimento, siquidem negotio facili repletae foueae turresque exustae. Ipse quoque Alexander fuga sibi consuluit eo tutior, quia nequaquam tanti aestimatus, ut eum uictor principe loco persequi deberet. Nam secundis partibus reseruatum ut itineris obstructi iniuriam acceptam ulcisceretur, rectum autem in Arabas iter direxit. Quorum rex in loca proelio oportuna sese contulerat, deinde subito conuerso equitatu maxima ui ac multitudine effuse ac sine ordine ruentes hostium turmas inuasere. Certatum acriter quoad Antiochus restitit; renitebatur enim, quamuis exercitus eius quasi more pecorum obtruncaretur. Vbi uero et ipse cecidit — nam prae ceteris sese offerre solebat periculis — auersi omnes, quorum maxima pars incerto fugae dispersa extinguitur, reliquis in uicum cui Ana nomen coactis atque alimentorum inopia consumtis, uix paucissimi ex his tantae cladi superfuere. Compare with Bellum [I.12.1] Hoc successu Areta etiam a Damascenis ad regnandum expetitur, ut Coelesyriae imperitaret, quo Ptolomaeum excluderent quem maxime infestis odiis persequebantur, nec Iudaeam immunem reliquit incursionis, de qua, uictor licet superato Alexandro, secundum utriusque tamen partis conuentum discessit ac reuertit in sua. Alexander autem Pellam euertit et Gerasam petiit iterum de Theodori possessionibus aliquas sibi adiungere parans eamque sibi bello uindicauit. Inde in Syriam progressus Gaulanen et Seleuciam et Gamelam euertit, ultus superioris belli contumeliam, ipsasque Antiochi munitiones diruit. Quibus ex locis iter in Iudaeam conuertit ac praeter spem cum gaudio totius gentis suscipitur pro mirabili successu rerum gestarum. Vbi parta bellandi quies exordium tribuit aegritudinis, atque aliquantulum quartanis febrium uicibus affectus, leuato paulisper incommodo, dum negotia repetit militaria nec modum seruat, animo ualidior quam corpore, comminuit omnem suae uigorem salutis uiresque absumsit atque ita mortuus est. Compare with Bellum [I.12.2] Viginti itaque et sex annis uario rerum euentu aduersum innumeros bellorum tumultus regnum tenuit et duobus liberis superstitibus decessit. Quos impares regni aestimans gubernaculo summam rem uxoris propriae delegauit sollicitudini, quoniam eam acceptiorem populo cognouit atque hoc apud uniuersos inuenisse gratiam, quod etiam ipsa ab immanitate uiri semper alienam sese faciendam existimauerit, ut non solum refugeret flagitiorum consortia, sed etiam resistendo eius iniquitatibus totius in se plebis conuerteret beniuolentiam. Nec improuida uiri sententia fuit. Nam regnandi ius mulier inoffense exercuit sine ullo feminei sexus impedimento et acquisiuit moderandi gratiam sacrae legis obseruatione. Nam dum attentior circa templum cura exercetur et remissa ministeria fraudi sunt, creuit imperii uigor. Nec tamen affectu infracta materno regni cupido, siquidem ex duobus liberis electus unus ad speciem regnandi, non potestatem, Hyrcanus uocabulo, natu senior, ingenio remissior, Aristobolum uero, acriorem animo, expertem potestatis emolliebat priuati humilitate. Compare with Bellum [I.12.3] Adsuerunt se Pharisei mulieri genus hominum secundum legis doctrinam exercitum, secundum qualitatem affectus callidum, auidum negotiorum, pecuniae appetens. Qui captantes elatam mulierculam, secundum scientiam iuris diuini, extollendo suam fecere, ut pleraque etiam regni negotia ipsis committeret, adhiberent quos uellent, quos uellent excluderent atque aulico exuerent ministerio. Quid plura? Ita sese insinuauere, ut commodorum omnium fructus ad eos peruenirent; sumtus et molestiae mulierem solam afficiebant. Nec mediocris mulieri spiritus, ut maxima quaeque auderet ac supra feminei sexus condicionem proelia disponeret, siquidem et praestantissimam de suis manum parauit et peregrini exercitus copias ingentes coegit, ut non solum domi tuta ad omnem regnandi securitatem foret, uerum etiam exteris esset potentibus formidabilis. Ea tamen reliquis praestabat omnibus, sed Phariseis quasi inferior obtemperabat. Compare with Bellum [I.12.4] Erat Diogenes in regno eius qui de potentissimis Alexandri amicis familiaritati eius inhaeserat. Eum adorsi obtruncauere memorantes ipsius consilio octingentos illos in medio urbis ab Alexandro cruci suffixos, in ceteros quoque facinoris auctores ut pergeret ultio mandatum. Necabantur itaque quos Pharisei praecipiebant, non quos societas sceleris inuoluerat. Quo metu perterriti plerique, quibus huiusmodi pericula intendebantur, et maxime praestantiores opibus aut dignitatibus ab Aristobolo intercessionem implorauere, ut matrem ab exsecutione praecepti seuerioris ad molliora inflecteret. Ille sibi gratiam parare cupiens non detrectauit. Mulier, aegre licet, oranti tamen filio cessit, ut contuitu honorum quos gesserant, qui in huiusmodi inuidiam arcessebantur, supremae necis sententia mitigaretur atque eos tantum, quos obnoxios suspectaret patrando flagitio incentores fuisse, urbe egredi iuberet. Qui accepta uitae securitate per agros dilapsi. Compare with Bellum [I.13.1] Eodem tempore causa accidit ut Damascum iuuentus dirigeretur, quoniam Ptolomaeus frequentibus incursionibus incolas memoratae urbis terebat, cuius negotii necessitas occupauit de exercitu Alexandriae ualidam manum. Cleopatram quoque Tigranes, qui Armeniis imperitabat, in urbe cui nomen Ptolomais obsidione clauserat. Eum muneribus Alexandria mulcebat ut a se auerteret. Quem Lucullus facta inruptione in terras Armeniorum redire infectis rebus coegit consultius ducentem sua tutari quam aliena adiungere. Compare with Bellum [I.13.2] Tantis itaque intenta negotiis Alexandria in morbum incidit. Quam occasionem rapuit Aristobolus ad suas artes et congregata manu, conspirantibus secum quos feruor naturae ad praerupta quaeque audendum cupienti adiunxerat, thesauros occupat eorumque copiis inuitat ad militiam uoluntarios, ac pretio componit ut in omnia quae uellet fidem praestarent atque infulas regni induit. Turbatus animam Hyrcanus matrem lacrimis conueniebat. At illa spirans ferociam filios et uxorem Aristoboli in castrum reclusit, cui nomen primo Baris postea Antonia appellatum, de quo supra memorauimus. Coepta Alexandriae celeri eius obitu destituuntur. Compare with Bellum [I.13.3] In hereditatem omnem Hyrcanus successit, qui uiuente adhuc matre dignitatem induerat sacerdotii, Aristobolus uirtute et sapientia praestabat, res usque ad contentionem atque in congressionem deducta. Vbi consertum, plerique relicto Hyrcano illum alterum bello meliorem secuti. Hyrcanus comitantibus secum qui bello reliqui fuerant confugit in Antoniam repertisque filiis et uxore Aristoboli per obsides salutem inuenit, quia ne quid asperum in suos fieret Aristobolus pacto consuluit. Conuentum fratrum huiusmodi fuit, ut regno Hyrcanus cederet atque ad Aristobolum ius omne imperii transiret, nec tamen Hyrcanum inhonorum relinqueret, sed regni exsortem honore alio fungi sineret, quem ipse impertiuisset. Transactio huiusmodi etiam religione templi sacrata adsensionem utriusque tenuit uoluntariam. Inde cum gratia discessum ac, se inuicem salutantes, Aristobolus in aulam regiam sese recepit, Hyrcanus aequanimiter in domum Aristoboli concessit. Compare with Bellum [I.14.1] Sed fuere quos metus hac rerum mutatione incesseret, qui se studuisse aduersus Aristobolum recordarentur, et prae ceteris Antipater. Is erat Idumaeus genus, maioribus apud suos clarus, non tenuis pecuniae et ideo praeualidae potentiae, arte mira factus ad contemnendam pecuniam propter conciliandam gratiam. Qui Hyrcanum consiliis suis perterritum, quod nullam salutis suae spem tutam haberet, qui imperio decessisset, nisi transfugio sibi consuleret, ubi ad suas artes inclinauit, insinuat Aretae regi fouendum auxilio uirum, qui circumuentus foret ut regno decederet. Decorum hoc fore regi, si arbiter fieret imperii restituendi, multoque pulchrius, si circumscripto, cui primitiua regni competerent, dolo sublata reformari iuberet. Illum uersutum et callidum et ideo suspectum uicinis, hunc mitem et quietum, qui pro summo beneficio acciperet, quicquid sibi ab externo tribueretur, cui frater etiam regnandi ius ademisset. Praeparatam itaque regis Aretae gratiam Hyrcano adnuntians fugiendi spem detulit et uiam demonstrauit, ut secum peteret Petram in finibus Arabiae sitam, quo in loco regem adirent. Qui precibus Antipatri donisque inflexus plurimam bellatorum manum Hyrcano adiunxit ut regno restitueretur. Erant fere peditum equitumque quinquaginta milia, a quibus prima pulsus congressione Aristobolus Hierosolyma confugit, ibi quoque intutus aduersus tantam hostium multitudinem, quae clausum expugnauisset, nisi Scaurus ductor Romani exercitus alterius belli occasione, quod aduersus Tigranen gerebatur, soluisset obsidionem missus a Pompeio, cui recepti Mitridatis ultio grauis bellique in socerum transferendi propositum exarsisset, qua causa Syriam infestari per Scaurum praeceperat, cum ipse Tigranen atque Armeniam urgueret. Compare with Bellum [I.14.2] Scauro itaque aduenienti Damascum, quam Metellus et Lollius funditus euerterant, occurrere fratrum legati sibi quibusque Romanae opis auxilium implorantibus, et quamuis inferior esset uiribus Aristobolus, praeponderauit tamen pecuniae oblatione. Venditur summa proeliaris certaminis talentis CCC et iustitia postulati pretio pensatur, qua pecunia sibi adnumerata denuntiat Scaurus Hyrcano regique Arabiae discedere ab obsidione, aut si permanerent scirent sibi aduersus Pompeium et Romanos bello certandum. Eo terrore obsidio soluta, Aretas Philadelfiam petiit, Scaurus Damascum reuertit. Aristobolus autem uix dudum idoneus propulsando periculo manum collegit, hostem insequitur et ad Papyronem, id uocabulum loco, VI milia hostium simul et fratrem Antipatris Fallionem proelio fudit. Hyrcani atque Antipatris spes lapsae, quibus fiducia omnis in Arabiae uiribus erat. Compare with Bellum [I.15.1] Sed ubi Magnus Pompeius obire Syriam coepit et Damascum aduenit, a Romanis, quorum auxiliis infracti de manibus uictoriam amisere, opem postulant Pompeiumque adeunt tamquam iusti arbitrum et minime auarum pecuniae. Allegationibus itaque, non muneribus ut ante niti coepere, quoniam integer animus aduersus corruptelam pecuniae laqueis auaritiae non capiebatur et gratuito odisse poterat fraterno insidiatum honori. Et ideo his eum adorsi querellis, quibus et Aristobolo inuidia fieret, quod indignus aliena inuaserit, et Hyrcano gratia conciliaretur, cui uel merito uitae uel aetatis suffragio regnandi ius competeret adstipulante praesertim matris auctoritate, quae et iudicium eligendi habuit et ius conferendi.
