Nullum itaque reliquum futurum, si iste euaderet doctus uenena parricidalia suorum uisceribus infundere, mutare mentes hominum, qui etiam Feroram semper amantissimum fratris Herodis in necem eius parricidio funesto exsuscitauit. Compare with Bellum [I.45.2] Ad haec cum plurima alia excitandae commotionis gratia Nicholaus addidisset, ubi sermonem absoluit, interrogatus a Varo est Antipater, si respondere uellet. Nihil aliud rettulit, nisi: ‘Deus mihi testis est quia nihil laesi.’ Tum Varus uenenum proferri atque id dari iussit uni de his qui iam rei mortis essent adiudicati, quo epoto statim mortuus est. De quo relatum ad Caesarem est et in uincula Antipater imperio patris ducitur. Compare with Bellum [I.45.3] Nec tamen ab insidiis uacuus erat. Nam tum maxime Salomes periculum dolis temtabat directis epistulis, quas Salomes nomine Antipater conposuerat, plenis in regem contumeliarum atque ad Acmen ancillam Iuliae, quae uxor Caesari erat, per Antifili seruulum perferri iusserat, quas Acme sibi redditas regi transmitteret. Ac paene in mulieris perniciem fraus conualuerat, ni reperta esset epistula Acmes ad Antipatrum, quae dolum prodidit, scripta in hunc modum: ‘Sicut uoluisti, patri tuo scripsi et epistulas illas direxi, nec dubito regem in periculum sororis insurrecturum. Compare with Bellum [I.45.4] Tu uicem restitue optato effectu potitus.’ His litteris deprehensis rex in suspicionem deductus, quod etiam Alexander pari arte conpositis a fratre esset adpetitus epistulis, et nimia commotione exasperatus aegritudinem grauem contraxit. Quo se uidens urgueri periculo Antipan unum ex filiis heredem imperii testamento scripsit praelatum Archelao et Philippo senioribus liberis, quoniam ipsos quoque Antipater dolis atque fallaciis suspectos patri fecerat. Caesari legauit M talenta donis muneribusque additis, in uxorem et filios, libertos atque amicos quingenta contulit. Nec Salomen sororem munerum suorum expertem reliquit. Compare with Bellum [I.45.5] Procedebat in deterius aegritudo atque accessu temporis asperabatur, quam inbecilla senectus suis incommoditatibus acerbabat cotidie, siquidem non minus LXX grauatum annis corpus, crebro quoque maerore animi adflictum gerebat tot parricidiis conuulneratus, quae aut deprehendisse in filiis extremae miseriae erat aut intulisse. Immedicabilis tamen aegritudinis feruor, quod superstes Antipater metuebatur. Compare with Bellum [I.45.6] Contemtus quoque in dies uilior, quod imagines Caesaris atque animalium similitudines contra legem templo adpositae detrahebantur, auctoribus maxime Iuda atque Matthia iuuentutis doctoribus, qui conspirantibus sibi uenisse tempus aiebant, quo uiolatae legis iniuria uindicaretur. Dare poenas sacrilegum, qui putaret fas esse quicquid potestati liceret, nec religione inclinatum sed elatum superbia in penetralibus templi faciendi quod uellet libidinem pro iure exercuisse. Et quamquam uis diuina ultionem adceleraret, tamen pulchrum uideri si etiam templo sacrati libertatem suam in defendendis paterni ritus obseruationibus adprobarent. Nec periculi metu quemquam reuocari oportere, cum etiam mori pro lege patria insigne inmortalitatis sit. Compare with Bellum [I.45.7] Primique adorsi auream aquilam supra fastigium portae adfixam detrahere, conprehensi atque ad regem perducti cum interrogarentur, cui oboedire cupientes tantum facinus adorsi forent, responderunt: ‘Legi paternae.’ Et iterum quaerenti quo freti laetiores adessent, cum ad mortis uocarentur periculum, rettulerunt, pietatis et deuotionis praemiis, quorum remuneratio pro ritu patrio mortem expetentibus persolueretur. Compare with Bellum [I.45.8] Nec diutius ferre potuit responsionis constantiam, sed indignatione super aegritudinem factus, ut infirmitatem uinceret, in conuentum populi processit. Ibique tamquam sacrilegii reos ad plebem referens accusare coepit, quod maiora de factis talibus suspectarentur. Quae etiamsi non probarentur, tamen cuncti sibi quisque metuentes auctorum qui conprehensi forent luenda supplicio deprecabantur, nec pergendum in ceteros, ne quaestio plures atque alienos et innoxios perturbaret. Rogatus itaque in praesentes sententiam tulit ut uiui exurerentur. Compare with Bellum [I.45.9] Vnde incommoditas aucta et grauioris aegritudinis uis diuersis totum corpus eius passionibus depascebatur. Febris erat uehemens, prurigo intolerabilis, continui ac sine ulla intermissione interiorum dolores uiscerum, colo medius uexabatur, hydrope grauabantur uestigia, abscondita corporis scatebant uermibus, spasmi totius corporis, anhelitus grauis et suspiritus perniciosi cuiuis indicio erant, quod iniusti parricidii et sacrilegae damnationis poenas reposceretur. Non cedebat tamen animo et uiuendi cupiditate passionibus reluctabatur. Petitae trans Iordanen Callirrhoes aquae calidae nihil profuerant. Asphaltius lacus plerisque medicabilis sine ullo profectu aegrum tenebat. Vbi dum oleo plurimo foueretur, laxato resolutus corpore morientium specie oculos inuertit, et uox defecerat nec sensus manebat, sed excitatus strepitu conclamantium resumsit. Compare with Bellum [I.45.10] Et ad sua regredi cupiens ubi ad regionem loci qui appellabatur Hiericho aduenit, atro felle exagitatus et ipsi quodammodo morti minitans immane facinus excogitauit, quo uelut inferiae sibi populi mitterentur. namque ex omni Iudaea congregari iamdudum praecipiens quosque nobiliores, ut ex singulis uicis in unum conuenirent, ubi imperio obtemperatum, claudi eos intra hippodromum iussit et accersita Salome atque eius Alexa uiro legatum sanguinis mandauit, asserens laetitiae populis gentis Iudaeae suam mortem futuram et ideo commentum se, quo praeclarissime suum epitafium celebraretur; deposcere a suis, ut cum ultimum exhalasset spiritum, statim eos omnes qui clausi tenebantur necari iuberent. Ita neminem futurum in uniuersa Iudaea atque omni domo, cui mors eius esset inlacrimabilis, cum uniuersis domestici luctus hereditatem dereliquisset, qui dum suorum deplorant necem iusta regi uiderentur persoluere, atque ita publicorum laetitia uotorum domesticis doloribus inpediretur. Ac ne forte scelesta imperia mandata exsecutio destitueret, quinquagenas dragmas iussit militibus dari, ut tali sceleris inposita mercede ferale ministerium milites non recusarent, conpensaturi exsecutionis horrorem remunerationis emolumento. Compare with Bellum [I.45.11] Cedebat prope iam tantae incommoditatis suppliciis, sed expetebat funestae responsa legationis, quae rettulit de Acme supplicium sumtum ad Herodis querellam, Antipatrum quoque conuictum parricidii morti adiudicatum, tamen si pulso patria, regno pater fugae potestatem tribuere uellet, Caesar iuberet sententiam sceleri ferens, consilium pietati relinquens. Soluerat natura parricidii necessitatem. Nam recreatus paulisper permissa sibi utendi ut uellet potestate, dum de genere necis tractat, distentus doloribus propriae diem mortis praeuenire desiderauerat. Poposcit itaque malum pariterque gladium, ut eo pomum solitus incidere refectionis aliquid assumeret, et paulisper se attollens cubituque adnixus leuauit dexteram cupiens sese ferire, sed occurrit Achiabus et inpediuit ictum, luctuque tota concrepuit domus, ut obisse Herodes foris aestimaretur. Exultauit Antipater ad sonum planctus et a custodibus postulauit ut uinculis resolueretur. Sed praepositus ei muneri non solum abnuit quod rogabatur, sed etiam regi adnuntiauit. Exclamans ille insultari sibi adhuc uiuenti percussores direxit qui Antipatrum interficerent, caesumque in Hyrcania sepeliri iussit. Atque iterum mutauit testamentum regemque Archelaum instituit seniorem ex fratribus, Antipan tetrarcham reliquit. Compare with Bellum [I.45.12] V itaque diebus Antipatro superstes defecit, XXXVII annis, ex quo a Romanis imperitare iussus est, regno potitus; ex quo autem Antigonum sustulit regni aemulum, annos XXXIIII in imperio exegit, utinam tam domestico usu quam publicis laetus successibus. Namque ita foris secundae ei res adspirauerunt, ut priuatus in regnum adscisceretur, eoque permulta usus annorum curricula, quod difficile, saluo potestatis usu decederet relinquens liberis imperii successionem, quam ipse a suis non acceperat, sed intra domum infelicissimus, quam acerbo suorum sanguine et luctu repleuit. Nec tamen exsecutionem inuenit ultimae crudelitatis, hoc uno Salome obliterante criminum suorum ludibria superiora, quod eos quos percuti rex iusserat omnes dimisit, dicens regem praecepti feralis postea paenituisse reuocatisque mandatis superioribus praecepisse ut ad sua omnes dimitterentur. Compare with Bellum [I.46.1] Deinde postea facta in amphitheatro militum et reliqui populi congregatione de obitu regis indicium factum. Processit Ptolomaeus, qui regis amicitiae inter fidissimos quosque usque in extremum adhaeserat, et anulum deferens, quem defuncti digito detraxit, conlaudat regem et populum admonet tranquillitatis. Aperitque epistulam, qua precatus fidelissimos sibi milites hortabatur, ut successori suo beniuolentiam exhiberent et gratiam. Apertis etiam tabulis testamenti recitatur Philippus Trachonitidis regionis et finitimorum locorum heres nuncupatus, tetrarches Antipas, rex Archelaus, ita tamen ut ad Caesarem deferri anulum suum atque ei arbitrium et firmamentum omnium dispositionum suarum reseruaretur, ac tunc demum ratum esset testamentum suum si Caesar probasset. Reliqua secundum priora sua testamenta custodiri praecepit. Compare with Bellum [I.46.2] Continuo adclamatio facta militum Archelao plaudentium, circumuallatur ilico stipatorum ambitu, promittunt beniuolentiam, spondent fidem. Post haec conpetenter atque magnifice funus curatum omni ambitu regalium diuitiarum praemisso ac pompae funebris celebritate. Lectus erat auro totus et gemmis insignitus, stratum refulgens murice, corpus adopertum purpurea diploide, quam internectebat fibula lapidibus pretiosis coruscans, diadema adhaerebat uertici supraque corona aurea, sceptrum in dextera, ut uiuentem putares. Praeibat agmen Thracium Germanique et Galli stipatores regii militarem seruabant ordinem. Pari modo succincti armis ac si in bellum prodirent, sed ora maesti et dolentibus similes prosequebantur. Reliqua manus praegrediebatur ornatu solito et cultu adsueto comitantibus pariter ducibus et centurionibus. L etiam seruorum et libertorum regiae domus aspergebantur aromata, ut suaui odore tota fragraret uia. Lectum filii regis et propinquorum uis maxima circumfundebantur. Sepultus est in Herodio ut ipse mandauit, quod aberat CC stadiis ab eo loco, in quo finem uitae inuenit, magno obsequio per tantum spatii deductus uniuersorum sed non omnium pari affectu. Metus enim officium non uotum extorserat, dolor intra se saltem liberam habebat sententiam. Hunc finem habuit Herodes. Compare with Bellum

English translation, version 1.0: Prologue and Book I chapters 1–46, ending at [I.46.2].(English translation, version 1.0: Prologue and Book I chapters 1–46, ending at [I.46.2].) Prologue [Prol.1] I too have set out in writing, in the form of a history, the four books of Kingdoms contained in sacred Scripture, down to the captivity of the Jews, the destruction of the wall, and the triumphs of Babylon. The prophetic account also briefly recounts the deeds of the Maccabees. Josephus is an outstanding narrator of the remaining events, in historical style, down to the burning of the temple and the spoils of Titus Caesar. If only he had been as attentive to religion and truth as to investigating events and restraint in expression! For he showed himself a partner in the faithlessness of the Jews even in the account he made public of their punishment. Though he deserted their arms, he did not abandon their sacrileges: he tearfully lamented their misery, but did not understand the cause of that very misery. [Prol.2] Hence we have taken it upon ourselves, relying not on the resources of talent but on earnest faith, to press a little further into the history of the Jews beyond the sequence of sacred Scripture. Like people seeking a rose among thorns, we seek to draw out, from amid the savage crimes of the impious, paid for at a price worthy of their impiety, something of reverence for the sacred law or of the marvel of the sacred order: things that afforded protection in adversity or honour in prosperity even to unworthy heirs. At the same time, let it be clear to everyone that they themselves were the authors of their own disaster, a sign of wickedness within their own ranks. First, they drew the attention of the Romans, who were occupied with other concerns, towards themselves and invited them to learn of their kingdom, though it would have been better for them to remain unknown to the Romans. They sought friendship without intending to keep faith, violated the peace though unequal in valour, and finally made war when all their hope lay in walls rather than strength. For being shut in under siege is pitiable for anyone; even when a siege goes well, it tends more often to increase dangers than to reduce them. [Prol.3] And lest anyone think that we have undertaken a task devoid of faith and superfluous, let us therefore consider the whole Hebrew people through their rulers, so that it may become perfectly clear whether, from the loins of Judah onward, the succession of his descendants never faltered, or whether it stumbled in the sequence of rulers but endured in him for whom all things remained in store, and who was himself the hope of the nations. From this, then, I shall begin. Book I [I.1.1] Resentment at sacrilege sparked the Parthian war, which was long and repeatedly fought between the Maccabean leaders and the nation of the Medes, with victory passing from side to side. For King Antiochus, called the Illustrious, son of King Antiochus, once he had added Egypt too to his dominion, grew arrogant because the uncertainties of war had turned out well for him. He had ordered that the rites of the Hebrews be disregarded and their mysteries profaned, and had dared enact this at the request of very many of the Jews.Compare with Bellum [I.1.2] Mattathias the priest could not endure this. He not only abstained from the sacrilege himself and refused to obey the royal edict, but also came upon one of his own people offering sacrificial victims to idols and ran him through with a sword. Gathering a band and taking the Hasideans as allies, he and his sons killed some who violated ancestral custom and the ordinances of the law, and drove out many more. He also advocated taking up arms on the Sabbath, lest they too be deceived by the same device: many of them had already fallen unavenged when enemies attacked them, because they refused to engage in war on the Sabbath. Successful deeds gave him power, and to the end of his life his zeal for defence and the vigour of his devotion persisted. But when he understood that his last day was upon him, he summoned his fellow citizens and, with his children standing beside him, urged them to defend their homeland and the worship of the temple. He left Judas Maccabaeus as their leader, to succeed to his care and concern.Compare with Bellum [I.1.3] It is not the business of the present work to recount how often he, vigorous in war, sound in counsel, and keener than all the others in faith, routed countless enemy forces with a small band. In brief, however, this much may be told. After repeated successes, he roused a great multitude of enemies against himself. Surrounded by them on every side, he thought retreat shameful; as his companions fled, he rushed into battle. He killed those he had advanced against, but was surrounded from the flank and slain, yet not before avenging his own death.Compare with Bellum [I.1.4] Jonathan succeeded him, his equal in valour no less than his brother by birth. After many exploits in war and services in sacred matters, witnessed and approved in the purification of the temple, he was shut up in an enemy city under a fraudulent assurance of friendship and killed not long afterwards. John too, the elder brother, and Eleazar, younger than the others, did not shrink from death for religion.Compare with Bellum [I.1.5] After them Simon assumed supreme command. He came to it no novice, but already proved by the triumphs he had shared with his brothers. If only he had been as perceptive in guarding against deceit as he was strong of hand and thoroughly tested in the arts of war! For after his valour had won him treaties of friendship with Roman commanders and the kings of nations, he was treacherously invited to a banquet by his son-in-law Ptolemy. Amid the tables and cups, he was surrounded along with the two sons present with him, stripped of his weapons, and given over to impious slaughter.Compare with Bellum [I.1.6] But John, Simon’s son, called Hyrcanus, forestalled the plot and hurried to the walls of a neighbouring city. There the people were awaiting him because of his father’s outstanding services, and also out of hatred for the enemy’s crime. He had scarcely entered the city when Ptolemy was already there. But when Ptolemy tried to enter by another gate, he was repulsed and decided to yield to the crowd. Jonathan at once assumed his father’s priestly office. From the worship of divine things he proceeded at once to the duties of family devotion and the care of protecting his kin, wishing to rescue his mother and brothers from danger.Compare with Bellum [I.1.7] Though he prevailed in battle, rightful feeling prevailed over him, preventing him from taking the fortress where they were confined. For whenever Ptolemy saw himself hard pressed, he placed the young man’s mother and brothers on the walls, to be thrown down at once unless Jonathan abandoned the war he was waging. The young man, who conquered by summoning his courage, was conquered by the fear born of family devotion; pity for his kin checked the anger roused against his enemy. His mother, however, ready for torture, stretched out her hands, pleading not for help to save her but for the consolation of vengeance. She feared that her son would fear more for his mother than he would devote himself to avenging his father. Such a death would take the place of immortality for her, avenging her husband and making her impious son-in-law pay the penalty for his monstrous crime. But the young man fought more within his own self than against his enemy. Whenever he thought of his father, he flared up; then again, when he saw his mother being beaten and made ready for death, he softened. He checked his attack, drew back his step, because feeling pulled him back. During the delays of the siege, the year of rest prescribed by the law arrived: the seventh year. Family devotion yielded to religious observance; the siege was lifted. But Ptolemy’s savagery was all the more aroused: he ordered that the very people whose exposure had saved him from destruction should have their throats cut. He immediately put himself beyond reach of vengeance by fleeing to Zeno, called Cotylas, king of Philadelphia, to protect himself with his support.Compare with Bellum [I.1.8] Nor did Antiochus remain inactive: he resented the fact that his armies had been made a mockery of by Simon, Jonathan’s father. Eager to extinguish Jonathan’s power while it was still beginning to rise, he came with a great force and besieged Jerusalem and Hyrcanus. Hyrcanus repelled with gold the man whom he could not repel with iron. Opening David’s tomb, as Josephus attests, he took out three thousand talents of gold; of these he paid three hundred to Antiochus, so that he would lift the siege and go away, bought off by the payment. And to lessen the odium of the deed, Hyrcanus is said to have been the first to establish guesthouses with that money, to receive poor travellers on their arrival.Compare with Bellum [I.1.9] He also took advantage of the difficulties Antiochus faced in making war on the Medes, avenged his loss, and brought many cities of Syria under his control. He also surrounded Samaria, where Sebastia was later founded, with siegeworks and entrusted its capture to his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus. Their protracted siege drove those shut inside to dreadful hunger and the hideous diet of human corpses. Driven by this necessity, they decided to seek help from Antiochus, called Aspondius, and drew the man who brought them aid into sharing their misery. For, defeated in battle by the brothers, he escaped death by flight. The Samaritans, however, were enslaved when their city was captured and destroyed in a sudden siege. Spurred on by this course of successes, Aristobulus and Antigonus did not let their onslaught cool, but continued, by war, to compel neighbouring peoples to join them, until envy arose and a savage war flared up: the inhabitants of the region conspired together and mustered a strong force. Defeated, however, that force gave John profound tranquillity thereafter, and itself repose.Compare with Bellum [I.1.10] In the thirty-first year, Hyrcanus ended his days, having enjoyed the benefit of a long peace and leaving five children alive, something many count a blessing. An outstanding ruler, admirably self-controlled, he never left even chance events any opportunity to cast a shadow over his deeds. He entrusted the affairs of supreme power to his wife, judging that she would direct public affairs more prudently; he held, with a certain inward foreknowledge, that his sons would not last long.Compare with Bellum [I.2.1] Nor was his judgement mistaken. For Aristobulus, the eldest of the brothers and the most headstrong in mind, turned the primacy of the priesthood into royal power. He was the first to take it upon himself to wear a diadem, four hundred and seventy-five years and three months after Israel, returning from Babylon and freed from servitude, had regained its own land. In his arrogance, unwilling to assign his other brothers a share, he favoured Antigonus alone with the appearance of honour, because he seemed to love him. His mother had complained that she was excluded from power and deprived of what her husband’s judgement had awarded her; he put her in chains. Fierce in his murderous hostility to his kin, he went so far in inhumanity that he kept both her and his brothers, bound in the same way, under close guard. They would have been driven almost to the very extremity of death by hunger, had Aristobulus not paid sooner for his wicked murder of kin. First his savage mind was roused against Antigonus himself and turned from love to hatred: he would kill before all the others the one man whom he promised a share in his rule. So little is affection worth among the wicked that evil suggestions soon wrench it away.Compare with Bellum [I.3.1] It is therefore fitting that we should not pass over the course of his cruelty, so that John’s judgement may be vindicated even after his death. He had by no means thought that supreme control of public affairs should be entrusted to his eldest son, whom he foresaw departing with such frenzy from the law of family devotion and the rule of justice. I do not know whether this was from observing his character or through a grace innate in the chief priests, whereby some knowledge of things to come was imparted to them even when they were less than worthy. A pitiful crime, that there were people who begrudged brothers the love of nature! From this the first taint of evil arose; envy was followed by fabrications of this kind. [I.4.1] At first they had devised other accusations, which Aristobulus did not believe. Out of love he softened the slander, attributing the bitterness of the accusation to envy. They therefore mingled falsehoods with truths, so that the details they had taken up to give an appearance of truth might ensnare him despite his resistance.Compare with Bellum [I.5.1] The Feast of Tabernacles was being celebrated in the lands of the Jews in accordance with the law: a festal day, that is, full of reverence, on which the customary sacrifice was offered. On that day Antigonus returned home, distinguished by his military exploits, and on his arrival happened to find his brother unwell. At once he made for the temple—for what would he put before religion?—still girded in his military dress and surrounded by an escort similarly equipped. There he prayed earnestly to the Lord for his brother’s health, and then hastened diligently to his brother. From this a slander was concocted with bitter gall, and a still more bitter outcome prepared.Compare with Bellum [I.6.1] For at once these thoroughly wicked men approached the king and stirred up his resentment: Antigonus had arranged a procession of armed men more splendid than was customary for private persons, to make a show before the crowd and ensure that no one dared oppose his designs. So great a display, they alleged, sought nothing but the king’s murder and the power to seize his rule. A sick mind, worn down by an ailing body, was easily induced to find credible what was asserted as true, especially since a day consecrated to religion excluded suspicion of a lie, the procession stirred resentment, illness added fear, and the band of armed men completed his conviction that the crime would be committed.Compare with Bellum [I.6.2] Accordingly, before any attempt at the crime of murdering his kin had been proved to him, he ordered his guards to take their places, armed, in a dark underground passage. They were to strip Antigonus of his armour as he arrived and, without awaiting the king’s command, kill him on their own authority. A message had, however, been sent ahead ordering him to come unarmed. Aristobulus’s wife reversed the sense of this instruction. Through the messengers, whom she had bound to her conspiracy, she had Antigonus informed that his brother had been delighted by the beauty of the arms in which he had recently appeared, but had been unable to examine them closely because of his illness. He now asked him to bring to his brother all the military attire he had assembled for himself: it would please the king if he came armed.Compare with Bellum [I.6.3] Antigonus did not foresee the deceit. He obeyed the message all the more eagerly because he wished to please both his king and his brother. Aristobulus lay ill in the fortress first called Baris and later Antonia, a name bestowed from Antony the triumvir, together with the status of a city. When Antigonus drew near and entered that dark passage, the king’s guards saw that he had come armed. Suddenly attacking the young man, they carried out their orders and overwhelmed him unawares.Compare with Bellum [I.6.4] The place was called Strato’s Tower, and it is widely believed that this name deceived Judas, who was an Essene by origin. An ancient account records that, whether through the uprightness of his life or through mystical observance, he had often foretold things to come.Compare with Bellum [I.7.1] When, as we have learned, he saw Antigonus passing by to visit his brother, he said to those numbered among his disciples: “Ah! Now it is good for me to die, since truth has died for me. Antigonus is alive, though he must be killed today; but the place appointed for his murder is Strato’s Tower, six hundred stades from here. It is already the fourth hour of the day. The time therefore rules out belief in the foretold death.” After saying this, he began to ponder more intently how his judgement had deceived him. Not long afterwards word came that Antigonus had been killed in the underground passage at Strato’s Tower. This place was customarily called by the same name as the one on the coast at Caesarea.Compare with Bellum [I.7.2] Once this crime had been committed, Aristobulus reflected on the wickedness he had perpetrated and fell ill. The murder of his kin was before his eyes, turmoil in his mind; there was no respite in which he could disregard it. Grief lodged deep in his entrails. Envy turned to pity because he had killed an innocent man in violation of the bond between brothers. The enormity of so great a crime ulcerated his mind: no sleep was granted to his eyes, no rest to his mind. The wound crept onward with unseen pain; cares and anxieties seethed in his sick heart and wounded his feeble limbs. All too deep sighs shook him with repeated groans.Compare with Bellum [I.8.1] Thus, through excessive grief, the violence of his illness reached the point where his entrails convulsed and he vomited blood from his mouth. A court boy attending to the king’s needs carried it outside. Unwittingly, for what happened was by chance rather than by design, he came to the place where Antigonus had been killed. There, on the still-wet stains of the slain brother’s blood, he poured out the slayer’s blood. At once there was a cry and groaning from the onlookers, because it seemed that, by some profound dispensation of the Lord, the blood of this most wicked murderer of his own kin had been poured out as a libation to the slain man. Aroused by the sound, he asked the cause. When silence met him, he drew it out by persistent questioning and an outburst of indignation. When he learned it, his eyes flooded with tears, and, groaning with all the strength he had, he said: “A fitting return is being paid for what I have deserved. For I, the deviser of so impious a crime, could not escape God’s eye. Vengeance follows hard upon the outrage, and the fitting price for my murder of kin is already being exacted from me. Farewell, body. How long will you hold a soul forfeit to my brother and mother? Why do I pour out my blood to them little by little? If there is any family devotion, let all hands hurl their weapons against me; let all sons and brothers pierce me with the sword that avenges family devotion. Let this victim, guilty of murdering his kin, be slaughtered and sacrificed to the violated bond of kinship; let the guilty flesh vomit all its blood at once. Let the demon that drove me to dare so impious and savage a crime not be sated by the torments of my entrails and a slow wasting away.” With these words, his reign and his life came to an end, after he had exercised royal power for scarcely a year, the power for which he had not shrunk from murdering his kin.Compare with Bellum [I.9.1] At once the woman released the dead man’s brothers and freed them from their chains. She made Alexander king, since both his greater age and his moderation were thought to favour him. As soon as he gained the kingdom, he killed the brother whom he had perceived to be too eager for it. The remaining brother, intent on life and safety rather than kingship, he spared and left free from public business.Compare with Bellum [I.9.2] Immediately, as restless character will do, he exchanged peace for war. In an encounter with Ptolemy Lathyrus he killed very many of the enemy, but victory fell to Lathyrus. His mother Cleopatra, however, deprived him of the fruit of victory: he was compelled to withdraw into Egypt to escape his mother’s threat. Alexander seized upon his absence. While seeking to invade parts of his kingdom, he also turned Theodorus against himself, for he had annexed the most important parts of Theodorus’s possessions. In a sudden attack, therefore, Theodorus seized the royal wealth and routed ten thousand Jews in battle. Alexander nevertheless rose above the blow, added still more of the enemy’s territory to his dominion, and subjected the peoples of the captured cities to servitude.Compare with Bellum [I.9.3] Domestic sedition interrupted these successes in war. A quarrel arising at banquets developed into war—a plague of a kind familiar among Jewish men, that they rouse themselves to arms from the sport of feasting. Had foreign auxiliaries not been at hand for the king, the sedition would have prevailed. With difficulty, however, it was suppressed by the foreign force, and nearly eight thousand Jews were killed. From there he made for Arabia; some of its cities were subdued, and tribute was imposed on the Moabites and the Gileadites by right of victory. Returning from there to Amathus, he found the fortress empty of defenders, Theodorus being stupefied by his many successes, and took it without delay.Compare with Bellum [I.9.4] Obodas, king of the Arabs, did not remain wholly inactive, however, nor did he long allow his kingdom’s losses to go unavenged. By laying an ambush at the right place, he destroyed Alexander’s entire army, trapping it in the depths of a valley and crushing it beneath a great column of camels. Alexander nevertheless escaped. Fleeing from the battle, he sought refuge in the city of Jerusalem, hated by his own people: those whom fear of his power had previously held down had seized the occasion of his misfortune to renew their hatred. Their discord was neither concealed in silence nor expressed in words alone. They fought not one battle but many, in which nearly fifty thousand Jews died, killed by Alexander. He was more destructive to his own people than to his enemies, and victory brought him the greater loss, since in conquering he had worn down the strength of his own kingdom. Hence even he no longer delighted in his victories. Turning away from battle, he dealt craftily with his subjects, no longer to oppress them with arms but to press them with words, and to dispel their various grievances through speech alone. He nevertheless made no progress in winning favour, since his crimes outweighed his pretences. Those who had suffered his savagery regarded his sudden turn to repentance and the inconsistency of his character with suspicion.Compare with Bellum [I.10.1] Finally, thinking that his feigned gentleness was meant to ensnare them, they stirred King Demetrius to war against Alexander, to come to their aid. Battle was at hand and was not deferred, although Alexander alone had to contend against two armies with inferior numbers. Accompanied by a thousand cavalry and six thousand infantry whom he had hired, and summoning to war ten thousand Jews united in his cause, he met the enemy near the city of Shechem. They had three thousand cavalry and forty thousand infantry. Each side tried to win over the other’s force. When Demetrius saw that the hired men would not abandon their allegiance, and Alexander found that none of the Jews whom Demetrius had joined had laid aside their hatred of him, they judged that the matter must be decided by arms.Compare with Bellum [I.10.2] Demetrius gained the upper hand in war, though at the cost of much of his own men’s blood. For the hired men on the opposing side fought outstandingly, maintaining their valour and allegiance to the point of death. Seeing himself abandoned, his bands cut down, Alexander withdrew into the mountains. But, contrary to both men’s expectations, the appearance of victory came to one, its fruit to the other. Demetrius was stripped of his support by the departure of the Hebrews who had invited him into the alliance, and six thousand of them joined Alexander: adversity, in a way characteristic of human nature, inclined them to pity. Demetrius therefore yielded to the man he had defeated in war, seeing him now fit for battle as the Hebrews gradually flocked to him, while he himself was left with few men.Compare with Bellum [I.10.3] Demetrius’s victory stirred fear of domination in those accustomed to freedom. Alexander’s savagery returned along with his security. His rule over his own people and the practice of war were restored. When he asked them what he could do to win the goodwill of the people, they replied that he should die. After suffering such grievous things, they would scarcely perhaps be reconciled even with him dead, so as to lay aside their hatred of the deceased. Roused by these words and their habitual rebellion, he killed many and forced the rest into the city called Bemeselel. Its capture brought a scourge more bitter than usual, with cruelty carried to such a savage extreme that he crucified eight hundred of their number in the middle of the city and ordered their wives and children to have their throats cut before their eyes.Compare with Bellum [I.11.1] He watched this reclining amid his concubines, cheerful among wine and cups, but drunk more on blood than on wine. By this deed alone he terrified the people more than by war, so that the following night eight thousand Jews departed beyond Judaea, their flight to end only with Alexander’s death. Horror at so great an evil brought quiet to the kingdom.Compare with Bellum [I.11.2] But when there was respite from domestic battles, Antiochus’s expedition against the Arabs became a cause of disquiet to him: he considered it a source of terror and danger to himself. This was the Antiochus also called Dionysius, Demetrius’s brother, the last in the line from Seleucus. Wishing to deny him passage, Alexander dug huge trenches between the city of Antipatris and the coast at Joppa, raised a very high wall, and set wooden towers upon it. He wasted his efforts, at great labour to his own men and no hindrance to the enemy, for the trenches were easily filled and the towers burned. Alexander himself also took thought for his safety by flight. He was all the safer because he was by no means considered important enough for the victor to pursue him as his first priority. Vengeance for the affront of obstructing his route was reserved for later; Antiochus directed his march straight against the Arabs. Their king had taken up a position favourable for battle. Then, suddenly turning their cavalry about, they attacked with overwhelming force and numbers the enemy squadrons rushing on loosely and without order. The fighting was fierce as long as Antiochus stood firm: he held out even though his army was being slaughtered like cattle. But when he too fell—for he was accustomed to expose himself to danger before the others—all turned to flee. Most of them scattered in aimless flight and were killed. The rest were driven into a village called Ana and perished from lack of food; scarcely a handful of them survived so great a disaster.Compare with Bellum [I.12.1] Following this success, Aretas was also sought as king by the people of Damascus, to rule Coele-Syria and exclude Ptolemy, whom they pursued with the bitterest hatred. Nor did he leave Judaea untouched by invasion. Although victorious over Alexander, he withdrew from it in accordance with an agreement between the two sides and returned to his own lands. Alexander, however, destroyed Pella and made for Gerasa, intending once again to annex some of Theodorus’s possessions, and claimed it for himself by war. Advancing from there into Syria, he destroyed Gaulane, Seleucia and Gamala, avenging the humiliation of the previous war, and demolished Antiochus’s fortifications themselves. From these places he turned his march towards Judaea and, contrary to expectation, was received with joy by the whole nation because of the remarkable success of his deeds. There, respite won from warfare brought the onset of illness. For a while he suffered recurring quartan fevers. When his illness eased briefly, he resumed military affairs without keeping any moderation; stronger in spirit than in body, he wore down all the vigour of his health and exhausted his strength, and so died.Compare with Bellum [I.12.2] Thus for twenty-six years, with varying fortune, he held his kingdom against countless upheavals of war and died leaving two children alive. Judging them unequal to steering the kingdom, he entrusted supreme control to the care of his own wife. He knew that she was more acceptable to the people and had won everyone’s favour because she too had always thought it necessary to keep herself apart from her husband’s inhumanity: she not only shunned complicity in his crimes but, by resisting his injustices, turned the goodwill of the whole people towards herself. Nor was her husband’s judgement improvident. The woman exercised the right of rule without giving offence and without any hindrance from her sex, and gained favour in governing through observance of the sacred law. For while closer care was devoted to the temple and neglect of its services incurred blame, the vigour of her rule grew. Her desire for kingship was not, however, broken by maternal affection. One of her two children was chosen to have the appearance of kingship, but not its power: Hyrcanus, the elder by birth and the more easy-going in temperament. Aristobulus, more spirited in mind, she kept from power and subdued through the lowly status of a private person.Compare with Bellum [I.12.3] The Pharisees attached themselves to the woman: a class of men practised in the teaching of the law, cunning in disposition, eager for business, and hungry for money. Using their knowledge of divine law, they played upon the conceited little woman and won her over by flattery, so that she entrusted even many affairs of the kingdom to them. They brought in whom they wished and excluded whom they wished, stripping them of service at court. What more need be said? They insinuated themselves so far that the fruit of every advantage came to them; the woman alone bore the expense and trouble. Nor was the woman’s spirit slight: she dared the greatest undertakings and planned battles beyond the condition of her sex. She prepared a force of the finest of her own men and assembled vast numbers of foreign troops, so that she would not only be safe at home in complete security of rule but would also be formidable to foreign powers. Yet she who surpassed all the rest obeyed the Pharisees as though their inferior.Compare with Bellum [I.12.4] There was in her kingdom a Diogenes who, as one of Alexander’s most powerful friends, had remained close to him. They attacked and slaughtered him, recalling that it was on his advice that Alexander had crucified those eight hundred in the middle of the city. Orders were given that vengeance should proceed against the other instigators of the crime as well. Thus those whom the Pharisees designated were killed, not those whom complicity in the crime had implicated. Terrified by this fear, many who were threatened with such dangers, especially those outstanding in wealth or rank, begged Aristobulus to intercede. He was to turn his mother from carrying out the excessively severe order to milder measures. Wishing to win favour for himself, he did not refuse. Reluctantly though she did so, the woman nevertheless yielded to her son’s plea: out of regard for the honours held by those exposed to such odium, the sentence of death was to be mitigated. She was merely to order out of the city those she suspected of bearing responsibility as instigators of the crime. Having obtained assurance of their lives, they dispersed through the countryside.Compare with Bellum [I.13.1] At the same time an occasion arose for sending the young men to Damascus, since Ptolemy was wearing down its inhabitants with frequent incursions. The demands of this affair occupied a strong force from Alexandra’s army. Tigranes, who ruled the Armenians, had also shut Cleopatra within the city called Ptolemais under siege. Alexandra sought to appease him with gifts, to turn him away from herself. By invading the lands of the Armenians, Lucullus forced him to return without accomplishing his purpose: he judged it wiser to protect his own possessions than to annex those of others.Compare with Bellum [I.13.2] Intent on so many affairs, Alexandra fell ill. Aristobulus seized the occasion for his schemes. He gathered a force, joined in conspiracy by those whom ardour of spirit had brought to his side in his eagerness to dare every reckless undertaking, and seized the treasures. With their resources he invited volunteers to military service and bought their agreement to maintain allegiance in whatever he wished; he put on the insignia of kingship. Troubled in mind, Hyrcanus appealed to his mother in tears. Breathing ferocity, she shut Aristobulus’s children and wife in the fortress first named Baris and later called Antonia, which we mentioned above. Alexandra’s undertakings were left unfinished by her swift death.Compare with Bellum [I.13.3] Hyrcanus succeeded to the whole inheritance; while his mother was still alive he had assumed the dignity of the priesthood. Aristobulus excelled in valour and wisdom. Matters were brought to a dispute and then to an encounter. When battle was joined, most deserted Hyrcanus and followed the other, who was the better man in war. Accompanied by those who had survived the battle, Hyrcanus fled into Antonia. Finding Aristobulus’s children and wife there, he secured his safety through these hostages, since Aristobulus took precautions by agreement lest anything harsh be done to his family. The brothers’ agreement was as follows: Hyrcanus was to relinquish the kingdom, and the whole right of rule was to pass to Aristobulus. Aristobulus was not, however, to leave Hyrcanus without honour; though excluded from the kingdom, he was to be allowed to hold another honour that Aristobulus himself would bestow. This settlement, also consecrated by the sanctity of the temple, secured the voluntary assent of both. They then parted in goodwill. After greeting one another, Aristobulus withdrew into the royal palace, and Hyrcanus went calmly into Aristobulus’s house.Compare with Bellum [I.14.1] But this change of affairs brought fear to some who remembered that they had taken sides against Aristobulus, and above all to Antipater. He was Idumaean by origin, distinguished among his people through his ancestors, a man of no small wealth and therefore of very great power. He was remarkably skilful at disregarding money in order to win favour. His counsels terrified Hyrcanus: a man who had relinquished rule could have no secure hope for his safety unless he sought protection by taking refuge elsewhere. Once he had bent Hyrcanus to his schemes, he suggested to King Aretas that help should be given to a man who had been ensnared into relinquishing his kingdom. It would be becoming to a king, he argued, to act as arbiter in restoring rule, and much finer still to order the restoration of what deceit had taken from a defrauded man to whom the birthright of kingship belonged. The one brother was shrewd and cunning, and therefore suspect to his neighbours; the other gentle and quiet. He would accept as the greatest benefit whatever an outsider bestowed on him, when even his brother had deprived him of the right to rule. Announcing to Hyrcanus that he had secured King Aretas’s favour, Antipater held out hope of flight and showed the way: Hyrcanus should go with him to Petra, situated in the territory of Arabia, where they would approach the king. Won over by Antipater’s pleas and gifts, the king gave Hyrcanus a very large force of fighting men to restore him to his kingdom. They numbered about fifty thousand infantry and cavalry. Driven back by them at the first encounter, Aristobulus fled to Jerusalem. Even there he was unsafe against so great a multitude of enemies: they would have captured him within it had Scaurus, commander of the Roman army, not lifted the siege on the occasion of another war, waged against Tigranes. He had been sent by Pompey, in whom fierce vengeance for the reception of Mithridates had blazed up, together with a resolve to carry the war against Tigranes’ father-in-law. For this reason he had ordered Syria to be ravaged by Scaurus, while he himself pressed Tigranes and Armenia.Compare with Bellum [I.14.2] As Scaurus approached Damascus, which Metellus and Lollius had utterly destroyed, the brothers’ envoys met him, each side begging for the support of Roman aid. Although inferior in strength, Aristobulus nevertheless outweighed his opponent by the money he offered. The decision of the contest in war was sold for three hundred talents, and the justice of the claim was weighed by its price. Once this money had been counted out to him, Scaurus ordered Hyrcanus and the king of Arabia to withdraw from the siege: if they remained, they were to know that they would have to fight a war against Pompey and the Romans. This threat dissolved the siege. Aretas made for Philadelphia, and Scaurus returned to Damascus. Aristobulus, who had scarcely been capable of warding off danger a moment before, gathered a force and pursued the enemy. At Papyron, as the place was called, he routed six thousand of the enemy in battle, together with Antipater’s brother Phallion. The hopes of Hyrcanus and Antipater collapsed: all their confidence had rested in the forces of Arabia.Compare with Bellum [I.15.1] But when Pompey the Great began to travel through Syria and arrived at Damascus, they sought help from the Romans, whose aid to their opponents had broken them and snatched victory from their hands. They approached Pompey as an arbiter of justice with no greed for money. They therefore began to rely on arguments, not gifts as before: a mind proof against the corrupting power of money was not caught in the snares of avarice and could hate, without payment, a man who had plotted against his brother’s honour. So they approached him with complaints calculated to arouse odium against Aristobulus for unworthily seizing what belonged to another, and to win favour for Hyrcanus. The right to rule belonged to him whether by the merit of his life or by the claim of his age, supported above all by his mother’s authority: she had had both the judgement to choose and the right to confer it. Aristobulus did not stay away long. Though he saw nothing in the Great man’s mind that would suit his schemes, he nevertheless presumed upon his purchase of Scaurus and boasted of their association. He therefore came clad in royal attire and surrounded by a more extensive display of pomp than usual. Distrusting the justice of his case, he meant to prevent any presumption that he would acquiesce and deny any hope that he would obey. But he could not long endure the Roman consul’s exalted position: though without a kingdom, the man was accustomed to command kings. When they reached the city called Diopolis, Aristobulus withdrew elsewhere, his swollen royal pride scorning the haughtiness of Roman dignity.Compare with Bellum [I.15.2] Aristobulus’s withdrawal gave no small cause for offence. The consul was so deeply stirred that Roman arms were immediately turned against Judaea, joined also by many Syrian auxiliaries. When Aristobulus learned that he was approaching the city of Scythopolis and then Coreae, where the territory of Judaea began, he fled into Alexandrium, a strongly fortified stronghold on a very high mountain. Learning this, Pompey ordered him to come down. But Aristobulus considered it unbecoming to obey a command as though from a master; immoderate in spirit, he thought he should face danger rather than obey an order. Looking down, however, upon the Roman camp packed with men, and warned by his followers not to provoke those to whose name and power almost the whole world had submitted, he came down. He used many arguments to establish that the kingdom had rightfully passed to him: it was owed to him by the bond of birth, or by the army’s judgement in following the stronger man and deserting the coward, or by the outcome of battle, or by the agreement of the treaty. He then returned to the fortifications. Again, when Hyrcanus had approached the consul, Aristobulus was summoned to judgement and presented himself. But seeing that the hearing was still being deferred, he returned to the stronghold. Poised between hope and fear, he thought that by obeying Pompey’s commands he could turn him to favour himself; yet he kept withdrawing into Alexandrium lest he again be forced to relinquish his rule. The king’s cunning did not escape the Great man. He ordered him to leave the fortifications and bind himself to do so by letters given to each of their keepers. Aristobulus obeyed commands he did not dare reject, but immediately hid himself within the walls of Jerusalem and began to prepare war against the Romans.Compare with Bellum [I.15.3] Pompey in turn pursued him as he fled, pressed him within his defences, and gave him no time to make preparations for war. News that Mithridates had ended the war by his death focused the Great man’s attention. Pompey was in the territory of the city of Jericho when word of the matter arrived. Near the city is a place where balsam is produced, growing upon shrubs which the farmers’ boys cut with sharp stones; through these incisions liquid drips, beautiful in its dew-like tears. From there the veteran soldier arranged his ranks and moved camp towards evening. At first light he stood before the walls of Jerusalem and unexpectedly poured in his armed forces.Compare with Bellum [I.16.1] Astonished by the sight of the deployment, the strength of the men and the eagerness of the soldiers, Aristobulus came forward of his own accord to beg pardon, offering money, the city and himself. Bending his words to a humbler tone of supplication, he had softened the consul’s indignation. But his plea proved fruitless because fulfilment of his promise was lacking: not only was the money refused, but Gabinius, who had come to claim what had been offered, was even shut out of the city. War descended upon them.Compare with Bellum [I.16.2] For the Great man placed Aristobulus under guard and began to survey the city walls and examine more closely where he might attempt an entry by force. But he observed the strength of the walls, which could not be stormed, and that the temple within the city was surrounded by fortifications hardly inferior to them. Those who entered would face a double danger, from the temple’s defenders and from the men holding the walls’ defences. For some time he hesitated, doubtful in mind and uncertain in judgement. Suddenly sedition arose within the city: Hyrcanus’s allies wished to admit Pompey, while Aristobulus’s defenders resisted. The former sought to open the gates to the Great man, the latter to bar them and wage war to prevent the Romans from taking away their king.Compare with Bellum [I.16.3] But those on the weaker side yielded to the greater number, whose ranks fear of Roman power had swelled. They withdrew into the temple and broke down the bridge that lay between city and temple, joining them by an open passage. The Roman army was thus admitted into the city, and with their own hands the Jews opened its gates to those who would soon storm both city and temple. David’s words were fulfilled: “God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple.” Thus they voluntarily handed over their royal quarters and relinquished the palace buildings. Piso, a man distinguished among his own people and experienced in military service, was charged with holding the royal palace and the rest of the city with a strong force. He carried this out diligently, as though he had led the Roman army there to defend these places rather than to occupy them.Compare with Bellum [I.16.4] For the assault on the temple, however, since resistance was stubborn, the Great man prepared the Jews—Hyrcanus’s allies, that is—so that, if possible, the Romans would not profane another people’s mysteries, and so that the Jews would fill the ditches with their own hands. In impious service and shameful obedience, their hands laboured at the basket, their minds at sacrilege. Yet the heaping up of material achieved nothing, since Aristobulus’s supporters resisted from the walls and hindered the work from above. Pompey’s first efforts would have been fruitless had he not, when the sacred days of religious observance came round, ordered his men to press on with heaping up mounds of earth. On those days it was the Jews’ ancient observance to refrain from all work. For only the practice of engaging in hand-to-hand combat had become customary even on the Sabbath: if battle was forced upon them and their lives faced the utmost peril, the Jews thought they must decide the matter by the sword; against other forms of conflict they had a religious scruple. Already the rampart had risen, already the siege engines had been brought up. The king’s men fought back, emboldened by the height of the walls; even when engaged in combat, they did not give way as the Great man came nearer.Compare with Bellum [I.16.5] Pompey marvelled at the men’s fierce spirits, the wall’s beauty and size, and the priests’ duties, nowhere relaxed amid the fury of war, as though there were profound peace. Nothing was lacking in the customary sacrifices. Amid the warriors’ missiles and the deaths of the slain, the blood of sacrificial victims was poured out; a victim was placed upon the altars. Those stationed before the altar were struck down. A third month already found the contest still undecided. Faustus, son of Cornelius Sulla, was the first, along with two centurions, one named Furius and the other Fabius, to break into the temple after a tower in the walls had been knocked down. Each had his band following him. Surrounding the temple’s interior on every side, they ran through with their swords whomever they found. Those fleeing were cut down; others, resisting, were slaughtered.Compare with Bellum [I.16.6] There was no mercy. Yet this savagery of the combatants did not interrupt the priests’ service. The enemy stood over them with drawn swords, but they carried out their accustomed duty without any disturbance. No kind of duty was suspended. Whatever belonged to the customary rites of purification, whatever concerned the observance of sacred worship, was fulfilled. So great was their care for their service—and if only it had been in the service of true devotion and faith! Still greater dangers also arose from their own people, which the Hebrews inflicted on one another. Inside, the fighting was fiercer, and the danger from the rebels nearer and twofold. A foreign enemy pressed from the front, a domestic one from the rear and the sides.Compare with Bellum [I.17.1] Thus, shut in on every side, some hurled themselves down, while others were consumed in the fires of their homeland. The priests, however, persevered in their duties to the very end, urging one another not to put the duty of religion below the protection of their lives. It would be well for them to give to devotion what was owed to necessity, and most noble if they could be buried in their homeland’s bosom. What good would it do to escape and outlive religion? Rather, to die together with their sacred service was a glorious deed. If anyone abandons it through fear of danger, that is sacrilege; if he fulfils it, that is sacrifice and the victory of devout suffering. Thus the priests, wearing their sacred fillets, were sacrificed among their own sacrificial victims; clad in their priestly robes, they lay on the ground among the bodies of the slain. Twelve thousand Jews were cut down there; few Romans were killed, more were wounded.Compare with Bellum [I.17.2] Yet amid that misery the Jews lamented nothing more deeply than that those previously hidden sacred mysteries had been uncovered and made manifest to the nations. Indeed, Pompey set aside such superfluous concerns. As he toured the burned ruins, intent rather on triumph, followed by many of his men, he saw the second tabernacle, which was open only to the chief priest on his customary entry. Looking inside, he saw the lamp, the table, the incense burners, the tablets of the covenant and the cherubim above them, a great quantity of spices scattered about, and two thousand talents of sacred money. Although these included a great deal of gold, he remained free of all greed and ordered that the treasure, and any sacred vessels also found, be kept untouched. On the day after the destruction he ordered the temple attendants to cleanse the temple’s interior and celebrate the customary sacrifices. He also gave Hyrcanus the primacy of the priesthood, having used his ready assistance in the exigencies of the siege. For though unfaithful to his own people, he was faithful to the Romans so that his own homeland might be stormed—but I think no one can be called faithful who has been unfaithful to his own people. Thus, in his own war, he gave far from perfunctory help to the enemies of his own people, if only by drawing away from Aristobulus’s alliance the multitude outside the walls that was supporting him. To all the ways in which Pompey proved an outstanding commander, whether in forestalling Aristobulus and diminishing his authority or in bringing the war swiftly to an end, he added this distinction: he kept moderation in victory. He bound the conquered to himself more by kindness than by terror, and executed only the instigators of the war with the axe. He also imposed tribute on the conquered, appointed a commander for Judaea, and fixed its boundaries.Compare with Bellum [I.17.3] Judaea was thus confined within its own boundaries. He also restored Gadara, which the Jews had destroyed, at the request of Demetrius, who had asked this favour for his homeland from his patron. In this matter, as in many others, Demetrius held a standing with the Great man beyond the usual measure of freedmen, even to the point of arousing envy. Pompey decided to take Aristobulus, his children and his father-in-law with him to Rome as captives. But one of the royal offspring escaped his guards on the journey and returned home. His name was Alexander; he was older than his brother and had two sisters. Thus the younger Antigonus and his sisters were taken to Rome; Pompey made for Cilicia and thence for Rome.Compare with Bellum [I.18.1] Meanwhile Scaurus, who held command in Syria, recovered the cities the Jews had invaded: inland, Scythopolis, Hippos, Pella, Samaria, Jamnia, Maresa, Azotus and Arethusa; on the coast, Gaza, Joppa, Dora and the place formerly called Strato’s Tower, afterwards named Caesarea under Herod’s rule, when he both adorned it and changed its name. Scaurus was preparing war against the Arabs. Holding Judaea between the Euphrates and Egypt under his jurisdiction, and Syria too, restored to its own boundaries, he wished to invade Petra, the capital of the kingdom of Arabia—whether from a desire for plunder, as I am more inclined to think, or for the sake of extending dominion. Hampered by the difficulty of the terrain, he could not break into it, but devastated many places both near the city and far away. While his army lingered in those places, hunger overtook it. A pitiful disaster would almost have occurred had Hyrcanus not supplied food to the struggling Romans through Antipater, and had he not, on Scaurus’s advice, urged Aretas to end the war with money. Thus the Arab rid himself of the enemy with three hundred talents: he bought off Scaurus. This was the price of his withdrawal. The affair strengthened Hyrcanus’s alliance with the Romans and fostered the security of profound peace, since through his efforts the Roman army had passed from severe scarcity to an abundance of grain in hostile territory and had found help at hand.Compare with Bellum [I.19.1] But Alexander, having escaped the Great man’s chains, first secretly gathered a suitable force over some time, then began openly to range through Judaea. Hyrcanus was thrown into alarm and lost confidence in his position; the Romans were pressed by concern lest the war grow. For Alexander had even resolved to rebuild the wall at Jerusalem that the Great man had destroyed. He had almost begun the work when Gabinius, who had succeeded Scaurus, energetically disposed of the other matters by which he had spread the terror of his name, and judged that Alexander’s attempts must be met. Alexander too thought he should not withdraw, but dared to decide the matter in battle with ten thousand infantry and fifteen hundred cavalry. He also repaired the strongholds of Alexandrium, Hyrcania and Machaerus, to serve as refuges for himself if circumstances demanded, or as obstacles to the enemy, since Arabia, not altogether faithful to the Romans, was nearby.Compare with Bellum [I.19.2] To meet him more quickly, Gabinius sent Mark Antony ahead with part of the army, to hinder the enemy’s march until he himself arrived with the entire force. Antipater came with picked men; Malichus and Pitholaus, supported by separate bands of Jews, also joined their strength to Antony’s. When Alexander saw them assembled—for Gabinius too was now present—he changed his plan and decided to fall back. But when he was no longer far from Jerusalem, he was forced to engage in battle, defeated, and fled. Nearly three thousand of his men were killed; the rest were captured or scattered. Scarcely a few remained with Alexander, to share his flight rather than dare further rebellion.Compare with Bellum [I.19.3] Finally, seeking peace from Gabinius, he even handed the strongholds over to the Romans, so that they would have no cause for suspicion. In this war Antony’s valour shone outstandingly, though everywhere he gave a distinguished demonstration of his courage.Compare with Bellum [I.19.4] Gabinius divided Judaea into five districts, to diminish the power from which arrogance arose in whoever gained control of affairs. The honour of the priesthood remained with Hyrcanus because of his gentle temperament, but Gabinius entrusted the care of the whole district of that region not to one man but to the people of Jerusalem in common. The other districts were assigned in the same way, apportioned among the leading citizens of Gadara, Amathus, Jericho and Sepphoris. Thus nothing would be left to the power of individuals, and the discharge of the districts’ duties, which called for public oversight, would not falter. This was welcomed both by the Romans, to relieve their fear of rebellion, and by the Jews, to lay aside resentment: the Hebrew people would live not under a king but under leading men, on the model of the Roman republic. There no single man commanded; rather, the best men, to whom office had fallen by lot, governed in turn, without kingdoms but arbiters of kings.Compare with Bellum [I.20.1] This was thought a prudent measure against the nation’s restlessness. But Aristobulus’s escape and return to Judaea stirred up very great disturbances. Many flocked back to him, attracted by the favour of an old friendship or by desperate circumstances for which they sought a remedy in public discord: they wished to mingle the lowest with the highest, and their other hopes had failed. On his return he began to build fortifications and repair Alexandrium. Learning this, Gabinius sent Sisinnius, Antony and Servilius with part of the army and stopped the work that had begun. For Aristobulus abandoned the fortifications and prepared for war. Since the force he led was greater in numbers than in experience, he rid himself of the burden of the unarmed multitude and mustered only eight thousand armed men. Pitholaus too joined him, having come voluntarily from Jerusalem with a thousand men. Battle followed—for the Romans were upon his neck—and for some time the fighting was vigorous. Roman valour nevertheless prevailed. Five thousand Jews were killed; Aristobulus broke through the line with a thousand men and withdrew into the defences of the stronghold of Machaerus, while two thousand scattered elsewhere. The Romans attacked the stronghold, but were held off for nearly two days, since Aristobulus fought with all his strength in the extremity of danger. Yet he could not hold out longer. Captured with his son Antigonus, whom he had taken with him when escaping from captivity, he was sent to Gabinius, and by him they were sent on to Rome. The senate put Aristobulus under guard but sent his children away to Bithynia. Gabinius is said to have indicated in letters that this had been promised to Aristobulus’s wife, to reward her diligence in handing the fortifications over to him.Compare with Bellum [I.21.1] After these events in Judaea, Gabinius thought he should dare some undertaking and prepared an expedition against the Parthians. But threatening developments on King Ptolemy’s side turned his advance back. For Gabinius changed his route from the Euphrates to Egypt, using in every matter the necessary services of Antipater and Hyrcanus—but Hyrcanus through Antipater. They helped the army with money, grain, arms and auxiliaries as well. Above all, the engagements around Pelusium would easily have deterred Gabinius had the Jews, familiar with the terrain and every aspect of that kind of warfare, not attended to everything. But while the army lingered, Alexander, Aristobulus’s son, was again preparing to throw himself into the other Syria as though into an unoccupied province. He would have done so had Gabinius not been stirred by the reports to hasten his return and send Antipater ahead to draw very many Jews away from Alexander’s alliance. Relying on their numbers, Alexander was preparing to destroy all the Romans he had found in the region. Even though many of the Jews had dispersed through Antipater’s intervention, he had not laid aside his audacity. He attacked with thirty thousand men around Mount Itabyrion, but fled when ten thousand were cut down. The scattering of the remainder ended the war. Gabinius arranged the public affairs of Jerusalem at Antipater’s discretion and departed. He subdued the Nabataeans in battle and secretly released Mithridates and Orsanes, who were fleeing from Persia; publicly, however, he told the soldiers that they had escaped by flight.Compare with Bellum [I.21.2] Crassus succeeded Gabinius. Before setting out for the Parthian war, he took away all the gold in the temple at Jerusalem and ordered that the two thousand talents Pompey had left untouched should also be removed. His joy did not last long: once he crossed the Euphrates, he lost his army and was himself killed.Compare with Bellum [I.21.3] Elated by this success, the Parthians thought they should cross into Syria. Cassius vigorously met them with an ambush and drove them from the boundaries of the province entrusted to him, inflicting no small loss upon the enemy. They had come on without restraint, thinking that no one would dare oppose them, and he had got ahead of them and caught them in narrower places. Thus, after many of their men had been cut down, they abandoned the war. Having repelled the enemy and secured the province, Cassius rushed into Judaea. He destroyed Tarichaeae and sold thirty thousand Jews into slavery. He also ordered Pitholaus to have his throat cut, suspecting him of a deceitful design to support Aristobulus’s side. Nor was Antipater uninvolved in that decision: he wished to exclude a rival for power as completely as possible.Compare with Bellum [I.22.1] He took as his wife a woman named Cypris, born to the most illustrious rank among the women of Arabia, and by her had four male children and one female. The males had these names: the first was called Phasael, the next Herod, the third Josephus, the fourth Pheroras; the daughter was Salome. For this reason a man outstandingly fitted to win the alliance of the powerful through gifts and friendship had secured the favour of the king of the Arabs above all others: he invoked the bond of kinship through the wife he had taken from the lands of Arabia. When preparing to fight Aristobulus, he sent his sons to the aforesaid king of the Arabs as pledges of mutual love. The king received them as an inviolable deposit, kept them in his house with the same care as his own children, and later returned them to their father when they were requested.Compare with Bellum [I.22.2] But while Aristobulus, defeated in war, was held in chains, his son Alexander refrained from battle under the terms of peace by which Cassius, about to return to the Euphrates, had bound him. The frontiers of Persia were troubled by no Parthian incursion, and an appearance of soothing tranquillity in the regions of the East relieved human anxieties. Caesar poured into Italy from the regions of Gaul beyond the Alps and drove Pompey and the senate across the Ionian Sea. Excluded from Italy, the Great man made for Emathia and ordered Roman forces from various places to follow him there, to prepare for war. Intent on these affairs, he had left Aristobulus in chains at Rome. Caesar was between the city of Rome and Pompey, following the Great man by short routes from the Flaminian Way to the Appian Way, to catch either the man himself or his army. He released Aristobulus from his chains, gave him military units as well, and sent him to Syria to bring Judaea to his side and press Pompey from the rear. But at the beginning of his attempts, once he reached the place, Aristobulus was killed by poison and left the undertaking unfinished. His death was attributed in common report to Pompey’s supporters. Thus Caesar’s arrangements were frustrated and Aristobulus’s ambitions defeated, in a strange variety of reversals: he had been safer as an exile among enemies, a captive in chains, than among his own citizens, master in his chamber, king at a banquet.Compare with Bellum [I.22.3] When Pompey learned that Aristobulus had tried to renew war against him in Judaea, he also ordered Aristobulus’s son Alexander to have his throat cut, deeply suspicious of his support for Caesar’s side. He gave the order to Scipio. In obedience, Scipio brought the accused before the tribunal to display the appearance of a trial. Accusers were also produced, and sentence was pronounced against a man who had disturbed the Roman republic by arms. Thus he was to be thought convicted of rebellion and struck with the axe, in the manner of enemy commanders, by the authority of law rather than in execution of an order.Compare with Bellum [I.23.1] When the deaths of both became known, Ptolemy, who had taken in Aristobulus’s brothers and his wife Alexandra, sent his son Philippion to the city of Ascalon to summon those mentioned. On arriving, Philippion received Antigonus and his sisters to take them to his father. Through familiarity and companionship a little flame of love stole upon the young man—surely forgivable, if tyrants knew how to forgive—and he took one of the sisters as his wife. His father Ptolemy could not endure this: he killed his son and married his own daughter-in-law. An outstanding censor of morals, who condemned in his son a marriage for which his consent had not been sought, so that he himself might be defiled by murder of kin and incest! Affairs changed when Pompey was killed: fleeing Caesar’s arms, he had offered his head to be cut off by an Egyptian eunuch. Yet he presented his head with the endurance fitting for a man who had so often conquered so many peoples. Seeing in his defeat the lot of an exile, a plaything of human reversals, he offered his neck to the sword, to receive death as his thanks from the man to whom he had given a kingdom.Compare with Bellum [I.23.2] After his death a change took place: many of the Great man’s friends sought Caesar’s friendship, and above all Antipater, endowed to an incredible degree with the ability to win the friendship of anyone he wished. For everyone needs resources, especially in preparations for war, when men who were enemies and opponents very often become all the dearer.Compare with Bellum [I.24.1] For Ptolemy, king of Egypt, had broken faith and was being pressed by Caesar himself in the gravest warfare. Mithridates of Pergamum, repulsed with all the force he had brought by the obstacles at Pelusium, had settled in the city of Ascalon. Despairing of passage and with his attempt frustrated, he no longer dared commit himself to battle on unfavourable ground and with inferior strength. Antipater first enlisted the Arabs to help him, then brought with him a strong, well-armed force of three thousand Jews. He also roused the powerful men of Syria to his aid: Ptolemy, who lived in Lebanon, Iamblichus, and another Ptolemy. Relying on their alliance, other peoples too were stirred to war. Supported by these additional forces, Mithridates approached Pelusium and, when denied passage, began a siege. There Antipater gave a distinguished demonstration of military ability. While the townspeople resisted and both sides fought with all their strength, he was the first to break into the city with his men, through a breach in the part of the walls where he himself was fighting, and he captured it.Compare with Bellum [I.24.2] Yet this was not the end of his labour and assistance. As the army advanced further inland, the Egyptian Jews around the district called that of Onias wished to resist and block its passage. Antipater again not only averted battle but brought it about that the very people who had prepared arms against them supplied the army with the necessities of human life. Hence the people of Memphis too turned their minds from battle and willingly joined Mithridates’s alliance. Having passed beyond the more suspect places, Mithridates thought he must engage the remaining Egyptians. The ground was more open, but the men of that region, whose settlement was called the Army of the Jews, were stronger. He fought so vigorously that he put himself in headlong danger and would almost have been killed had Antipater not seen the whole right wing, where Mithridates was, hard pressed by the enemy and enclosed on another side by the river, with no escape for the men. From the left wing Antipater rushed upon those pursuing the retreating Mithridates and pursued them until the entire body of the enemy was destroyed. In that battle Antipater lost only eighty of his men, Mithridates more than eight hundred; his own escape was beyond expectation. This disaster befell in a single moment. Antipater received many wounds in his body and won outstanding testimony to his valour before Caesar, particularly from Mithridates, who not only gave an account of his deliverance but proclaimed Antipater’s courage.Compare with Bellum [I.24.3] Greatly delighted by these things, Caesar received Antipater with honour among his friends, as was fitting. Then, after arranging what needed to be settled in Egypt and advancing into Syria, he bestowed on him honours of the Roman state. He also granted exemption from taxes and imparted other pledges of his favour, as to a man he had found worthy. At Antipater’s recommendation, he also willingly confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood.Compare with Bellum [I.25.1] Antigonus too met Caesar in Syria. It would have been fitting for him to lament either the misfortune of his father, who had been killed by poison at the hands of Pompey’s friends, or the execution of his brother, whom Scipio, with the utmost cruelty, had struck down with the axe as though he were a criminal. Instead, he acted from envy rather than grief. With the most vehement complaints he piled up accusations that Hyrcanus and Antipater were occupying the possessions of others, which had been criminally wrested from himself and his brothers. He had been made an exile from his father’s dwelling; the land where he was born was denied him. Yet the wrongs done to him seemed more tolerable: far more bitter were those Hyrcanus and Antipater inflicted upon the whole nation of the Jewish people. They claimed favour for their successes in Egypt, although no diligence arising from an innate goodwill towards Caesar had prompted their service in helping Mithridates. Rather, fear arising from the consciousness of their alliance with Pompey had wrung it from them, to provide a shield against offence.Compare with Bellum [I.25.2] Against these charges Antipater offered not words in return but the proof of deeds. He tore his clothing and, bare of garments but covered in wounds, displayed the signs of his proven valour to the eyes of those around him, his cloak ripped open. “Look,” he said, “let these testimonies to my ill will towards Caesar defend the accused: they shine like lights of the soul.
