At Herod’s departure he offered thirty talents as gifts of hospitality and accompanied the king as far as Zephyrium.Compare with Bellum [I.38.7] Upon returning home, the king immediately summoned the people and addressed them in this manner.Compare with Bellum [I.39.1] “Hebrew citizens, my reason for going to Rome proved both useful and fruitful: Caesar was to judge my sons, so that I, who was angry, should not hear the case alone. I went to Caesar so that the man who had restored my kingdom might pronounce upon my successor. He added to his benefits by doing what was difficult: restoring almost lost sons to their father, and restoring to brothers concord, which stands above kingship. I therefore return richer than when I set out. I have learnt to be a better father, because my sons have learnt to be better children, through Caesar’s benefit. For he determined that my sons’ succession should depend upon my decision: lest the privilege of succession engender arrogance, I myself should appoint as my successor the man I chose, the man who had deserved it, the man who had honoured his father more. I shall imitate Caesar, for by acquitting my younger sons he made them equal to my elder son. Thus today I appoint my three children kings together. Age supports the one, noble birth the others. Let their number trouble no one: the greatness of the kingdom is abundant enough for even more. Let God first judge my decision; then you too should join in. Honour fittingly those whom Caesar has united and their father appointed, so that their honour is neither excessive nor too low. The one inflates, the other exasperates. Let each be granted what is appropriate to his share. For a man does not so much please the person he honours beyond measure as wound the person to whom he denies his due. Often both are offended where flattery shows preference. I am certainly father to them all: honour paid to my sons is surely a favour to their father. Yet if anyone honours my children beyond measure, he is answerable to me also on my children’s behalf, for he brings about their downfall. Excessive honour supplies the means for audacity. Do I envy my children? Far from it. But I prefer them to have less power with goodwill than very great power with sedition. What belongs to arrogance or rapacity soon slips away; what belongs to goodwill is held for a long time. I shall therefore take care to attach relatives and friends to my children as guarantors of concord, through whose exhortation they may clothe themselves in mutual affection. For, while every evil utterance readily infects the hearer’s mind, continual conversations and prolonged familiarity especially tend to pour a plague into minds, which soon passes, as by contagion, into the conduct of those living together. Even if their conduct is tranquil, just as a pool, though calm, can rise in surges when stirred by winds, so a good nature is tossed by wicked advisers. I therefore think that each man ought to place his greatest hope for himself in me, for what accrues to my children is not lost to me. Each tribune or soldier should show greater reverence to the father of his commanders. I am the one, I am the one who will repay you all even for what you have bestowed upon my sons. If I observe upright efforts, I shall reward them in deeds. Ill will will receive its price, losing its reward even with the man it thought it should flatter. But you, good sons, consider first the sacred obligation of nature, whose affection binds even beasts and compels even wild creatures to love their kin. Mutual love remains among untamed animals, and beasts redeem their own by endangering themselves. Revere Caesar too, who has made you friends instead of enemies; and thirdly myself, who prefer to ask when I can command. Remain brothers; do not cast off what you were born. I give you the dress and splendour of rulers, but more precious is the inviolate seal of your love that I urge upon you. If family devotion remains, kingship delights; if affection is absent, rule is worthless and often harmful. Thus, while I put you to the test, for the present you have the honour of kingship, not the kingdom. If you love your father, the right will follow. Yet demonstrate your love for me among yourselves: as rulers you will enjoy everything by which kingship usually delights, while the burdens of rule and the mass of affairs will await me alone, even if I am unwilling. It is therefore to your advantage to wish what I wish, since I both wish for what is yours and consider it mine.” With these words he kissed his sons, so as to bind them to one another with a single kiss of love. Having done so, he dismissed the assembly.Compare with Bellum [I.40.1] Many departed happy, pleased by the concord between the brothers, but discord returned with the brothers, all the graver because their greater rank aroused more envy and supplied greater power to do harm. Mariamne’s sons resented being placed on an equal footing with the son of a private woman whose lineage knew nothing of kingship. Antipater, on the other hand, disdained having the hope of kingship divided between himself and his brothers, and envied his brothers, for whom even a lower place was scarcely reserved instead of the first. But he concealed and veiled himself, covering his hatred with a show of favour, while their every design lay open in their speech even to those who did not seek it, their tongue too ready and lavish with secrets. Whatever they had said reached Antipater at once; much that they had not said was also fabricated. The messenger added a great deal by way of amplification. Antipater was the architect of everything by which his brothers were assailed. His life was nothing other than a meeting place of cunning devices, a stage of wickedness, a plot of crimes, a mystery of disgraceful deeds. He planted informers, suborned witnesses and feigned a defence, carrying about the mask of a brother as though in a theatre, so as to shake off the lighter charges and yield to the graver ones, thereby deceiving his father more and stirring him more violently against his brothers. Above all, he skilfully aggravated the odium of a plan to kill their father and seize the kingdom, matters more suspicious to kings through fear of danger. Yet, lest the charges seem less credible to the king without anyone to rebut them, he first attempted to refute them himself and then wished to appear constrained by manifest evidence of the facts. With the case pleaded on both sides, as though nothing had been lacking in the trial, their father would be roused all the more against his sons as men convicted. For nothing lent greater credibility to the assertions than that Antipater was thought to be his brothers’ defender. Through this fraud he courted the favour of very many and inclined even his father’s mind towards himself.Compare with Bellum [I.40.2] Whatever was daily taken from his brothers’ share of their father’s affection was transferred to him. He drew away the king’s friends and relatives, and especially estranged the king’s brother Pheroras and his sister Salome from their nephews, so that they not only failed to defend them but also assailed and hated them. Alexander’s wife Glaphyra added material for hatred. With womanly insolence in her present circumstances, she had begun to exalt herself in proud disdain because she surpassed everyone in the distinction of her lineage. Thus she set herself above everyone in the royal palace as though their mistress, habitually boasting that her father and grandfather were kings, and especially that Darius Hystaspes was the summit of her maternal line. She insulted the king’s sister Salome and his wife Dosis for their low birth, which caused them grief and brought hatred upon herself. She similarly exasperated the other women joined to the king for their beauty rather than the nobility of their birth. For Herod delighted in very many women, not only according to royal custom but also by the practice of the Jews, as though with a certain licence for error: they use the figures of their ancestors as a cover for their own vices. Alexander was therefore burdened by his wife’s insolence.Compare with Bellum [I.40.3] Aristobulus too assailed his wife with the same words as Glaphyra: she was of lowly standing, could not be compared with royal offspring and was unequal to Glaphyra. It was a reproach to him that his brother enjoyed marriage to a woman of royal birth, while he himself had fallen below his birth by cohabiting with a private woman. Madman, to disturb his own bonds of kinship with abuse! Stung by these insults, Aristobulus’s wife reported them to her mother in tears. Salome in turn reported to King Herod what she had learnt through her daughter.Compare with Bellum [I.40.4] But he, thinking it better to warn his sons than destroy them, summoned them. In part he terrified them with a commander’s authority, in part he urged them with a father’s affection to love their brother and not be divided as enemies, forgiving past offences and threatening correction for future ones. Lamenting that they were assailed by many fabricated accusations, they pleaded and at the same time promised that henceforth their very deeds would lend credibility to their defence, if only their father would look at what was done and not rashly believe what he heard. For wicked informers would not be lacking so long as a credulous listener was available.Compare with Bellum [I.40.5] With these and similar words they softened their father. Although for the moment they drove away the fear that threatened them, they nevertheless increased their sorrow, seeing themselves pressed by Pheroras and Salome: the one their paternal uncle, the other their father’s sister, plotting against those whom they should have defended. For a grave fear was added by their very great influence with their brother. Except for the diadem, Herod had shared almost the whole power of the kingdom with his brother, and had bestowed no small wealth upon them both, especially Pheroras. Indeed, he put away a hundred talents each year, apart from the region situated beyond the Euphrates that multiplied his abundant revenues. He had also been appointed tetrarch by Caesar at Herod’s request and granted kinship with the king’s wife, since he had taken the queen’s sister in marriage. After her death, with the king’s elder daughter betrothed to him, he would have gained the favour of a son-in-law had he not, captive to love for a young slave woman, declined marriage to the royal girl. Exasperated by this affront, Herod gave his daughter to a man who later died in the Parthian war.Compare with Bellum [I.40.6] Nevertheless, when Pheroras was accused before him of having assailed his brother’s life with poison—a suspicion from which he had not been free even while his wife was alive—Herod willingly acquitted him after an interrogation first of very many people and finally of his friends had found him innocent of the deed of which he was accused. He also pardoned his planned flight: the confessions of his household disclosed his intention to carry off the slave woman he loved and flee to the Parthians. Alexander had breathed a little more freely while Pheroras was being assailed and Pheroras himself was assailing Salome for having promised to marry Syllaeus, Obodas’s man, who was the king of Arabia’s procurator and most hostile to Herod.Compare with Bellum [I.40.7] But when both were pardoned their offence, the storm of the household settled upon Alexander and enveloped him in grave danger. For Antipater, the savage plague and tempest of the whole palace, raged, bearing down upon his brother by every means and even through the concerted action of his relatives. His father’s sober state of mind was so disturbed that he loudly declared Alexander was standing over him with a sword. A scene of this kind had been brought forward: Alexander had enticed three eunuchs with more lavish gifts into his favour and participation in a shameful deed. One of them habitually served the king’s drinks, another brought in the dishes at dinner, and the third watched over the royal bed and never went away once Herod had lain down. When this was revealed, the eunuchs were compelled by torture to disclose the degrading acts of obscene lust. Unable to conceal the amorous promises either, they disclosed the words with which they had been solicited and the reward for illicit intercourse, so that a plan to murder his father might be believed beneath the disgrace. Through the charm of youth he possessed beauty of form and the strength of his years, whereas Herod was weak and already burdened by old age, dyeing his hair lest he reveal his years. Alexander could transfer the right to reign from Herod to himself whenever he wished. He promised immense rewards, and so they should place their hope in a young man, not in a decrepit old man whose end nature itself was hastening.Compare with Bellum [I.40.8] These things moved Herod deeply, but above all the eunuchs’ disclosure that had informed him that a body of soldiers, commanders of the army and centurions were conspiring with Alexander. Indeed, he was so agitated that he thought no kind of cruelty should be passed over, trusted no one and suspected everyone. Punishments were swifter than the investigation of crimes, and the death of the accused preceded judgement. Everywhere those assailed by any suspicion were seized for punishment. False accusations raged. Many, wishing to please the king, denounced the accused; but immediately the very men who had denounced others were themselves denounced and led to the place of punishment with those they had accused. Thus Herod had grown savage towards everyone, so that anyone left alive was suspect, the king thinking himself safe only if the human race should fail. He was irreconcilable towards the accused, distrustful of friends, arrogant towards his household, pitiless towards those on trial, fearful of everything, so that he frequently changed his quarters and spent sleepless nights. Exasperated by all these things, he suddenly bound Alexander in chains, surrounded him with guards and summoned his friends for interrogation. Those who denied the charges died under torture; those who remained silent in turn were torn with wounds to the very end of life because they confessed nothing that agreed with the suspicions. Yet some, overcome by the bitterness of the tortures and punishments, asserted that the young men had resolved to kill their father while he was intent upon hunting and to go to the city of Rome without delay, so as to evade punishment by flight. Although this was supported by no evidence, their father turned it to the consolation of his savage purpose, wishing to have just grounds for his son’s chains.Compare with Bellum [I.40.9] Alexander therefore considered that his father’s ears were barred against every defence of him, and that matters could in no way be brought to the point where Alexander could rely on his own innocence, assailed as he was by so great a mass of false accusations. He thought he should meet the most wicked informers with similar skill, deceiving the fraudulent fabricators of false accusations by cunning and arraigning on a false charge those by whose false accusations he believed himself oppressed. He therefore wrote four booklets in which he confessed the invented crime of having assailed his father’s life, and named as accomplices in plots of this kind many of those by whom he himself was assailed. In the same booklets he named Pheroras and Salome especially: she too had broken into the young man’s bedroom in the dead of night, enticed him against his will and compelled him, despite his resistance, to commit incest. He sent the booklets to the king as though disclosures of his own crimes, implicating in them all the king’s most powerful companions and friends. Archelaus arrived hastily in Judaea at the right moment to bring his son-in-law and daughter whatever help and support he could. But, foreseeing that access to a lawful defence was barred before the most hostile father, he restrained his agitation by cunning. For as soon as he entered the royal palace, already within Herod’s sight and hearing, he began shouting loudly as though beside himself with fury: “Is that sorcerer, my son-in-law, still alive, still enjoying this light? Where is he, I ask? Where shall I find that murderous creature who plotted against his father, so that I may tear him apart with my own hands? A kinsman must kill the man who wished to kill his kin. What will he do to his father-in-law if he has not spared his father? Who will point him out? I shall first tear out the scoundrel’s entrails, then add my daughter to her fine bridegroom. Even if she was not an accomplice in the crime, she is not free from its contamination, since she enjoyed marriage to a would-be murderer of his father. I do not acknowledge a daughter who failed to detect her husband’s devices and failed to show herself such a daughter-in-law to her father-in-law as to make his son subject to him. I joined her to him not to serve crime but to share marriage, so that she should show herself a coheir of favour, not a helper in crime. I am surprised at you, Herod, if that Alexander, who plotted against his father, still lives. I thought he had already paid the just penalty and should not have been put off: why should a man who has confessed to attempting his father’s murder be kept alive any longer? But perhaps this too belonged to divine providence, that the judgement of both parents should condemn the man who, in you, violated the family devotion of both. I shall not refuse to act as avenger, though I was preparing to proclaim the vengeance already exacted. Nor do I except my daughter, whom I myself betrothed in that ill-fated marriage, relying upon you as guarantor. For I entrusted her not to her husband’s character but to your faithfulness. Let her give an account of why she disregarded her guarantor and loved her husband. We must now judge them both. If you are resolute in exacting satisfaction for so great a grief, gird yourself. Father, set family devotion aside: it is indeed no task for fathers to wish for, but neither one to disregard. If family devotion softens you and nature bends you, let us exchange roles, so that I may act upon your son and you upon my child in the execution of this mutual service.”Compare with Bellum [I.40.10] Blustering in this manner, Archelaus swayed Herod and gradually softened his furious resolve, so that Herod entrusted himself to Archelaus as one who shared his suffering and his mind, and gave him the booklets Alexander had written to read. Attending to each detail, Archelaus understood that they had been piled together from grief rather than founded on truth. With deep calculation he began gradually to diminish the odium of the attempted murder of a father and to transfer responsibility for the charges to those named, especially Pheroras. Thus, when he perceived that the king was not averse to his opinion, he said: “We must consider whether the young man has perhaps been assailed before you by the plots of so many wicked men, rather than you by the young man. For what reason had he to assail your life, when you had granted him the honour of kingship and reserved for him the right to reign and the hope of succession? Why should he seek what he already had, or how could he be ungrateful for such great gifts? What else would he achieve by your death but seek his own danger, which he could not fear while you lived but would fear once you were dead, from those very men by whom, even while under his father’s protection, he dreaded the destruction of his own life? That age lies open to deceit: it is readily deceived and circumvented by the plots of fraudulent men. Old age scarcely withstands cunning, and yet often even the prudence of the old is ensnared by the devices of deceivers. Therefore, if more mature experience has often been assailed, what wonder if a less mature age could not come to its own aid when it was pressed by throngs of conspirators?” Those men, then, were the disturbers of the royal house, the inciters of the young men, the sowers of discord. They had brought the young man to despair of his safety, so that he had indulged his anger, aimed at vengeance rather than acquittal, and yielded something to his agitation.Compare with Bellum [I.40.11] With these words Herod had begun gradually to relent and soften his indignation towards Alexander, but to be moved more violently against Pheroras, since the four booklets portrayed him as the agent of every crime and architect of the whole scene. Seeing that the king had inclined his mind towards Archelaus and bestowed upon him above all others the favour of intimate friendship, Pheroras went to him, begging him to restore the king’s mind to reconciliation with him. But Archelaus said that he was entangled in very many bonds of crime, by which he was clearly proved to have plotted against the king and assailed the young man. There was no room for pardon unless, laying aside the cunning of denial, he did not hesitate to confess the charges to the brother who loved him and ask his forgiveness. Archelaus would not fail such a course with whatever efforts he could make.Compare with Bellum [I.40.12] So, changing his clothes and bathed in tears, a pitiable sight, he clung to his brother’s feet, begged pardon and confessed his wickedness. He did not deny anything of which he was accused but acknowledged it all: madness had caused so great a fall, since excessive fury of love for the woman he cherished had blazed up within him. With Pheroras thus established as both accuser and witness of his own crimes, Archelaus, as though in reward for the fabrication of an argument that would serve his own purposes, entreated Herod to soften his anger out of regard for nature and forgive his brother, setting the right of nature above vengeance. Nor was it strange if, in very great kingdoms as in great bodies, some part often became inflamed: it should be treated with gentler medicines, not cut away. His own brother too had laid much graver plots against him, but for the sake of kinship he had remitted what was owed to his grief. The more he lightened the ungrateful man’s punishment, the more he aggravated his case.Compare with Bellum [I.40.13] By adding these and similar arguments, he did indeed soften Herod into forgiving his brother, but himself remained seemingly implacable towards his son-in-law. Indeed, he threatened to tear his daughter away from him and raged with such violent indignation that Herod himself thought his son’s offence against him sufficiently expiated. He begged the avenger of his injuries and himself intervened for his own accused son before his father-in-law, asking him to renew the marriage afresh. Archelaus persisted: Herod could join his daughter-in-law to anyone else he wished except Alexander, on whose account even his wife was discredited. By this device he impelled Herod much further, so that he thought his son would be restored to him if his marriage were not dissolved. Alexander dearly loved his wife, by whom he had also had children, sweet to their grandfather and dear to their parents. This would be the gift of a son restored to him, since to no small extent a good wife restrained her husband’s errors or compensated by her attentiveness for the odium of his crimes. If she were torn away from him, her husband would have no remedy to keep him from rushing headlong into every wickedness. For criminal audacity was usually softened when checked by affection at home. At length, with difficulty, Archelaus relented, was himself reconciled to his son-in-law and reconciled his father to him. By this design he rescued his son-in-law from death, receiving his acquittal as a reward while pretending to condemn rather than intervene. Had he thought to plead for him, he would undoubtedly have obtained nothing. Archelaus added that Alexander ought to go to Rome to clear himself of what his father had suspected in him, since Archelaus himself had written everything to Caesar. I think this too was contrived, so that in this way, when Alexander had cleared himself, he might be commended to Caesar and the plots Antipater had prepared against his brothers might be exposed.Compare with Bellum [I.41.1] By this design the faction was dissolved and there was a change to joy. A banquet was renewed as a sign of the reconciliation achieved. Archelaus, its author, was presented with seventy talents, a golden seat adorned with gems and chosen eunuchs, with royal magnificence. A concubine named Pannychis was also given and accepted as a gift. At the king’s prompting, his relatives likewise bestowed most splendid gifts upon Archelaus. Nor did any of his companions go without a gift: Herod bestowed very much upon all these men of his, according to each man’s deserts. As Archelaus returned to his kingdom, Herod also accompanied him with his powerful men as far as the most splendid city in Syria, named Antioch.Compare with Bellum [I.41.2] Alexander would have escaped had a man far more practised in devices than Archelaus not thrust himself into Judaea: a Laconian by birth named Eurycles, excessively greedy for wealth yet ready to disdain it as business required whenever the hope of gaining more shone forth. Indeed, not content with the resources of Laconia, he had set his mind on royal lavishness. Skilled in the hunt, he approached Herod with rich gifts, preparing the way for the most ample repayment. Although he obtained far more than he had offered, he was still not satisfied unless he became bloodstained and bought the king’s favour through impious intrigues. Thus, in a manner and practice familiar to Greeks, by flattering the king and praising everything about him—not only what had no claim to praise but even what was entangled in vice—he soon attained his most intimate friendship, so as to be chosen among the foremost confidants of his secrets. The privilege of his homeland also supported him, since the Jews regard the Spartans as brothers, joined to them by kinship of descent.Compare with Bellum [I.41.3] Once he knew the vices of the royal house, the father’s suspicious mind and the brothers’ hatred of one another, he used novel devices to pretend he was dear to everyone and was regarded as faithful to each. But he shaped his efforts according to the king’s disposition or the value of gifts, so as to be more closely attached to Antipater and circumvent Alexander by cunning and plots. With a show of friendship he exasperated both: the kingdom was owed to the one by the privilege of age, while the other, endowed with the nobility of his maternal line, was rightly superior and had no equal partnership with the offspring of the vilest debauchery. Captivated by these words as a younger man, delighting in what was said to him without weighing what in turn was being fabricated about him before Antipater, Alexander poured himself out to Antipater’s hireling and his own betrayer. With an unsteady disposition and incautious affection, he opened his mind, complaining that his father was the author of his troubles. He had taken his mother from him and dishonoured the kingdom, which he wished to divert from Alexander although it was owed to him through his grandfather and the distinctions of his ancient lineage. The legitimate sons were being defrauded of their right of succession, and a bastard preferred as the reward for illicit intercourse. But God’s judgements would not long remain still: the man who had killed an innocent wife would himself soon be deprived of the rule he had gained through his wife. The Laconian conveyed these things to Antipater without delay, having also deceived Aristobulus into being caught in the snares of the same complaint. For a price, he brought them before the king in an accumulated heap, saying that he could not keep silent about so monstrous a deed and that, in return for the gift of hospitality, he was repaying the benefit of the light of life, which the sons were proceeding to take away. Had he himself not called them back by pretending to offer more faithful counsel, their father would long since have been killed by Alexander’s sword and the kingdom left vacant for unworthy heirs. Nor did Alexander feel a religious scruple about the atrocity of killing his father, since he considered it the greatest crime that they still held their grandfather’s and mother’s deaths unavenged. The complaints of the slain confronted and pressed him, demanding that they avenge so terrible a deed: funeral offerings for the slain were required of him; blood was demanded. Their succession ought not to be contaminated by his receiving the kingdom from the man who had killed their forebears. He would renew the proceedings before Caesar, not with the same reverence as before, but so that Caesar himself might learn all the king’s secrets: wealth acquired through blood and a province undermined. He would recall his grandfather from the underworld and set forth his mother’s most bitter murder, so that an outsider might be appointed successor to the kingdom.Compare with Bellum [I.41.4] Eurycles had roused the king, but Antipater, thinking little of one man’s report, also suborned other accusers against his brothers. They were to say that a conversation had taken place with Jucundus and Tyrannus, former commanders of the cavalry, and that plots had been laid against the king out of grief at their removal: danger was at his neck unless he took precautions quickly. Herod did not delay: he had them seized at once and interrogated them severely, but they were found to have confessed nothing of the charges. Since such grave things could be fabricated with impunity before a man who professed himself an avenger of crimes but disregarded false accusations, there was no lack of people to devise plots of this kind, believing they would be more acceptable to the father. For a letter was also produced as though sent by Alexander and Aristobulus to the commander of a fortress, asking him to allow them to take refuge there after the king had been killed, until they could defend themselves with arms against their pursuers and prepare protection with other resources. The fortress commander was tortured and confessed nothing.Compare with Bellum [I.41.5] Nevertheless, although no evidence of the intended crime existed, Alexander and Aristobulus were placed in custody as though guilty. Eurycles was rewarded with fifty talents and regarded as the author of the king’s safety and life.Compare with Bellum [I.41.6] It is fitting not to pass over the Coan either. He had crossed to Judaea in Eurycles’s time and was one of Alexander’s most faithful friends. Thinking that he knew of Alexander’s attempts, the king considered that he should be questioned about whether what the Spartan had disclosed about the young men agreed with the truth. But, pledging an oath, he gave assurance that he knew nothing of the kind about them; yet it did the young men no good. Herod put an end to the questioning, lest the man, if questioned more severely, diminish the odium of the denunciation and undo Eurycles’s deceit by denying it. Thus he was excluded by Herod as though unworthy of belief. For the good father gladly heard his sons accused but did not allow them to be defended; he delighted when they were assailed and took offence when they were cleared. The Spartan, however, enriched by royal rewards, paid the price of his false accusations once he reached Achaea.Compare with Bellum [I.41.7] Salome could not clear herself of having agreed to marry Syllaeus the Arab. But when she betrayed her son-in-law’s confidential warning to look to her own safety and escape her brother’s agitation, since she was being accused on suspicion of reporting the king’s plans to the Arab in the hope of their future union, she obtained pardon for her offence and turned the entire storm of royal savagery upon the young men. Submerged in that final and inescapable shipwreck, they paid the penalty. They were therefore bound, and, what was harder for them than chains, the brothers were separated from one another. Volumnius, master of the soldiers, and Olympus, a man among the king’s friends, were sent to accuse them before Caesar. Although offended that a father sought the punishment of his sons, Caesar nevertheless thought a father should not be denied authority over his children and granted him licence. But he added advice: it would be better to assemble a council of the king’s relatives and the provincial governors, and for the inquiry to proceed by their common judgement as to whether the sons had laid any plots against their father. If they were proved to have attempted their father’s murder, they should be put to death; but if accused of flight or lighter offences, the punishment should be more moderate.Compare with Bellum [I.41.8] Granted this power to kill his own children, but on condition of a trial and with an admonition to moderation, Herod immediately hastened to the city of Berytus, which Caesar had prescribed for holding the trial. The provincial governors assembled in accordance with the instructions sent to them by the Roman ruler Caesar. Saturninus and the legates took their seats, among them the procurator Volumnius, followed by the king’s relatives and friends, Salome and Pheroras too, and the leading men of Syria. Archelaus alone, king of Cappadocia, was excluded, charged with suspect favour towards his son-in-law, while the young men’s accusers and those who plotted against them constituted the court. But what semblance of a trial was there, when the accused were not allowed to appear for themselves and were accused in their absence? For Herod perceived that if they were merely seen, they would be acquitted, human nature being inclined to pity, especially where there was a privileged claim upon natural affection. Moreover, if Alexander were allowed any opportunity of defence, he would easily demolish the charges.Compare with Bellum [I.41.9] Thus, with them banished to a village of the Sidonians, the accusation was directed against them as though present. Their father charged them with plots laid against him; no proof was offered, no evidence of attempts. The accuser faltered, although no one contradicted him. Unsupported on every side, he gathered together kinds of insult to arouse odium, so that those who sat in judgement might consider them graver than death. But no one discussed them, no one dared examine what was alleged by a father and commanded by a king. The appearance of family devotion prejudged the case; the right of power terrified them. He asked their opinions, confident of victory, unaware that in a trial of this kind the victor was more wretched than those so bitterly condemned. Saturninus condemned the young men because nothing else was permitted, but moderated his sentence, declaring that care should be taken lest, if two of the three brothers were killed, the death of the two be attributed to the third. Timidly, indeed, but he had stated the cause: that brother was the author of his brothers’ danger. A few out of many followed him. Volumnius, however, muttered a deadly judgement, and after him everyone, weighing what the king wanted with such a man to lead them, pronounced a sentence of death, with differing feelings indeed but the same outcome. Flattery had extorted it from some, hatred instilled it in others: either they sought the king’s favour, or they wished the cruelty of a murderer of his own children to be visited with a graver punishment, since in his victory he would have won so bitter a triumph over himself. Yet no one recoiled as at an actual deed and pronounced judgement as though moved by it. For it was the semblance of a stage, not the discipline of a court, to condemn absent men, to condemn without witness or informer, solely by the privilege of nature, which was usually directed towards safety rather than danger. All Syria and all Judaea were stunned, and with minds aghast awaited the end of so great a tragedy. For, although Herod’s cruelty was known, no one could believe that he would persist to the point of killing his own children. But in him the savage force of his mind was restrained by neither sea nor land. Thus, as though celebrating a triumph, he dragged his sons from place to place, going to the illustrious city of Tyre and from there crossing by ship to Caesarea, carrying about the wretched spectacle of the murder of his own children, until some pretext could be found for their most bitter death.Compare with Bellum [I.41.10] The whole army was moved, but fear restrained their indignation. There was in the royal army a man of long service named Tiro, who had a son attached to Alexander. He was a most indulgent father and for that reason dear to his child, since family devotion has a certain universal charm and especially draws one’s own people to love. He was also more inclined in his attachment to the king’s young sons because they loved his son. Overcome by indignation beyond measure and troubled in mind, he began to cry out that justice was being oppressed, truth excluded, religion abolished, the rights of kinship confounded and natural affection overwhelmed by injustices. At last, advancing into the king’s very presence, he charged him to his face with being wretched for thinking that the most wicked men should be believed against his sons. Pheroras and Salome were chosen as counsellors: what faithfulness could come from those who knew that they had very often been condemned to death by the king? What else were they doing but looking to vengeance, so that, bereft of suitable successors, he would incline towards the one weaker than the others, who could easily be removed? The royal army itself would pursue with hatred the man to whom the death of his two brothers had been paid. There was no one untouched by pity for innocent youth. Moreover, many of the commanders were no longer restraining their indignation but making it known.Compare with Bellum [I.41.11] After giving their names, he finished speaking. They were immediately seized with Tiro. Tryphon, one of the servants of the royal palace, who possessed the skill and practice of a barber, suddenly made a disclosure against himself through some foolish impulse. He asserted that Tiro had devised a plan and persuaded him to press his razor into Herod’s throat until he killed him while shaving his beard as usual. It would bring him a very great reward, which Tiro promised from Alexander’s gifts. Tiro was brought forward with his son, and the informer was interrogated at the same time. They denied the charge, while the informer offered nothing further. Since there was no manifest assurance of the facts, no supporting argument and no indication to serve as proof, Tiro was ordered to be tortured more violently. Then his son, pitying his father’s sufferings, promised to disclose everything if his father’s safety were granted him. When the king promised pardon, he declared that his father had prepared the king’s murder at Alexander’s instigation. Many thought this had been contrived for the occasion to save Tiro through such a disclosure by his child; others said it had been given as the truth. But Herod adjudged the doubtful as certain, as though afraid that the opportunity to murder his own children might escape him.Compare with Bellum [I.41.12] He therefore summoned the people and assembled the commanders, poured forth his complaint about the plots discovered with the gravest agitation, and roused the populace to kill them. There Tiro, his son and the barber were killed with stones and clubs.Compare with Bellum [I.42.1] Alexander and Aristobulus too were sent to the city of Sebaste, which was not far from the city of Caesarea, and strangled at the king’s command. Such was the end of Mariamne’s sons.Compare with Bellum [I.42.2] Antipater did not rejoice long in their death. With them removed, he flattered himself that his succession was beyond doubt; but the grave hatred of the whole nation soon blazed against him, since it was plain to everyone that his brothers had fallen through his intrigue. No small fear also followed as he considered how numerous the offspring of the slain grew day by day. Alexander had left his sons Tigranes and Alexander, born to him by Glaphyra; Aristobulus was survived by Herod, Agrippa and Aristobulus, born of Berenice, Salome’s daughter. Herodias too survived, and Mariamne’s daughters, whom their sex would not hinder and desire for the kingdom would stir. Terrified by these things, Antipater placed his hope in fraud and cunning and tried to bind each man to himself more and more with gifts and presents, even attempting to buy the favour of Caesar’s friends and household. But, on the contrary, even affairs at home turned against him. For, with the passage of time, the king gradually softened towards his grandchildren born to Alexander and Aristobulus and displayed remorse for his deed, pitying those whose parents he had killed.Compare with Bellum [I.42.3] Indeed, one day he gathered his friends and relatives and, his face bathed in tears, said to them: “I see my years advancing, and I cannot look without tears upon these little ones, the offspring of unhappy fathers, whose grief I have caused. Let me not leave them in a worse condition than that in which I took away their parents. Some affliction robbed me of their fathers, but nature and pity commend these children to me more and more: the one because they are my grandchildren, the other because they are bereft of their parents. My sons may have wronged their father: what have my grandchildren done to their grandfather? I have been an unhappy enough father; I ought to be a more attentive grandfather. I shall try to provide for my grandchildren after my death. If only I had also provided for myself in my sons! But the deceit of our common enemy and adversary may have crept upon them. We must take care that their perils do not involve these children too, and that I have not at one stroke both lost my sons and struck down my grandchildren. Let us provide defenders for those from whom we took them away. I shall therefore betroth your daughter, Pheroras, to the elder of Alexander’s sons, and appoint you as his father; and Aristobulus’s daughter to your son, Antipater, so that in this way you may become a father to the orphan girl. Her sister too shall marry my Herod, born to me by Mariamme, Hyrcanus’s daughter. This,” he said, “is my decision: that the successive generations of my posterity should be joined to one another by marriage, so that none may be suspect to another and I myself may look upon my grandchildren with more tranquil eyes than I looked upon their parents.”Compare with Bellum [I.42.4] With these words he joined the right hands of those mentioned and, kissing each, burst into tears. While the others rejoiced, Antipater took this so hard that he immediately betrayed his grief even in his face. No small anxiety gripped him as he saw that Alexander’s sons had stronger support than the others, backed as they were by King Archelaus and Pheroras, who held the tetrarchy. He perceived that hatred of himself was growing, while pity supported the grandchildren.Compare with Bellum [I.42.5] Nor could he receive Aristobulus’s daughter into his house, lest the continual sight of her, evidence of his crime, offend him. He did not dare approach his father, lest he provoke a man susceptible to every suspicion by suggesting that the bonds of the agreed marriages should be dissolved. Yet he subtly ventured to beg his father to look to his interests, so that he should not be exposed, powerless, with the bare name of kingship, against the resources of two powerful men, a king and a tetrarch. He should at least support the honour he thought fit to confer upon his son, so that the appearance of kingship should not pass to Antipater and its strength to them. Nor did he suspect only the sons of Alexander and Aristobulus: he thought everyone stood in his way who, born of Herod’s different wives, seemed even in silence to lay claim to the succession to the kingdom. They were numerous. For nine women enjoyed marriage to the king, of whom only two were childless; the others had offspring. Antipater raised up his mother Dosis, Herod his mother Mariamme. Antipas and Archelaus were the sons of Malthace, a Samaritan woman, and she also had a daughter, Olympias, who was joined to Josephus in lawful marriage. Cleopatra of Jerusalem too had borne Herod and Philip to Herod, and Pallas had borne Phasael. The king also had other daughters, Roxane and Salome, whose mothers were respectively Phaedra and Elpis. The full sisters of Alexander and Aristobulus, whom Mariamne had borne to Herod, also survived, as we mentioned above.Compare with Bellum [I.42.6] Fearing Herod’s numerous offspring, therefore, Antipater finally succeeded, though with difficulty, in having Aristobulus’s daughter joined to himself and his own son to the daughter of his paternal uncle Pheroras. At his first attempts the king had been greatly moved that he should begrudge the marriage alliances arranged for the grandchildren bereft of their father’s help. Such was his influence through flattery that he dissolved the agreed marriages.Compare with Bellum [I.42.7] Salome, by contrast, when she wished to marry Syllaeus, could not obtain this from her brother even with the support of Livia, Caesar’s wife, but was unwillingly married to a certain Alexander, one of the king’s friends.Compare with Bellum [I.42.8] With the king’s arrangements overturned, therefore, Antipater exulted in spirit as a man who had provided for himself as he wished, and surpassed everyone in cunning. Yet he could in no way suppress the hatred against him; instead he inflamed it, since he sought to secure protection for himself through terror.Compare with Bellum [I.42.9] He had attached his father’s brother Pheroras to himself as a fellow worker in his intrigues. Not long afterwards Herod expelled Pheroras from his house when he refused to be torn from his own wife, towards whom Herod was particularly hostile because of the injuries that woman had inflicted upon his wife Dosis. Pheroras, however, embraced the affront and withdrew to his own territory, over which he presided as tetrarch, firmly resolved never to return to Herod while Herod lived. Indeed, even when he learnt that Herod was afflicted by a grave illness and repeatedly begging him to come, since the king thought he had certain things to entrust to him as a dying man, Pheroras did not think him worth visiting. Although struck by this injury, when the king recovered from his illness against expectation, he nevertheless came to Pheroras with a brother’s affection on learning that he was ill. He shared his suffering attentively, and, when he died, conveyed him to Jerusalem and conducted his funeral with much weeping and splendid pomp. Yet these signs of attentive love did not dispel the opinion that he had attacked him with poison. Such was his cruelty even towards his own family. Nor was it difficult to believe that a man who had killed his sons could have killed his brother.Compare with Bellum [I.43.1] Thus one of the killers of Alexander and Aristobulus found this end to his wickedness. Beginning with him, punishment passed to Antipater, the author of the crime. For Herod was stirred by the complaints of the freedmen, who asserted that their patron had been killed with poison. In his more diligent inquiries he learnt that Pheroras had received from his wife a drink made from Arabian juices, thought to be a love potion, and that it had been poison, supplied through Syllaeus’s efforts and immediately turned to destruction. He therefore proceeded to interrogate very many people.Compare with Bellum [I.43.2] Hence one of the slave girls cried out under torture that almighty God should transfer every torment to Antipater’s mother, the director of all the crimes. Through her, Antipater and Pheroras had held secret meetings day and night and drunk to intoxication, so that on returning from the king’s banquet they drank the whole night through.Compare with Bellum [I.43.3] It was rightly suspected that this was neither idle nor free from an attempt at conspiracy, especially since the slaves and servants had been sent away. Such prolonged gatherings were a great bond of association and an indication of conspiracy, all the more suspicious to kings in the secrecy of solitude and silence of night. There it had been arranged that Antipater should go to Rome and Pheroras to Perea. They were revealed to have been accustomed to discuss this frequently with one another, because after Alexander and Aristobulus Herod would turn to killing them. Wretched men that they were to have thought Herod hated his sons’ designs against their father: he was pursuing heirs to the kingdom. Those removed were not rivals for power but partners in misery; all the danger and hatred had passed to themselves. He would not spare even women’s sex, since he had not spared his beloved Mariamne or the children born of her. They had no remedy except to withdraw somewhere further away, so as to escape the fury of so great a beast at least by flight. Frequent complaints by Antipater to his mother were added: he lamented that he burned under the odium of the royal succession, since the savagery of kingship had fallen chiefly upon himself, so that he could no longer endure it. Devoted to the most abject services, he was pressed by the utmost dangers. Not only had the right to reign been lost to him, but the course of the years of his life had also run out. He was of more mature age, his head already grey, while his father grew young again. It was vain to hope for the inheritance of a man who might perhaps be preserved long enough even to outlive him. What advantage would the succession bring him as an aged heir, when the numerous offspring of Alexander and Aristobulus sprang up before him like a hydra whose severed heads grew again? His father’s will had deprived him even of the common right: given the appearance of kingship, which he would hold temporarily as a deputy, he could appoint none of his sons to succeed to his rule but would be obliged to hand the kingdom over to Herod, Mariamme’s son. Thus he had been given the appearance of kingship to endanger him, not to benefit him, making him suspect to his predecessor and burdensome to his successor. Finally, the king himself, vigorous in his prolonged old age and intent upon slaughtering his own family, was the executor of his own will, so that no one should survive who could succeed. He was borne by grave hatred against his sons and no less against his brother: he had given Antipater a hundred talents not to speak with his uncle. Pheroras had replied: “For in what have we injured him? Am I too a successor?” Antipater was said to have answered that Herod had no grounds for offence but fabricated them himself. He was a savage beast, not sated even by deaths, who could not endure any love remaining between relatives. “If only, with everything lost, we could escape him stripped of everything but our lives! But that is impossible.” Therefore they needed secret conversations for the present. A time would come when they would employ manly vigour of mind and alertness of judgement, and the service of an avenging right hand.Compare with Bellum [I.43.4] These answers were given by slaves under torture, and Herod believed them, especially because he had spoken of the hundred talents to Antipater alone and no intermediary had been present at their conversation. Ablaze with indignation, he therefore dragged very many, including the innocent, to torture, lest any of the guilty be left behind.Compare with Bellum [I.43.5] Antipater the Samaritan was summoned for torture because he was Antipater’s procurator, and was tormented in various ways. The interrogation revealed that poison had been sent from Egypt through a certain Antiphilus, a companion, and that he had given it to Antipater’s friend Theudion, through whom it was delivered to Pheroras. The king’s son Antipater had entrusted Pheroras with carrying out the deed: while he himself was in the city of Rome, his father Herod was to be killed, so that at that time no suspicion of the murder would fall upon the absent man. But Pheroras had entrusted the poison he received to his own wife for the time being. A second accusation of poisoning thus returned against Pheroras’s wife. The king immediately ordered her to come and bring the poison. The woman went out as though to bring what was requested, and threw herself from the top of the buildings to escape the burden of the double charge and forestall disclosure of the matter and the bitterness of interrogation by her death. But since deadly vengeance for the intended murder of his father was being hastened for Antipater, she did not fall on the crown of her head, which would readily have killed her, but landed on another part of her body, so that death was postponed. Nevertheless, the woman was unconscious and stunned, since she had fallen from a high place. Herod ordered that she be given a little time to recover until she came to herself, and promised pardon if she would disclose the sequence of events plainly. It was not for nothing that she had thrown herself down: conscious of a great crime, she had sought a shorter way through punishment. If she confessed, all her crimes would go unpunished; if she denied them, torments would be heaped upon her and even burial denied.Compare with Bellum [I.43.6] When she had recovered a little, she said: “For whose sake should I still keep silent about these secrets, now that Pheroras is dead? To him I owed faithfulness in keeping silent, and for his sake I would not have refused torments had they been necessary. But he is now free from torture, and, if correction of an error may win pardon, free from guilt. What, then, compels me to wrap truth in lies? Or should I do so to comply with Antipater’s wishes? Am I to spare him and not myself? A fine reward indeed we owe the man who has brought us all to these torments through his crimes! Hear me, king, with God presiding, who alone is the judge of my truthfulness, for I have resolved to conceal nothing. Hear me, I say, but first recall how you sat weeping beside your brother in his peril and fulfilled every duty of devoted brotherhood towards Pheroras. Moved by these things, as soon as you departed he called me back to him and said: ‘Woman, I have strayed no little distance from affection and concern for my brother. I hated one who loved me so, and wished to kill one so unable to bear grief at my peril. He cannot bear a death that comes by chance, though I was pressing an undeserved death upon him. I was deceived, I confess, by Antipater’s cunning, but I shall pay the price of his design. Quickly bring the poison you have, which he left for me, and pour it out before my eyes, so that at least I may not carry a murderous intention against my kin to the underworld. Let repentance be a correction of what it was criminal to prepare. Quickly, I say, woman, so that I may at least forestall death, since I could not forestall guilt.’ Then I brought the poison and emptied it before him. Yet I kept a little of it for myself, since I feared you, so that, if it were disclosed, there would be a remedy: poison prepared for that use.”Compare with Bellum [I.43.7] With these words she produced the box containing the poison that remained. Antiphilus’s mother and his brother were subjected to interrogation. They confessed that Antiphilus had brought the box full of poison from Egypt, having received it from his brother, who was living in Alexandria as a physician. Mariamme too was discovered to have known of the plots being prepared against her husband, and this was made plain by her brothers’ confessions under torture. Hence the younger Herod paid the price of his mother’s audacity: his father, who had appointed him to follow Antipater in the succession to the kingdom, thought he should be erased from the will. This was indeed no small error on the elder Herod’s part, to punish one person for another’s discovered crime; yet the younger Herod’s punishment was not unjust either. For it seems that divine foresight provided for his exclusion from kingship, not yet as deserved by his deed but as the price of his future wickedness. For who could have endured him as king, when as tetrarch he was so insolent as to be intolerable?Compare with Bellum [I.43.8] Another kind of poison was also added, which Antipater’s freedman Bathyllus brought to Pheroras and his wife, compounded from the juices of serpents and the venom of asps, so that if the first had not proved strong enough to kill Herod, they could use the second.Compare with Bellum [I.44.1] Letters fabricated against his brothers Archelaus and Philip were also found. These were sons of the king being educated in Rome. Antipater assailed them especially because he saw that they possessed no small wisdom and that the king’s fatherly affection inclined towards them; indeed, he had summoned them by letter to return home sooner. Antipater therefore thought that they stood in the way of his interests and pressed upon his devices, so that the hope placed in the young men would overshadow all the feigned efforts of his intrigue. He therefore composed letters in the names of powerful men whom he had drawn into his friendship while in Rome, and also paid others to write that the young men were assailing their father with hostile hatred and lamenting the deaths of Alexander and Aristobulus with excessive complaint.Compare with Bellum [I.44.2] As he secretly put letters of this kind before his father through the courtiers who served his crime, he used the same cunning as before to pretend to plead for his brothers, so as to weave the impious murder of his kin beneath the pretended protection of family devotion. When all these things were brought forward, the interrogations revealed most clearly that his father’s life had been assailed, and the letters that his brothers’ deaths had been sought. It was therefore decided to exact punishment from the author, whose later false accusation had betrayed that he pursued his brothers as rivals for the lawful succession, not as would-be murderers of their father: he was not defending his father but preventing anyone from sharing his kingdom. Meanwhile, although seven months elapsed between the evidence of his crimes and Antipater’s return, no indication of events became known to him, so fiercely did everyone’s hatred burn against him. Thus, knowing nothing of it all, he wrote from the city of Rome that he would soon be there and had been dismissed by Caesar with the highest honour.Compare with Bellum [I.44.3] Herod replied to this letter that he ought to hasten back, assured of his father’s affection. Not only had it diminished in no way through his absence, but so much favour had been added that for his sake his mother’s offence would be lessened. For, after discovering her complicity in her son’s devices, he had again expelled her from his house, stripped of the gains of royal generosity. He wrote as though he would relent in his indignation towards her, fearing that Antipater, on learning of his mother’s expulsion, would grow suspicious and take precautions. On reaching Tarentum, Antipater first learnt of Pheroras’s death and there mourned greatly. Some attributed this to family devotion, thinking he could not bear the grief of his uncle’s death. But he was groaning at the loss of the agent of his attempted murder of his father. Not only had the preparation of the crime failed; the poison had also remained, and this terrified him, lest it somehow come to the king’s knowledge and Herod expose the scene of the crime. He therefore crossed to the harbour of Caesarea, by no means free from graver care and anxiety, since his mother’s expulsion gave no small prejudgement against her condemned offspring. But his friends urged him on, thinking that whatever served Antipater’s interests should take second place to their longing for their homeland. Having also observed his disposition, by which he had been accustomed readily to sway his father through his counsels even when estranged from favour towards him, they urged him to present himself all the sooner to his father and the kingdom destined for him. No one would dare oppose him when he was present; only the opportunity of his absence had smiled upon them, so that they thought the king’s mind could be turned away from him. He should therefore forestall this quickly, lest by delaying he either offend a father who longed for him or further embitter a suspicious one by betraying his own lack of confidence. Thus he believed those who advised what he wanted rather than what he needed.Compare with Bellum [I.44.4] But when he entered the harbour and looked about without seeing anyone coming to meet him, he sensed that his presence was being shunned like a plague: amid the greatest throng there was the greatest solitude. No one dared meet him, some through fear, others through aversion, for by then hatred too had gained the authority to cease concealing itself. He began to reckon his crimes within himself and to be troubled by the goads of conscience. No place of flight or means of escape remained to him; surrounded as though by nets, he was held captive. He drew all his confidence from shamelessness, concealing everything so as to present himself unexpectedly to his father, rush into his embrace and discharge the duties of family devotion.Compare with Bellum [I.44.5] But his father stretched out his hands to push him away as he pressed forward and turned his head aside lest he be touched by the kiss of a would-be murderer of his father. He exclaimed that this too belonged to the madness of such a man: “To seek an embrace when you know yourself to be hated, to fill your father with horror of you and wrench away the sweetness of life by contact with your guilty body! Do not therefore touch or taint the man you have criminally assailed. First at least clear yourself, if you can; refute what has been discovered. I shall not shun a trial or allow you to be denied a hearing, nor shall I take upon myself the examination of your case, lest I leave you an opportunity for argument. Varus is conveniently here: prepare your defence before him. There is no room for delay. Tomorrow, though endowed with cunning and fraud, you have the opportunity to clear yourself.” Stupefied by fear of so great an outburst, Antipater dared answer nothing, nor could he. He went outside and wavered in spirit, since he had learnt nothing at all of what had happened and been disclosed before the king. His mother and wife later came to him and revealed everything. On learning it, he began to collect himself and prepare in his mind the means by which he would meet the accusation and lessen the offences.Compare with Bellum [I.44.6] The next day all the relatives assembled, and Antipater’s friends were present at the examination. Everyone who had made various disclosures about Antipater was ordered to be brought in. Letters from his mother were also read, in which she had written to her son to let him know that the scene of their crimes had been betrayed to his father. He should by no means come unless some force were summoned from Caesar to surround him with its protection. Assailed by the confessions of so many, he should not entrust himself to judgement but secure himself with arms. With these things added to the earlier evidence, Antipater entered, threw himself at his father’s feet and begged him not to regard him as condemned in advance. He was confident that, if granted a hearing, he would be free of the charge, if his father wished it.Compare with Bellum [I.44.7] His father ordered him to be silent and spoke before him in this manner: “I am certain enough that Antipater’s wickedness can seem pardonable to no just man, but I think I am all the more burdened before you, Varus. For I fear that you may hate me too for having fathered sons who would murder their father, whom not even their father could spare, although in this too I deserve pity rather, because I loved them even as they were. But I shall say nothing of those whom I myself exasperated and whose just allegations against this man I rejected. For they had no grounds for grief against me except that Antipater was preferred to them and received the privilege of sharing kingship, although he had not been born into it. I thought, however, that I was taking an elder son to protect the younger ones, but I brought in an enemy who would envy the nobler, provoke the young, deceive the weak and betray the unwary. I do not deny that they fell, but they should have been excused rather than pressed. Antipater took them from me too; this man compelled them too to plot against me. I grieved, I confess, that those to whom I had given the hope of kingship and reserved the succession devised wicked things against me. But in me they hated Antipater, not their father. Thus they died to their father’s grief and Antipater’s profit. Do you ask, Varus, who killed them? Learn whom their death benefited. The house was emptied for a stepmother’s son; the palace, which had had many successors, lay open for one man to succeed. Nor were his bloodstained spirit and impious mind satisfied by his brothers’ deaths. When he no longer had brothers to hate, he pursued his father. I reflect within myself: I, who had secured his inheritance, seemed myself to live too long to a man disgusted with his predecessor. I taught him what to want. Having removed his rivals for the succession, I was not tolerated when I delayed him. He would not wait for the kingdom but must obtain it by his father’s murder. He repaid me for taking him in when he had been cast out and preferring him to men of nobler birth. For upon which of them did I confer as much as upon him? While still alive, I yielded power to him and openly designated him heir in my will, something usually ruinous to kings: that someone should know he will succeed. I granted him fifty talents in revenues, gave him three hundred when he left for Rome, commended him to Caesar as though my only son, and kept nothing for myself for which I should fear a son who would murder his father. But this armed him all the more for his father’s murder, that he saw himself superior. What crime so great had his brothers committed, whom he drove to death? What evidence of this kind was discovered against them, comparable to what is found against him? Yet the would-be murderer of his father dares interrupt and clamour, and tries to wrap the truth in cunning. Beware, Varus, I warn you, beware his feigned tears and groans artfully contrived, wrung from no grief. This is the man who robbed me of the affection of family devotion, warning me in fabricated fear to guard against Alexander. He asserted that very many minds agreed with Alexander’s and that I should not rashly entrust my presence to everyone. He pretended to look about at everything, to escort me to bed, to investigate and examine each man. This was the dispenser of my sleep, the minister of my security, in whom I placed my consolation and through whose services I lightened my grief for the slain. I thought he would restore them to me too, remove my sorrow and hold family devotion before me. This was my protector, to whom I entrusted the guarding of my aged body. I do not know how I am alive, how I escaped so great a conspirator, with what allurements he deceived me, with what frauds he held me bound, so that I trusted myself to the one man against whom alone I should have guarded. It is incredible to me that I escaped. I do not seem to myself to be alive; I think it a dream. For who would believe either that he could become so ungrateful, when I had entrusted him with every power over me, or that I could escape if Antipater were unwilling? Yet I thought favour had made me safer. But what accursed misfortune is mine, that it makes those I have loved more rise against me! I lament the affliction of my house, Varus, I weep for its solitude, I groan at the force of so great a grief. Yet such is the bitterness of the crime of murdering a father that I shall allow no one to escape me who has thirsted for my blood, even if evidence of intended murder of their father is brought forth against all my sons.”Compare with Bellum [I.44.8] As he said these things, indignation and grief together cut off his voice. Antipater immediately raised his head, for he lay at his father’s feet as though struck and pierced by a grave wound. Not thinking to rise, he said: “You indeed accuse me in anger, father, but I have no greater defence than the testimony of your accusation: I have always guarded your safety. In your desire to accuse, therefore, you have supplied a defence for me. For how am I a would-be murderer of my father when you yourself acknowledge me as your protector? Or how am I circumspect and cunning if, as you allege, I devised my father’s murder, when it is the utmost folly to have contemplated what both is execrable among human beings and cannot go unpunished before God? At least my brothers’ example could have taught me that there would be no escape from so great a crime, since a crime of this kind finds no hiding place and evades no punishment: they too paid the penalty for such great ill will towards you. But some envy, as you say, may have impelled them to murder their father, because they saw me preferred to themselves. The nobility of their maternal line gave them the spirit to claim the kingdom as owed to them by succession from their mother and demand it back as though taken from them by you. What like this was there in me, who knew only to hope for the kingdom from you, seek your judgement and please you alone? What was there to impel me to dare anything against your life? Desire for the kingdom? But I was reigning. Suspicion of hatred? But I was loved. Grief at an injury? But I was preferred. If only fear of my preferment armed them to murder their father, I am acquitted, since those preferred know to hate the murder of a father, not to contemplate it. Unless perhaps some fear of you compelled me; yet, as your voice testifies for me, I knew only to fear for you. For what should I fear for myself, who was the minister of your security and dispenser of your rest? Or did lack of money and poverty compel me, as they commonly persuade the needy to brigandage? But you had given enough to abound not only for the present but for all time, and had sent me rich to Rome, so that the kings of kings declared that pre-eminence in rule lay with them, not pre-eminence in wealth. Indeed, I won for you that Fabatus, a director of Roman affairs and an intimate of Caesar. Though Syllaeus had courted him with immense sums to attack you, I changed him so that he became your defender and the betrayer of the man soliciting him. Through whom else, father, were those plotting against your life discovered? How then am I a would-be murderer of my father, who discovered your bodyguard Corinthus in hiding, removed him as he plotted and brought him from denial to confession? I could have avoided contemplating my father’s murder and yet enjoyed its fruits, had I kept silent. But even if I had the savagery of beasts and the fury of ferocious wild creatures, I could nevertheless have been tamed by such great benefits from you, so as to place no help except in the support of your safety. For everything you gave, I could at least repay you with love alone, protect you with my body and, if it were possible, enclose you within my inmost entrails. You had preferred me, less noble in maternal descent, to sons of nobler birth; you had also recalled my mother, an exile from the kingdom, into the kingdom, and now held me as a partner in your rule rather than a successor. Wretched man that I am, upon whom your generosity poured so many good things as to kindle envy! Most foolish man that I am, to have left you, father, if an opportunity was given to envy and power to conspirators! For, while I lingered long for your safety, I betrayed my own, and yet I have nothing to impute to myself. You ordered me to depart, father. For you I was abroad, father, lest Syllaeus deceive your old age, strip you of the kingdom while you lived and assail your safety before Caesar. Rome is my witness to family devotion; Caesar too, guardian of the world, censor of all and judge of my heart, was accustomed to call me a lover of my father. Bear witness, Caesar, to what I said of my father before you, before whom alone I could have harmed him. Bear witness for me, I say, you who had pronounced upon others and thought the murder of a father should be investigated, not disregarded. If only your presence would favour me! But you are absent and far away, and without you I am condemned by my father. Yet though absent, you are present in your letters. I offer your writings, which would-be murderers of their fathers usually fear; I carry your letter, which those who wish such murder not to remain hidden usually produce. Receive Caesar’s letter, father: let the man who recently avenged you instruct you himself. Receive Caesar’s writings, stronger than every argument. You recently used them for vengeance: use them now for safety. I bring these written characters as witnesses to my innocence. That right hand never deceived you; that right hand of Caesar placed the diadem upon you, it did not take it away. That mind of Caesar restored to you the kingdom you had cast aside. Caesar could have hated me first if he had found me like my brothers, but he examined me and pronounced me an interpreter of family devotion. Had I not been in Rome, Syllaeus would have won. To him I am condemned today; to him I, wretched man, pay the penalty. Remember, father, that I did not sail willingly. I already saw the pit of the conspirators being prepared for me, yet I preferred, father, that I should be endangered rather than you. Nor do I shudder at the danger to my life, but I grieve, father, to be endangered before you as though your enemy. Yet I am endangered if even Caesar’s testimonies are endangered before you: these, then, are the proofs I use in my defence. I do not appeal to Caesar as a man awaiting a hearing, but implore him as one already acquitted. If you think a trial must be held, here I am, father: I came to you after Caesar; I hastened to you from Caesar. If only I had never gone anywhere away from you! But you, father, unknowingly exposed me to dangers by ordering me to go. I am here, father, and I do not think the truth about your safety should be sought lightly from witnesses of lower standing. Let neither those who can fear torments nor those who can despise them prejudge the case. Scripture says, ‘Every human being is a liar.’ I offer the incorruptible testimonies of the elements. I come to you over seas and lands, never having suffered anything. Had I been guilty of attempting my father’s murder, I ought not to have escaped. Let heaven, which did not strike me with lightning, acquit me before you, father; the sea, which did not drown me; the earth, which did not swallow me. Through these I come to you safe, father, although even those who are not would-be murderers of their fathers often fail to escape them. The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram in its yawning chasm, yet they had not assailed the father who begot them. The earth suspended Absalom as he fled in the branches of its tree, lest he reach his father; had he reached him, he would have escaped. I have come to you and am still endangered. David avenged the son who would have murdered him because he could not save him. I do not ask to be avenged upon my enemies and false accusers by summoning them to torture. Let them escape the penalty for false accusation. I ask one thing, father: do not trust other people’s torments; inquire from me myself against myself. Hang up your accused: let the interrogation of truth proceed into my entrails, let the cords of interrogation descend into my body and its inner chambers, let the blood flow that is accustomed to cry out against the murder of a father, let fires be brought upon the guilty limbs. Why hesitate, father? If you spare me, you pronounce me innocent; if you refrain from torture, you acquit me of the crime. A man thought worthy of a simple death is no murderer of his father. Or if you spare me as your son and pity limbs begotten from yourself, those limbs are not yours that are instruments of cruelty.” Having said this, he ended his speech with much weeping and lamentable groaning, and with the greatest wailing moved Varus and everyone to pity. Herod alone was moved by no tears and himself refrained from weeping, implacable towards pardon, pressing for interrogation and seeking vengeance.Compare with Bellum [I.45.1] At the king’s command Nicolaus followed Antipater’s speech, to answer his cunning skilfully and draw those who had been moved back from pity by turning upon Antipater the odium of his brothers’ murder. He argued that, if anyone was moved by pity, they ought to pity those who had been killed by his fraud and demanded vengeance. If they acquitted one man, the whole royal house would be brought into danger: brothers, relatives by marriage, parents, the king himself, whose life he had not spared. Turning therefore to the cunning of orators, as though in a kind of peroration he summoned from the underworld the souls of the slain to fill the court benches with their pitiful complaint: they had died innocent, weighed down by suborned witnesses, fabricated letters and fraudulent words. Their father had been deceived into trusting a son whom he did not think capable of lying about his brothers. Now this man offered himself for torture, although he had not believed his brothers’ torments; he had weighed them down with chains and bound them so that they could not attend the hearing. Sentence had been passed against absent men; they had been killed far away, lest their father pity them. No one would therefore be left if this man escaped, trained to pour poison for the murder of kin into his own kin’s entrails and change men’s minds. He had even roused Pheroras, who had always loved his brother Herod so greatly, to kill him in a deadly murder of kin.Compare with Bellum [I.45.2] Nicolaus added very many other things to these to stir emotion. When he had finished his speech, Varus asked Antipater whether he wished to reply. He answered nothing except: “God is my witness that I have done no harm.” Then Varus ordered the poison to be brought forward and given to one of those already condemned to death. He drank it and died immediately. This was reported to Caesar, and Antipater was led away in chains at his father’s command.Compare with Bellum [I.45.3] Yet he was not free from plots. For at that very time he was trying by deceit to endanger Salome. Antipater had sent letters composed in Salome’s name, full of insults against the king, and had ordered them to be conveyed through Antiphilus’s slave to Acme, the slave girl of Julia, who was Caesar’s wife, so that Acme would forward the letters delivered to her to the king. The fraud nearly succeeded in destroying the woman, but a letter from Acme to Antipater was found that exposed the deceit.
