It was written in this manner: “As you wished, I have written to your father and sent those letters, and I do not doubt that the king will rise to endanger his sister.Compare with Bellum [I.45.4] You, having obtained the outcome you desired, repay the service.” When these letters were intercepted, the king was led to suspect that Alexander too had been assailed by letters fabricated by his brother with the same art, and, exasperated by excessive agitation, he contracted a grave illness. Seeing himself pressed by this danger, he named one of his sons, Antipas, as heir to his rule in his will, preferring him to his elder children Archelaus and Philip, since Antipater’s deceit and falsehoods had also made them suspect to their father. He bequeathed a thousand talents to Caesar, with gifts and presents added, and allotted five hundred to Caesar’s wife and children, freedmen and friends. Nor did he leave his sister Salome without a share in his gifts.Compare with Bellum [I.45.5] The illness grew worse and became more severe with the passage of time, while the disabilities of feeble old age aggravated it daily. For he bore a body weighed down by no fewer than seventy years and afflicted also by frequent grief of mind, wounded by so many murders of kin, which it was the utmost misery either to have discovered in his sons or to have inflicted. Yet the illness burned incurably because Antipater, still alive, was feared.Compare with Bellum [I.45.6] He also became more contemptible day by day: images of Caesar and likenesses of animals placed upon the temple contrary to the law were being torn down. The chief instigators were Judas and Matthias, teachers of the young, who told those conspiring with them that the time had come to avenge the wrong done by violation of the law. The sacrilegious man was paying the penalty: he thought that whatever power permitted was right, and, not bowed by religion but exalted by pride, had exercised his desire to do whatever he wished in the temple’s inner sanctuary as though it were a right. Although divine force was hastening vengeance, it nevertheless seemed noble that those consecrated to the temple should also demonstrate their freedom by defending the observances of their ancestral rite. No one ought to be deterred by fear of danger, since even to die for the ancestral law was a mark of immortality.Compare with Bellum [I.45.7] They were the first to attempt to tear down the golden eagle fixed above the top of the gate. They were seized and brought before the king, and when asked whom they wished to obey in attempting so great a deed, they answered: “The ancestral law.” When he asked again what they trusted in, that they appeared so cheerful when summoned to the danger of death, they replied that they trusted in the rewards of devotion and dedication, the recompense for which would be paid to those who sought death for the ancestral rite.Compare with Bellum [I.45.8] He could no longer bear the firmness of the reply. Raised above his illness by indignation, so that he overcame his weakness, he went out into the assembly of the people. There, bringing them before the people as guilty of sacrilege, he began to accuse them on the grounds that graver things were suspected from such deeds. Even if these were not proved, everyone nevertheless feared for himself and pleaded that the instigators who had been seized should pay with punishment and that proceedings should not be extended to the rest, lest the interrogation trouble more people, including those uninvolved and innocent. Thus entreated, he passed sentence upon those present, that they should be burnt alive.Compare with Bellum [I.45.9] His infirmity increased from this, and the force of a graver illness consumed his whole body with various sufferings. His fever was violent, his itching intolerable; there were continual pains in his inner entrails without any interruption, and he was tormented by colic in his middle. Dropsy weighed down his feet, his private parts swarmed with worms, and spasms of the whole body, heavy breathing and deadly gasps were signs to anyone that he was being made to pay the penalty for the unjust murder of his kin and the sacrilegious sentence. Yet he did not yield in spirit, and in his desire to live struggled against his sufferings. The hot waters of Callirrhoe, which he sought across the Jordan, had done him no good. At Lake Asphaltites, healing for very many, he lay ill without any improvement. There, while he was being soothed with copious oil, his body relaxed and lost its strength; he turned up his eyes in the manner of the dying, his voice failed and he lost consciousness. But, roused by the noise of those crying out, he recovered.Compare with Bellum [I.45.10] Wishing to return to his own lands, when he reached the region of the place called Jericho he devised a monstrous deed, driven by black bile and in a manner threatening death itself, so that peoples might be sent as funeral offerings to him. For he had already ordered the nobler men to be gathered from all Judaea, so that they should assemble from each village in one place. When his command was obeyed, he ordered them to be shut inside the hippodrome. He summoned Salome and her husband Alexas and entrusted to them a legacy of blood. He asserted that his death would bring joy to the peoples of the Jewish nation, and that he had therefore devised a way for his funeral commemoration to be celebrated most splendidly. He demanded of his family that, when he had breathed his last, they should immediately order all those confined there to be killed. Thus there would be no one in all Judaea or in any house for whom his death would be unmourned, since he would have left everyone an inheritance of mourning at home. As they bewailed the murder of their own kin, they would seem to be paying the king his funeral dues, and thus the joy of public wishes would be hindered by private griefs. Lest the wicked commands fail to be carried out, he ordered fifty drachmas to be given to each soldier, so that, with such a reward for crime set before them, the soldiers would not refuse the deadly service, offsetting the horror of carrying it out with the gain of the reward.Compare with Bellum [I.45.11] He was already almost yielding to the torments of so great an infirmity, but he awaited the replies brought by the deadly embassy. It reported that Acme had been put to death in response to Herod’s complaint, and that Antipater too had been convicted of attempting his father’s murder and condemned to death. Yet, if his father wished to grant him the opportunity to flee, expelled from his homeland and kingdom, Caesar would give the order, passing sentence upon the crime but leaving the decision to family devotion. Nature had removed the necessity of killing kin. For, briefly revived by the power granted him to act as he wished, while he considered the manner of death, he was racked by pains and had desired to forestall the day of his own death. He therefore asked for an apple and a sword together, to take some refreshment by cutting the fruit with it as he was accustomed to do. Raising himself a little and leaning upon his elbow, he lifted his right hand, wishing to strike himself. But Achiabus rushed up and prevented the blow. The whole house rang with mourning, so that outside it was thought that Herod had died. Antipater exulted at the sound of lamentation and asked the guards to release him from his chains. But the man in charge of that duty not only refused the request but also reported it to the king. Exclaiming that he was being mocked while still alive, Herod sent assassins to kill Antipater and ordered him to be buried in Hyrcania after his death. He changed his will again and appointed Archelaus, the elder of the brothers, king, leaving Antipas as tetrarch.Compare with Bellum [I.45.12] Thus he survived Antipater by five days and died, having held the kingdom for thirty-seven years from the time when the Romans ordered him to rule. From the time when he removed Antigonus, his rival for the kingdom, he spent thirty-four years in power. If only he had been as happy in life at home as in his public successes! For abroad prosperity favoured him so much that he was raised from private station to kingship and, after enjoying it for a great many years, died with his power intact, a difficult thing, leaving his children a succession to rule that he himself had not received from his own family. But within his house he was most unhappy and filled it with the bitter bloodshed and mourning of his own family. Yet he found no one to carry out his final cruelty. In this one act Salome effaced the disgrace of her earlier crimes: she released all those whom the king had ordered to be killed, saying that the king had afterwards repented of the deadly command, revoked his earlier instructions and ordered that they should all be sent home.Compare with Bellum [I.46.1] Then, after the soldiers and the rest of the people had assembled in the amphitheatre, the king’s death was announced. Ptolemy came forward, a man who had remained one of the king’s most faithful friends to the very end. Bearing the ring he had drawn from the dead man’s finger, he praised the king and urged the people to remain calm. He opened a letter in which the king appealed to the soldiers most faithful to him and exhorted them to show goodwill and favour to his successor. The tablets of the will were also opened and read: Philip was named heir to the region of Trachonitis and neighbouring places, Antipas tetrarch, and Archelaus king, on condition, however, that his ring should be conveyed to Caesar and that the judgement and confirmation of all his arrangements should be reserved to him. His will was to be valid only if Caesar approved it. He ordered the remaining provisions to be observed according to his earlier wills.Compare with Bellum [I.46.2] At once the soldiers acclaimed and applauded Archelaus. He was immediately surrounded by a ring of guards; they promised goodwill and pledged allegiance. After this the funeral was fittingly and magnificently arranged, with the whole display of royal wealth sent ahead and the splendour of a funeral procession. The bier was adorned entirely with gold and gems, its covering shone with purple dye, and the body was covered by a double purple robe fastened with a clasp glittering with precious stones. A diadem clung to his head with a golden crown above it, and a sceptre was in his right hand, so that one might think him alive. A band of Thracians went before him, and the Germans and Gauls, the royal guards, kept military order. Armed alike as though going out to war, they followed with sorrowful faces, as if grieving. The rest of the force went ahead in their usual equipment and accustomed dress, their commanders and centurions accompanying them. Fifty slaves and freedmen of the royal household also sprinkled spices, so that the whole road was fragrant with a sweet scent. The king’s sons and a very great crowd of relatives surrounded the bier. He was buried in Herodium, as he himself had commanded, two hundred stades from the place where his life had ended. Over so great a distance everyone escorted him with great ceremony, but not with equal affection from all. For fear had wrung out duty, not willing service; grief at least kept its judgement free within itself. Such was Herod’s end.Compare with Bellum
